# Irish data protection authority fines LinkedIn €310 million for GDPR breach

---

25 Oct 2024, 3:31 pm

[Share via email](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection# "Email")

[Share via linkedin](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3a%2f%2fwww.pinsentmasons.com%2fout-law%2fnews%2firish-data-protection-fines-linkedin-310-million%3Futm_source%3Dlinkedin.com%26utm_medium%3Dsocial%26utm_campaign%3DPM_share&title=Irish%20data%20protection%20authority%20fines%20LinkedIn%20%E2%82%AC310%20million%20for%20GDPR%20breach&summary=&source=Pinsent+Masons "LinkedIn")   [Share via x](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Irish%20data%20protection%20authority%20fines%20LinkedIn%20%E2%82%AC310%20million%20for%20GDPR%20breach&url=https%3a%2f%2fwww.pinsentmasons.com%2fout-law%2fnews%2firish-data-protection-fines-linkedin-310-million?utm_source=twitter%26utm_medium=social%26utm_campaign=PM_share "Share via X")   [Share via facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3a%2f%2fwww.pinsentmasons.com%2fout-law%2fnews%2firish-data-protection-fines-linkedin-310-million?utm_source=facebook.com%26utm_medium=social%26utm_campaign=PM_share&display=popup&ref=plugin&src=like "Facebook")   [Share via whatsapp](whatsapp://send?text=https%3a%2f%2fwww.pinsentmasons.com%2fout-law%2fnews%2firish-data-protection-fines-linkedin-310-million?utm_source=whatsapp%26utm_medium=social%26utm_campaign=PM_share "WhatsApp")   [Share via print](# "Print page")

[Follow Data, privacy & cyber](/account-settings?setting=subservicepagedataprivacycyber#fc392582-9c0e-4f28-9463-f2306c918459 "Save in your preference settings")

The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) has fined LinkedIn for breaching the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) when processing personal data of its registered users for marketing and analytic purposes.

The [decision](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/irish-data-protection-commission-fines-linkedin-ireland-eu310-million) followed an inquiry launched by the DPC after the French Data Protection Authority had submitted an initial complaint from a French non-profit organisation filed in August 2018. The DPC led the investigation in its role as the lead supervisory authority for LinkedIn, as LinkedIn’s EU business operations are headquartered in Ireland.

The inquiry examined LinkedIn’s processing of personal data for the purposes of behavioural analysis and targeted advertising of users who had created LinkedIn profiles. The personal data in question encompassed data provided directly to LinkedIn by its members and data obtained via its third-party partners relating to its members.

The decision concerns the lawfulness, fairness and transparency of the processing of this data. The DPC ordered LinkedIn to bring its processing into compliance with the GDPR and to pay an administrative fine of €310 million.

[Nicola Barden](/people/nicola-barden), a Dublin-based data protection law expert at Pinsent Masons, commented: “The decision focuses on basic data protection requirements that all controllers should comply with, and regulators tend to take a strict approach to this type of processing.”

The DPC found that LinkedIn did not validly rely on article 6.1 of the [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32016R0679) when processing the third party data of its members for the purpose of behavioural analysis and targeted advertising. Article 6.1 of the GDPR outlines the required legal basis for processing of personal data. The legal basis can be based on consent, contractual necessity or legitimate interests.

The DPC said that the consent obtained by LinkedIn from its users was “not freely given, sufficiently informed or specific, or unambiguous”. It also found that there was no contractual necessity for the processing of relevant data and that LinkedIn could also not rely on an overriding interest, as LinkedIn’s interests “were overridden by the interests and fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects.”

Accordingly, the DPC concluded that LinkedIn did not have a legal basis for processing data. Processing personal data without an appropriate legal basis is a violation of the data subjects’ fundamental right to data protection.

Additionally, the DPC found that LinkedIn had infringed the principle of fairness outlined in article 5(1)(a) of the GDPR. It stipulates that personal data may not be processed in a way that is detrimental, discriminatory, unexpected or misleading to the data subject.

“The decision puts other controllers on notice that if they are undertaking behavioural analysis or targeted advertising, they have to have a very clear lawful basis that meets the requirements under data protection legislation,” Barden said. “They also need to ensure that their lawful basis is set out in its public-facing privacy notice. Controllers relying on vague lawful bases and notices, will not meet the DPC’s expectations.”

“The GDPR compliance points that are the focus of the DPC’s findings also reflect the need for controllers to properly consider ‘data protection by design’ in respect of their data processing activities” said [Andreas Carney](/people/andreas-carney), a Dublin-based partner at Pinsent Masons. “The decision underlines the importance of reflecting on compliance requirements in the round and from the ground up.”

Before handing down the decision, the DPC had submitted a draft decision to the other GDPR enforcement authorities of the EU member states in July 2024, as required under article 60 of the GDPR. The other authorities did not object to the suggested fine and order.

The so-called ‘one stop shop’ mechanism under the GDPR is envisaged to allow businesses to deal with just one data protection authority (DPA) in relation to their EU operations, as opposed to DPAs across all EU member states.

The mechanism provides for one DPA to take a lead in investigating cross-border cases. However, it requires the lead authority to enter into dialogue with the other DPAs in the countries where data subjects have been impacted and makes provision for those other DPAs to input to the inquiries and to raise 'relevant and reasoned' objections against proposed decisions of the lead authority. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) has the power to issue binding decisions in cases where the lead authority and objecting authorities cannot reach a consensus.

The Irish DPC is often in charge of leading on data protection investigations in the tech business, as most large digital businesses have their EU headquarters in Ireland. However, decisions proposed by the DPC have often been [challenged by other national DPAs](/out-law/news/twitter-gdpr-dispute-resolved-by-edpb), usually for being too lenient.

“The DPC will likely be pleased that there were no objections to its draft decision from other supervisory authorities, after a run of criticism for its decisions in the last few years,” Barden said.

# EU privacy regulator fines LinkedIn 310 mln euro

By Reuters

October 25, 2024 9:05 AM UTC Updated October 25, 2024

A keyboard is placed in front of a displayed LinkedIn logo in this illustration taken February 21, 2023. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/illustration-shows-linkedin-logo/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjM6bmV3c21sX1JDMlVGWjlBNUg5MA%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

DUBLIN, Oct 24 (Reuters) - The lead European Union privacy regulator on Thursday said it had imposed a 310 million euro ($335 million) fine on Microsoft's [(MSFT.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/MSFT.O) professional networking platform LinkedIn over its targeted advertising practices.

The Irish Data Protection Commissioner (DPC) is the European Union's lead privacy regulator for most of the top U.S. internet firms due to the location of their EU operations in the country.

"The processing of personal data without an appropriate legal basis is a clear and serious violation of a data subjects’ fundamental right to data protection," DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle said in a statement.

Microsoft last year said it expected to take a charge of [about $425 million](https://www.reuters.com/technology/microsoft-flags-over-400-mln-charge-irish-privacy-violation-fine-linkedin-2023-06-01/) for a potential fine from the Irish regulator for its LinkedIn unit.

LinkedIn in a statement said: "While we believe we have been in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), we are working to ensure our ad practices meet this decision by the IDPC's deadline."

($1 = 0.9260 euros)

This webpage is the "Numbers and Figures" section of the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2026 (7th edition), with a cut-off date of 1 March 2026. It presents comprehensive statistics on GDPR fines imposed across Europe since 2018.

Key findings include:

Top 10 overall fines (all largely imposed by the Irish Data Protection Commission, which accounts for 9 of the top 10):
1. Meta Platforms Ireland Limited – EUR 1.2 billion (Ireland, 12.05.2023) – insufficient legal basis

4. Meta Platforms Ireland Limited – EUR 390 million (Ireland, 04.01.2023) – non-compliance with general data processing principles

Business sector insights: The highest average fines were levied in "Media, Telecoms and Broadcasting," "Employment," and "Transportation and Energy" sectors. The sectors with the highest number of fines are "Industry and Commerce" and "Media, Telecoms and Broadcasting." Few fines were issued in "Accommodation and Hospitality" and "Real Estate." The Spanish authority has issued over 80 fines against a particular Spanish telecommunications provider.

Country insights: Spain's Data Protection Authority has been the most active, issuing a total of 1,048 fines (+116 vs. the 2025 report). Italy, Romania, and Poland imposed between 106 and 490 published fines each, but together published fewer fines than Spain alone. The average fine in Spain is much lower than in most other countries. Differences in fine activity may be due to publication methods, staffing levels, or differing regulatory approaches (e.g., Sweden focuses more on consultation and reprimands before fines).

Types of violations: Fines are categorized into nine categories. The most frequent reason for fines was processing activities lacking a sufficient legal basis, followed by non-compliance with general data processing principles, insufficient technical and organisational measures, failures to fulfil data subject rights, and inadequate compliance with information obligations. Very few fines have been imposed for lack of cooperation with supervisory authorities or missing data protection officer appointments.

Outlook: GDPR enforcement is now part of daily work for European DPAs. Cooperation between authorities is well established, including enforcement against non-EU companies. --- SOURCE 2: Avoiding GDPR fines in 2025: Enforcement trends and tips ---
URL: https://www.scrut.io/hub/gdpr/gdpr-fines-penalties-us-eu-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Megha Thakkar (Technical Content Writer at Scrut Automation) serves as a comprehensive guide to GDPR fines and penalties in the US and EU, published on November 5, 2025. It covers the two-tiered GDPR fine structure, recent enforcement trends, how GDPR applies to US companies, US vs EU enforcement comparisons, common compliance failures, and practical strategies to avoid penalties.

**GDPR Enforcement Structure:** Each EU member state has an independent Data Protection Authority (DPA) that investigates, issues warnings, bans unlawful processing, and imposes fines. Violations follow a two-tiered system under Article 83:
- **Tier 1 (Article 83(4))**: Fines up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (whichever greater) for first-time or less severe infringements, including lack of parental consent for children's data, failure to implement data protection by design, not maintaining records, failing to report breaches within 72 hours, and not appointing a DPO.
- **Tier 2 (Article 83(5))**: Fines up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for serious/repeated violations, including unlawful processing, processing without valid legal basis, invalid consent, processing special category data, violating data subject rights, and unlawful cross-border transfers.

Under Article 82, data subjects can claim compensation for material and non-material damage (the ECJ confirmed no minimum threshold), opening the door for mass litigation. A €10,000 Article 82 claim was cited as an example.

**Recent Enforcement Statistics:** From May 2018 to August 2025, regulators issued over 2,800 GDPR fines totaling over €6.2 billion, with more than 60% (€3.8 billion) imposed since January 2023. Top enforcement countries by number of fines: Spain (107), Romania (61), Italy (41). Top by fine amounts: Ireland (€1.18 billion), Germany (€45.9 million), Italy (€32.4 million). The media/telecommunications/broadcasting sector is most exposed (4th consecutive year). Top five reasons for fines: insufficient security measures (86 fines), non-compliance with processing principles (74), insufficient legal basis (73), insufficient cooperation with authorities (25), and failure to fulfill data subject rights (18).

**Largest Recent Fines:** TikTok (€530M, Ireland, May 2025, insufficient legal basis), LinkedIn (€310M, Ireland, Oct 2024), Meta Platforms Ireland (€251M and €91M, Dec 2024 and Sep 2024, insufficient security measures), and Vodafone GmbH (€45M, Germany, 2025).

**GDPR Applicability to US Companies:** Article 3 states GDPR applies to any organization processing EU residents' data regardless of location. Eight of the 10 highest GDPR fines were imposed on US-based companies (Meta, Amazon, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Uber), totaling €3.9 billion (nearly 63% of all fines). Example: Clearview AI was fined €30.5 million by the Dutch DPA in 2024 and over €100 million total across seven fines since 2020. US companies must comply if they offer goods/services to EU/EEA residents or monitor their behavior.

**US vs EU Enforcement Comparison:** EU takes a proactive, rights-based approach treating privacy as a fundamental human right, with fines based on global turnover percentage (up to 4%). The US is reactive/complaint-based consumer protection, with fines per violation or per consumer. EU enforcers are national DPAs coordinated by EDPB; US enforcers are FTC and state AGs. The EDPB's Coordinated Enforcement Framework ran a 2024 sweep on "right to access" and a 2025 sweep on "right to erasure." The EU AI Act came into force August 1, 2024, with full applicability by August 2, 2027. In the US, CCPA (2018) inspired 19 other states to pass similar laws, creating a fragmented compliance landscape.

**Key Compliance Lessons:** Legal basis is paramount; security isn't optional; transparency equals trust; cooperate with authorities; compliance is continuous (not one-and-done).

**Common Compliance Failures:** Poor data security, ignoring legal basis and GDPR's seven principles, not fulfilling data subject rights, cross-border data transfers without safeguards (Meta's €1.2 billion 2023 fine cited), and failing to report breaches within 72 hours.

**Avoidance Checklist:** The article provides a 21-item checklist covering data mapping/auditing, valid legal basis for all processing, proper consent mechanisms, data minimization, privacy by design, DPIAs for high-risk processing, strong security measures, breach response plans with 72-hour notification, maintaining Records of Processing Activities (RoPA), appointing a DPO, third-party compliance, cross-border transfer mechanisms, employee training, continuous monitoring, and using compliance automation software.

**Automation Solution:** The article promotes Scrut's GDPR compliance platform (trusted by 1,500+ customers) with pre-built policy templates, pre-mapped controls, daily automated control monitoring, compliance gap analysis, automated evidence collection, vendor management, real-time dashboards, and GDPR expert access. Scrut positions automation as the fix for manual, error-prone compliance processes.
</summary>

**The 10 largest GDPR fines (2024-2025):**
1. TikTok — €530M (Irish DPC, May 2025) — Illegal transfer of EU user data to China
2. LinkedIn — €310M (Irish DPC, Oct 2024) — Unlawful behavioural profiling for targeted ads
3. Uber — €290M (Dutch AP, Aug 2024) — Transferring sensitive EU driver data to US without safeguards
4. Meta (breach) — €251M (Irish DPC, Dec 2024) — 2018 Facebook breach exposing 29M accounts

7. Enel Energia — €79.1M (Garante Italy, Feb 2024) — Telemarketing data misuse, unauthorized CRM access sharing
8. Amazon France — €32M (CNIL France, 2024) — Excessively intrusive employee monitoring
9. Clearview AI — €30.5M (Dutch AP, Sep 2024) — Illegal biometric database from 30B+ scraped images
10. Apotheka — €3M (Estonian DPA, 2025) — Health data breach affecting 750K+ people

1. The core problem is identifiable data, not weak firewalls — under GDPR, properly anonymized data is no longer personal data (Recital 26) and falls outside regulation scope entirely.
2. Cross-border transfers are the highest-risk scenario — three of the five largest fines (TikTok, LinkedIn, Uber) involved data transfers outside the EU; anonymizing before transfer eliminates the need for SCCs, adequacy decisions, or TIAs.

## GDPR Enforcement: Complete Guide for 2025

This webpage from CookieScript provides a comprehensive guide to GDPR enforcement, covering how the regulation is enforced, key regulatory bodies, enforcement evolution since 2018, common violations, penalties, fines, and business compliance responsibilities.

### Key Regulatory Bodies
- **Data Protection Authorities (DPAs):** National authorities in each EU member state that monitor compliance, investigate complaints, audit companies, and issue fines. Notable DPAs include France's CNIL, UK's ICO, Germany's BfDI, Spain's AEPD, and Italy's Garante.
- **European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS):** Supervises GDPR compliance within EU institutions and advises on new legislation.
- **European Data Protection Board (EDPB):** Coordinates enforcement across EU/EEA states, resolves disputes between DPAs, and ensures harmonized enforcement, especially in cross-border cases.

### GDPR Enforcement Process
Enforcement follows a four-step process: (1) complaint or DPA discovery, (2) audit of the organization's data handling, (3) decision with warnings, corrective orders, or fines, and (4) appeals (which rarely overturn fines). For cross-border cases, a lead supervisory authority handles enforcement, with the EDPB resolving disputes.

### Evolution of Enforcement Since 2018
- **2018:** Initial phase favored guidance over penalties with few small fines.
- **2019–2020:** First wave targeted Big Tech; France's CNIL issued the first major fine of €50 million to Google in 2019.
- **2021–2023:** Increased number and value of fines; heavy scrutiny of cross-border enforcement.
- **2024–2025:** Record-breaking fines, including the first billion-euro fine (€1.2 billion to Meta in May 2023 for unlawful data transfers to the US). Enforcement expanding beyond tech into finance, energy, and other sectors, with executives held personally accountable and growing attention to AI and cloud services.

### Penalties and Fines
- Minor violations: up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher).
- Serious violations: up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher).
- As of October 2025, total GDPR fines reached €6.7 billion.
- **Top fines:** Meta – €1.2B (2023); Amazon – €746M (2021); TikTok – €530M (2025, children's data); Meta – €405M (2022); Meta – €390M (2023).
- Spain has issued the most fines in the EU (1,021 fines totaling ~€120,750,450 as of September 2025), while Ireland has issued the largest fines (~€3.5 billion since May 2018) due to Big Tech headquarters.
- Small businesses and individuals can also be fined; e.g., Romanian DPA fined Dr. Max SRL €1,000 in September 2025.

### Most Common GDPR Violations
1. Lack of valid consent for data processing (most common)
2. Transparency issues (Article 5)
3. Inadequate security measures
4. Data breaches (72-hour notification requirement)
5. Improper international data transfers (Schrems II ruling invalidated EU-US Privacy Shield in 2020)
6. Failure to honor data subject rights
7. Poor cooperation with DPAs

### Most Targeted Industries
Tech & social media, finance, healthcare, and e-commerce & retail.

### Future Enforcement Trends (2025–2026)
Expected intensification in AI compliance (with the new EU AI Act), cross-border data transfers, enforcement against SMEs and startups, and real-time audits using new technologies.

### 10 Key Business Compliance Steps
1. Obtain lawful, explicit user consent (opt-in mechanisms)
2. Implement a clear and accessible Privacy Policy
3. Conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) when processing is high-risk
4. Keep a record of processing activities
5. Appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO) for large-scale processing
6. Implement data protection by design and default
7. Train employees on GDPR best practices
8. Respond to data subject requests within 30 days
9. Protect data against breaches (notify authorities within 72 hours)
10. Use a Consent Management Platform (CMP) like CookieScript

## EDPB Annual Report 2024 - Summary

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) published its 2024 Annual Report, titled "Protecting Personal Data in a Changing Landscape." The report covers the Board's activities throughout 2024, including its strategy, guidance, opinions, enforcement cooperation, and the work of its Secretariat.

### Key Highlights of 2024

**Strategy and Governance:**
- Adopted the new 2024-2027 Strategy in April 2024, structured around four pillars: (1) advancing harmonisation and promoting compliance, (2) reinforcing a common enforcement culture, (3) addressing technological challenges, and (4) enhancing the EDPB's global role
- Adopted the 2024-2025 Work Programme implementing the Strategy
- Zdravko Vukić (Croatia) elected as new EDPB Deputy Chair in June 2024
- Anu Talus served as Chair; Isabelle Vereecken as Head of Secretariat

**Consistency Opinions (28 total in 2024):**
- 20 opinions under Art. 64(1) GDPR (covering DPIA lists, codes of conduct, certification bodies, SCCs, BCRs, etc.) — bringing the total to 188 since 2018
- 8 opinions under Art. 64(2) GDPR on matters of general application, including:
  - **Opinion 04/2024** (Feb): Notion of "main establishment" of a controller — clarified that a place of central administration qualifies as main establishment only if it takes decisions on purposes/means of processing and has power to implement them; burden of proof falls on controllers
  - **Opinion 08/2024** (April): "Consent or Pay" models by large online platforms — concluded most current implementations are unlikely to meet GDPR's valid consent requirements; platforms should offer free alternatives without behavioural advertising, ensure transparency, and avoid excessive fees
  - **Opinion 11/2024** (May): Use of facial recognition at airports — only storage solutions with biometric data held by the individual or central storage with encryption key solely in the individual's hands were found compatible with data protection principles
  - **Opinion 22/2024** (Oct): Obligations regarding processors and sub-processors under Art. 28 GDPR — controllers must have identity information on all processors readily available; verification obligations apply regardless of risk level but extent varies by risk; controller retains ultimate decision on engaging sub-processors
  - **Opinion 28/2024** (Dec): Processing personal data to train AI models — confirmed legitimate interest can serve as legal basis under certain conditions, with a three-step test proposed; EDPB consulted the EU AI Office before adoption

**Statements on Legislative Developments (6 in 2024):**

**GDPR Enforcement Structure:** Each EU member state has an independent Data Protection Authority (DPA) that investigates, issues warnings, bans unlawful processing, and imposes fines. Violations follow a two-tiered system under Article 83:
- **Tier 1 (Article 83(4))**: Fines up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (whichever greater) for first-time or less severe infringements, including lack of parental consent for children's data, failure to implement data protection by design, not maintaining records, failing to report breaches within 72 hours, and not appointing a DPO.
- **Tier 2 (Article 83(5))**: Fines up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for serious/repeated violations, including unlawful processing, processing without valid legal basis, invalid consent, processing special category data, violating data subject rights, and unlawful cross-border transfers.

Under Article 82, data subjects can claim compensation for material and non-material damage (the ECJ confirmed no minimum threshold), opening the door for mass litigation. A €10,000 Article 82 claim was cited as an example.

**Recent Enforcement Statistics:** From May 2018 to August 2025, regulators issued over 2,800 GDPR fines totaling over €6.2 billion, with more than 60% (€3.8 billion) imposed since January 2023. Top enforcement countries by number of fines: Spain (107), Romania (61), Italy (41). Top by fine amounts: Ireland (€1.18 billion), Germany (€45.9 million), Italy (€32.4 million). The media/telecommunications/broadcasting sector is most exposed (4th consecutive year). Top five reasons for fines: insufficient security measures (86 fines), non-compliance with processing principles (74), insufficient legal basis (73), insufficient cooperation with authorities (25), and failure to fulfill data subject rights (18).

**Largest Recent Fines:** TikTok (€530M, Ireland, May 2025, insufficient legal basis), LinkedIn (€310M, Ireland, Oct 2024), Meta Platforms Ireland (€251M and €91M, Dec 2024 and Sep 2024, insufficient security measures), and Vodafone GmbH (€45M, Germany, 2025).

Example: Clearview AI was fined €30.5 million by the Dutch DPA in 2024 and over €100 million total across seven fines since 2020. US companies must comply if they offer goods/services to EU/EEA residents or monitor their behavior.

**US vs EU Enforcement Comparison:** EU takes a proactive, rights-based approach treating privacy as a fundamental human right, with fines based on global turnover percentage (up to 4%). The US is reactive/complaint-based consumer protection, with fines per violation or per consumer. EU enforcers are national DPAs coordinated by EDPB; US enforcers are FTC and state AGs. The EU AI Act came into force August 1, 2024, with full applicability by August 2, 2027. URL: https://gdpr-info.eu/issues/fines-penalties

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from gdpr-info.eu provides a comprehensive overview of fines and penalties under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). National authorities can or must assess fines for data protection violations, which are applied in addition to or instead of corrective powers such as orders to end violations, instructions to adjust data processing, and temporary or definitive limitations including bans on data processing. Processors may be subject to sanctions directly and/or in conjunction with the controller.

Fines must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive for each individual case. Authorities use a statutory catalogue of criteria when determining penalty levels, with aggravating factors including intentional infringement, failure to take mitigation measures for damage, and lack of collaboration with authorities. For especially severe violations under Art. 83(5) GDPR, fines can reach up to €20 million or, for an undertaking, up to 4% of total global turnover of the preceding fiscal year (whichever is higher). Less severe violations under Art. 83(4) GDPR carry fines of up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover (whichever is higher).

A key point is that the term "undertaking" is equivalent to its meaning under Art. 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). According to European Court of Justice case law, an undertaking encompasses every entity engaged in economic activity regardless of legal status or financing method. This means a whole corporate group can be treated as one undertaking, allowing total worldwide annual turnover to be used for calculating fines. Member States may also impose other penalties (often criminal) for violations not covered by Art. 83, which must also be effective, proportionate, and deterrent.

Violations can be revealed through proactive inspections by data protection authorities, employee or customer complaints, company self-denunciation, or press investigations. The page references the Enforcement Tracker for an overview of reported EU fines. It also links to relevant GDPR articles (Art. 58, 70, 83, 84), recitals (148-152), and external resources including the Article 29 Working Party's WP 253 guidelines on administrative fines, European Commission guidance, the Handbook on European data protection law, and expert analyses from JIPITEC, IAPP, and A&L Goodbody.
</summary>

<summary>
This is a legal news article published on the Fluxmans (a South African law firm) website on May 9, 2025, authored by Ryszard Lisinski and Brett Weinberg, discussing two major EU regulatory actions against tech companies over data privacy violations.

**TikTok Fined €530 Million:** Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined TikTok €530 million ($571 million) for illegally transferring European users' data to China — one of the largest penalties under the EU's GDPR. TikTok admitted in April 2025 that European user data was stored on Chinese servers, contradicting earlier statements to Irish regulators. The DPC found TikTok failed to verify that EEA user data remotely accessed by staff in China received protection essentially equivalent to EU standards, and that the company neglected to assess risks posed by Chinese national security laws. This publication from Simmons & Simmons (dated 24 April 2026) analyzes the Irish Data Protection Commission's (DPC) €530 million fine against TikTok for unlawful international data transfers to China, one of the most important post-Schrems II enforcement actions to date.

**Key Findings:**
- TikTok stored EEA user data on servers in Singapore, the US, and Malaysia, but allowed ByteDance personnel in China to access that data remotely for core functions (content delivery, security, R&D, analytics, payments, support, and content moderation), constituting a "transfer" to China.
- TikTok relied on SCCs plus supplementary measures and had prepared TRAs with a leading Chinese law firm. Its central legal argument was based on the territoriality principle in Chinese law — that Chinese authorities could not lawfully compel access to data only accessed remotely and not stored domestically.
- The DPC rejected this argument, finding that TikTok failed to adequately assess Chinese law and practices, failed to assess the level of protection afforded to EEA users' data, and failed to verify/guarantee essentially equivalent protection. The supplementary measures (including encryption and "Project Clover," TikTok's €12 billion data security initiative) were deemed general security measures that did not address the risk of Chinese authorities accessing data under problematic laws.
- TikTok could not rely on GDPR Article 49 derogations (contractual necessity, compelling legitimate interests) since those apply only to occasional/non-repetitive transfers, whereas TikTok's transfers were systematic, repetitive, and continuous.

**Fine Factors (Article 83(2) GDPR):** The DPC weighed the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement (systematic transfers over years affecting a very large number of EEA users, including sensitive data), the highly negligent character (despite TRAs being carried out), TikTok's high degree of responsibility given the scale of processing, and the categories of data involved (daily life, location, private communications, financial data, user-generated content potentially revealing special category data). **Key Takeaways for Organisations:**
1. TRAs must be substantively robust — merely preparing a TRA is insufficient; they must include detailed analysis of local law measured against the European Essential Guarantees and form a defensible basis for conclusions about essentially equivalent protection.
2. Supplementary measures must meaningfully address specific risks (such as government access under destination-country laws); general security measures alone are insufficient.
3. Article 83(2) factors provide a useful framework for organisations' own risk management — large-scale, long-term, core-service transfers involving sensitive data should receive enhanced scrutiny.

**Practical Steps:** Organisations should revisit TRAs for transfers to non-adequate countries, redesign supplementary measures to address government access risks (strong encryption with key separation, pseudonymisation, data minimisation), and adopt a risk-based approach. The article promotes CtrlTransfer, Simmons & Simmons' tool providing jurisdiction-specific analysis mapped against the European Essential Guarantees, TRA templates, and objective country risk scoring.

--- SOURCE 6: Into the Data Transfer Thicket: The Dutch Uber Decision and the Relationship Between GDPR Article 3 and Chapter V – European Law Blog ---
URL: https://europeanlawblog.eu/1xjmngct

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an opinion/analysis article from the European Law Blog (22 October 2024) by E J Kyriakides examining the Dutch DPA's enforcement decision against Uber and the legal relationship between GDPR Article 3 (territorial scope) and Chapter V (data transfer safeguards).

KEY ISSUE: The article addresses a lingering legal ambiguity: under what circumstances are GDPR data transfer safeguards required when a foreign firm is already subject to the GDPR. The classic transfer scenario involves a foreign company NOT governed by GDPR receiving EU data. But GDPR has extraterritorial effect (Article 3(2)), meaning foreign companies targeting the EU can also be subject to it.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:
- Article 3(1): Entities with an EU "establishment" are subject to GDPR
- Article 3(2): Entities without EU establishment are subject if they (a) offer goods/services to EU data subjects, or (b) monitor EU data subject behavior
- Chapter V (Articles 44-47) requires transfer safeguards including adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses (SCCs), binding corporate rules, etc.
- Under Schrems II, firms must independently assess whether transfer tools ensure "essentially equivalent" protection, potentially requiring supplementary measures
- Chapter V applies only to a "transfer" — a term the GDPR does not define

EDPB GUIDELINES (05/2021):
- Defined "transfer" as occurring when: (1) a controller/processor (exporter) is subject to GDPR; (2) the exporter discloses personal data to another controller/processor (importer); (3) the importer is in a third country (regardless of whether importer is subject to GDPR)
- Critically concluded NO transfer occurs when data is directly disclosed by an individual in the EU to a firm in a third country
- Companies subject to GDPR must still assess third country government access risks under other GDPR obligations (Articles 32, 33, 35)
- Not binding but highly authoritative

THE DUTCH DPA UBER DECISION (August 2024):
- Dutch DPA fined Uber €290 million — the largest fine ever from the Dutch DPA — for transferring French Uber drivers' data to the US without Chapter V safeguards
- Fine originated from an NGO (Ligue Des Droits De L'homme) complaint to the French CNIL
- Transfer involved Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) and Uber Technologies Inc (UTI, US parent)
- Uber relied on SCCs until August 2021, then determined SCCs were unnecessary because Article 3 directly applied to UTI's US processing; Uber had NO transfer mechanism from August 2021 until relying on the Data Privacy Framework in November 2023
- Two scenarios found to involve transfers: (1) EU drivers' data sent directly via Uber app to UTI for US storage; (2) data relating to GDPR rights requests where UBV and UTI collaborated
- Dutch DPA rejected Uber's defenses (direct collection, joint controllership, Article 49 derogations), holding transfers between joint controllers subject to GDPR in different countries are governed by Chapter V
- DPA departed from EDPB guidance by finding scenario one (direct collection from EU data subjects) constituted a "transfer," relying on the employment relationship between UBV and drivers and the asymmetry of power
- DPA argued Chapter V should be read broadly to counterbalance risks of diminished protection when data is processed abroad and difficulty enforcing against foreign entities
- DPA found Article 49(b-c) derogations inapplicable because transfers were ongoing, not "incidental" or "necessary"

ANALYSIS/NEXT STEPS:
- Uber is appealing; Dutch courts are likely to refer questions to the CJEU on the Article 3/Chapter V relationship
- The Dutch decision failed to articulate a clear legal standard for when direct collection by foreign providers subject to GDPR triggers Chapter V
- The article recommends that EU entities subject to GDPR under Article 3(2) in doubt apply Chapter V safeguards until the issue is settled
- European Commission has not yet issued SCCs for scenarios where the importer is subject to GDPR (current SCCs only apply when importer is NOT subject to GDPR)
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This GDPRhub page documents the Dutch Data Protection Authority's (AP - Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens) decision to fine Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI) and Uber B.V. (UBV) €290,000,000 for violating Article 44 GDPR. The decision was issued on 22 July 2024 and published on 25 August 2024.

**Key Facts:**
- Uber B.V. (UBV), based in the Netherlands, is part of the Uber group and serves as the EEA representative. Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI), based in San Francisco, US, is the parent company and joint controller for Uber drivers' personal data.
- Uber used a centralized IT infrastructure with servers located in the US. EEA-based drivers' personal data was processed in the US in two situations: (1) data collected through the driver app and stored on US-based servers (including account, location, criminal and health data, identity documents, and taxi licenses), and (2) when drivers exercised their GDPR rights, UTI was responsible for making data available to UBV.
- Uber previously used the European Commission's Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) but removed them from their joint controllership agreement effective 6 August 2021, arguing SCCs could not be used when processing falls directly under GDPR scope.
- The complaint originated from the French human rights group Ligue des droits de l'Homme on behalf of 172 Uber drivers, filed with CNIL (French DPA) on 12 June 2020, and forwarded to the Dutch AP due to Uber's main establishment in the Netherlands.

**Key Holdings:**
1. **Article 3 GDPR and Chapter V can apply simultaneously**: The DPA rejected Uber's argument that the territorial scope (Article 3 GDPR) and Chapter V (international transfers) were mutually exclusive. Chapter V is complementary to Article 3, preventing circumvention of EU data protection law. The DPA also rejected the WTO agreement argument.
2. **The processing constituted a transfer**: Applying the EDPB Guidelines 05/2021's three cumulative criteria, the DPA found all criteria met. The DPA rejected Uber's argument that drivers themselves were the exporters, finding instead that UBV was the exporter because drivers have little influence over processing purposes and means (terms are pre-drafted and non-negotiable).
3. **No valid transfer mechanism**: From 6 August 2021 to 27 November 2023, Uber had no lawful transfer mechanism. The DPA rejected Uber's interpretation of the European Commission's FAQ statements regarding SCCs.
4. **Article 49 GDPR exceptions did not apply**: The transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing (not incidental per Recital 111). The transfers were not "necessary" for contract performance per C-252/21 (Meta Platforms), as there were practicable, less intrusive alternatives (e.g., processing on EU servers).

**Fine details:** The DPA imposed a €290,000,000 administrative fine on the joint controllers due to the seriousness of the violation. This is the third fine the Dutch DPA has issued against Uber: €600,000 in 2018 for a data breach notification violation, €10 million in 2023 for a nontransparent privacy policy (which Uber has appealed), and this €290 million fine.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from CookieScript provides a comprehensive guide to GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) enforcement for 2025. It explains who enforces the GDPR, how enforcement works, how it has evolved since 2018, key regulators, penalties for non-compliance, and what businesses must do to remain compliant.

**GDPR Enforcement Overview:** GDPR enforcement is carried out by national Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) in each EU member state, along with the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) for EU institutions and the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) for cross-border coordination. Enforcement involves investigating complaints, auditing companies, issuing warnings, and imposing fines. For cross-border cases, a lead supervisory authority handles enforcement, with EDPB resolving disputes.

**Evolution of Enforcement (2018–2025):** Initially (2018), regulators focused on guidance over penalties. From 2019–2020, enforcement targeted Big Tech and social media, with France's CNIL issuing the first major fine (€50 million to Google in 2019). From 2021–2023, the number and value of fines increased with heavy scrutiny on cross-border enforcement. From 2024–2025, enforcement intensified with record-breaking fines, the first €1.2 billion fine (Meta in May 2023), expansion beyond tech into finance and energy, personal accountability for executives, and growing attention on AI and cloud services.

**Key Regulators:** National DPAs (e.g., France's CNIL, UK's ICO, Germany's BfDI, Spain's AEPD, Italy's Garante), the EDPS, and the EDPB. Supervisory Authorities have powers to investigate complaints, conduct audits, issue fines and corrections, and monitor international data transfers.

**Variations Across Member States:** Enforcement differs across EU countries due to decentralized DPAs with different resources and priorities. Spain has issued the most GDPR fines (1,021 fines totaling ~€120,750,450 as of September 2025), while Ireland has issued the largest fines (~€3.5 billion since May 2018) due to Big Tech headquarters locations. As of October 2025, total GDPR fines reached €6.7 billion.

**Penalties:** Minor violations: up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover. Serious violations: up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover. Top fines include Meta (€1.2B, 2023), Amazon (€746M, 2021), TikTok (€530M, 2025), Meta (€405M, 2022), and Meta (€390M, 2023).

**Common Violations:** Lack of valid consent, transparency issues, inadequate security, data breaches (72-hour notification requirement), improper international data transfers (Schrems II invalidated EU-US Privacy Shield in 2020), failure to honor data subject rights, and poor DPA cooperation. Most targeted industries: tech & social media, finance, healthcare, and e-commerce & retail.

**Future Trends:** Intensified enforcement expected in AI (with EU AI Act), cross-border data transfers, SMEs/startups, and real-time proactive audits.

**Business Compliance Responsibilities (10 steps):** Obtain lawful consent, implement a clear Privacy Policy, conduct DPIAs, keep records of processing activities, appoint a DPO, implement data protection by design and default, train employees, respond to data subject requests within 30 days, protect against data breaches (72-hour notification), and use a Consent Management Platform (CMP). The article promotes CookieScript's CMP as a solution with features including cookie banners, cookie scanning, consent recordings, Google Consent Mode v2 integration, and IAB TCF v2.2 integration. The GDPR Enforcement Tracker (maintained by CMS law firm) is recommended for tracking fines.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Avoiding GDPR fines in 2025: Enforcement trends and tips ---
URL: https://www.scrut.io/hub/gdpr/gdpr-fines-penalties-us-eu-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Megha Thakkar (Technical Content Writer at Scrut Automation) serves as a comprehensive guide to GDPR fines and penalties in the US and EU, published on November 5, 2025. It covers the two-tiered GDPR fine structure, recent enforcement trends, how GDPR applies to US companies, US vs EU enforcement comparisons, common compliance failures, and practical strategies to avoid penalties.

**GDPR Enforcement Structure:** Each EU member state has an independent Data Protection Authority (DPA) that investigates, issues warnings, bans unlawful processing, and imposes fines. Violations follow a two-tiered system under Article 83:
- **Tier 1 (Article 83(4))**: Fines up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (whichever greater) for first-time or less severe infringements, including lack of parental consent for children's data, failure to implement data protection by design, not maintaining records, failing to report breaches within 72 hours, and not appointing a DPO.
- **Tier 2 (Article 83(5))**: Fines up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for serious/repeated violations, including unlawful processing, processing without valid legal basis, invalid consent, processing special category data, violating data subject rights, and unlawful cross-border transfers.

Under Article 82, data subjects can claim compensation for material and non-material damage (the ECJ confirmed no minimum threshold), opening the door for mass litigation. A €10,000 Article 82 claim was cited as an example.

**Recent Enforcement Statistics:** From May 2018 to August 2025, regulators issued over 2,800 GDPR fines totaling over €6.2 billion, with more than 60% (€3.8 billion) imposed since January 2023. Top enforcement countries by number of fines: Spain (107), Romania (61), Italy (41). Top by fine amounts: Ireland (€1.18 billion), Germany (€45.9 million), Italy (€32.4 million). The media/telecommunications/broadcasting sector is most exposed (4th consecutive year). Top five reasons for fines: insufficient security measures (86 fines), non-compliance with processing principles (74), insufficient legal basis (73), insufficient cooperation with authorities (25), and failure to fulfill data subject rights (18).

**Largest Recent Fines:** TikTok (€530M, Ireland, May 2025, insufficient legal basis), LinkedIn (€310M, Ireland, Oct 2024), Meta Platforms Ireland (€251M and €91M, Dec 2024 and Sep 2024, insufficient security measures), and Vodafone GmbH (€45M, Germany, 2025).

**GDPR Applicability to US Companies:** Article 3 states GDPR applies to any organization processing EU residents' data regardless of location. Eight of the 10 highest GDPR fines were imposed on US-based companies (Meta, Amazon, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Uber), totaling €3.9 billion (nearly 63% of all fines). Example: Clearview AI was fined €30.5 million by the Dutch DPA in 2024 and over €100 million total across seven fines since 2020. US companies must comply if they offer goods/services to EU/EEA residents or monitor their behavior.

**US vs EU Enforcement Comparison:** EU takes a proactive, rights-based approach treating privacy as a fundamental human right, with fines based on global turnover percentage (up to 4%). The US is reactive/complaint-based consumer protection, with fines per violation or per consumer. EU enforcers are national DPAs coordinated by EDPB; US enforcers are FTC and state AGs. The EDPB's Coordinated Enforcement Framework ran a 2024 sweep on "right to access" and a 2025 sweep on "right to erasure." The EU AI Act came into force August 1, 2024, with full applicability by August 2, 2027. In the US, CCPA (2018) inspired 19 other states to pass similar laws, creating a fragmented compliance landscape.

**Key Compliance Lessons:** Legal basis is paramount; security isn't optional; transparency equals trust; cooperate with authorities; compliance is continuous (not one-and-done).

**Common Compliance Failures:** Poor data security, ignoring legal basis and GDPR's seven principles, not fulfilling data subject rights, cross-border data transfers without safeguards (Meta's €1.2 billion 2023 fine cited), and failing to report breaches within 72 hours.

**Avoidance Checklist:** The article provides a 21-item checklist covering data mapping/auditing, valid legal basis for all processing, proper consent mechanisms, data minimization, privacy by design, DPIAs for high-risk processing, strong security measures, breach response plans with 72-hour notification, maintaining Records of Processing Activities (RoPA), appointing a DPO, third-party compliance, cross-border transfer mechanisms, employee training, continuous monitoring, and using compliance automation software.

**Automation Solution:** The article promotes Scrut's GDPR compliance platform (trusted by 1,500+ customers) with pre-built policy templates, pre-mapped controls, daily automated control monitoring, compliance gap analysis, automated evidence collection, vendor management, real-time dashboards, and GDPR expert access. Scrut positions automation as the fix for manual, error-prone compliance processes.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: GDPR Fines Statistics 2026: Article 83 & Penalties ---
URL: https://deepstrike.io/blog/gdpr-fines-statistics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This DeepStrike blog article (published July 8, 2026, by Cybersecurity Architect Mohammed Khalil) provides a comprehensive analysis of GDPR fines statistics, enforcement patterns, and practical risk implications for privacy, legal, GRC, and security teams.

## Key Statistics
- Cumulative GDPR fines: approximately €6.31B across 3,195 listed fines per CMS Enforcement Tracker (July 2026), and approximately €7.1B per DLA Piper survey (January 2026) — these are separate datasets and should not be merged
- 2025 annual fines: approximately €1.2B (roughly matching 2024)
- Irish DPC cumulative fines: approximately €4.04B since 2018 (dominated by major tech company cases)
- Largest single fine: Meta Platforms Ireland €1.2B (2023, EU-US data transfers)
- Other major fines: Amazon Europe Core €746M (2021), TikTok €530M (2025, transfers to China), Meta/Instagram €405M (2022), Meta €390M (2023), TikTok €345M (2023), LinkedIn €310M (2024), Uber €290M (2024, Dutch DPA), Meta €265M (2022), Meta €251M (2024), WhatsApp €225M (2021)
- 443 EU breach notifications per day in 2025 (DLA Piper)

## Article 83 Fine Tiers
- Article 83(4): up to €10M or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover (certain controller/processor obligations, certification/monitoring bodies)
- Article 83(5): up to €20M or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover (core principles, lawful basis, consent, data subject rights, international transfers)
- Article 83(6): up to €20M or 4% (non-compliance with supervisory authority orders)
- These are maximum legal caps, not typical fine values; the GDPR text refers to "total worldwide annual turnover" (not "revenue") with a "whichever is higher" rule

## Country Trends
- Ireland leads cumulative euro totals due to lead supervisory authority status over major tech companies
- France/CNIL: 87 fines and approximately €55.2M in 2024
- Spain/AEPD: approximately €35.6M in 2024
- Germany has fragmented enforcement across federal and state authorities
- UK GDPR fines (ICO) must be kept separate from EU totals; UK fines often reported in GBP

## Key Enforcement Patterns
- The largest fines involve international transfers, lawful basis for behavioral advertising, transparency, and children's data — not just data breaches
- GDPR fines cover lawful basis, consent, transparency, data subject rights, transfers, security of processing (Article 32), breach notification, and processor obligations
- Average fine values are misleading due to mega-fine skew; scenario-based risk analysis is recommended
- A data breach does not automatically mean a GDPR fine; regulators examine controls, detection/notification timing, mitigation, cooperation, and documentation
- US and non-EU companies can face GDPR fines if offering goods/services to EU individuals or monitoring their behavior

## Practical Guidance
- Security testing (penetration testing, API testing, cloud security) supports Article 32 evidence but does not guarantee compliance or prevent fines
- Teams should focus on: lawful basis documentation, transfer governance (SCCs, TIAs), consent records, privacy notices, DPIAs, vendor/processor management, incident response, breach notification workflows, Article 32 controls, and documentation/evidence quality
- EU GDPR, UK GDPR, ePrivacy/cookie fines, CCPA/CPRA, civil compensation, breach costs, and cyber insurance claims are separate data categories that should not be merged

The article emphasizes that GDPR fine data should guide governance and security validation rather than serve as a penalty calculator, and includes extensive checklists for benchmarking fine exposure across security, privacy, and governance controls.
</summary>

This webpage documents the Irish Data Protection Commission's (DPC) investigation into TikTok over alleged violations of GDPR data transfer provisions. The case involves cross-border data transfer regulation under the General Data Protection Regulation, specifically concerning TikTok Technology Limited's unlawful transfer of personal data from the European Economic Area (EEA) to China.

**Timeline of key events:**

- **21 Feb 2025:** DPC submitted a draft decision under Article 60 of the GDPR to other EU and EEA supervisory authorities.

- **27 May 2025:** TikTok filed an appeal at the High Court against the EUR 530 million fine and the order suspending data transfers to China (under appeal).

- **13 Nov 2025:** High Court granted TikTok's application to stay the data transfer suspension order and corrective order pending appeal.
- **30 Apr 2026:** Supreme Court dismissed the DPC's appeal against the High Court decision granting the stay on the suspension and compliance orders against TikTok.
- **03 Jun 2026:** High Court upheld the DPC's findings on data protection violations and the EUR 530 million fine against TikTok.
- **30 Jun 2026:** High Court upheld the EUR 530 million GDPR fine and referred fining methodology questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union.

**Key details:**
- Implementers: Ireland
- Policy area: Data governance
- Policy instrument: Cross-border data transfer regulation
- Regulated economic activity: Platform intermediary (user-generated content)
- Government branches involved: judiciary (court, supreme court) and executive (data protection authority)
- Related regulation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation) data transfer requirements, in force since 25 May 2018

--- SOURCE 7: [PDF] Irish Data Protection Commission Fines TikTok Over EEA Data ... ---
URL: https://www.maynardnexsen.com/assets/htmldocuments/Irish%20Data%20Protection%20Commission%20Fines%20TikTok%20Over%20EEA%20Data%20Transfers%20to%20China%20w-047-0335.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 2 May 2025, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) issued a final decision finding TikTok Technology Limited in breach of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) for two key violations: cross-border transfers of EEA user data to China without legally adequate safeguards, and violations of GDPR transparency requirements.

TikTok was fined a total of EUR530 million (EUR485 million for the Article 46(1) GDPR transfer infringement and EUR45 million for the Article 13(1)(f) transparency infringement). TikTok must bring its processing into compliance within six months, and the DPC suspended any further transfers of EEA data to China if compliance is not achieved within that timeframe.

Key findings of the inquiry:
- TikTok initially informed the DPC it did not store EEA User Data on servers in China, but in April 2025 disclosed that limited EEA User Data had in fact been stored on servers in China since February 2025, meaning TikTok had provided inaccurate information to the inquiry.
- No EU adequacy decision exists for China, so transfers required safeguards under Chapter V of the GDPR (such as standard contractual clauses with supplementary measures), placing the burden on TikTok to verify, guarantee and demonstrate that Chinese law provides essentially equivalent protection to EU law.
- The DPC found TikTok failed this obligation, noting that aspects of Chinese law (including the Anti-Terrorism Law, Counter-Espionage Law, Cybersecurity Law, and National Intelligence Law) materially diverge from EU standards and preclude a finding of essential equivalence.
- For transparency, the DPC found TikTok's October 2021 EEA Privacy Policy inadequate because it did not name third countries (including China) to which data was transferred, and did not explain that transfers included remote access to data stored in Singapore and the United States by personnel in China.
- TikTok's updated December 2022 EEA Privacy Policy was found compliant, so the transparency infringement was limited to the period between 29 July 2020 and 1 December 2022.

The ruling underscores the importance of sufficient transparency and specificity in public privacy notices, as well as legally adequate safeguards for cross-border transfers of personal data to third countries.

## QUICK FACTS

* **Fine Amount**: €290,000,000
* **Date**: 22 July 2024
* **Primary Violations:** GDPR Breaches

  + Unlawful transfer of personal data to a third country without appropriate safeguards (Article 44 GDPR)

---

## Overview

The Dutch Data Protection Authority (Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, AP) has imposed a significant administrative fine of €290 million on Uber Technologies Inc. and Uber B.V..

The penalty addresses violations of Article 44 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The AP determined that between August 6, 2021, and November 27, 2023, Uber unlawfully transferred the personal data of its European Union drivers to the United States.

This was done without the appropriate legal safeguards required by Chapter V of the GDPR, such as an adequacy decision or Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs), thereby failing to ensure the continuity of the high level of data protection afforded under EU law.

---

## Details of the CASE

The AP's investigation identified Uber B.V. (UBV), based in the Netherlands, and Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI), based in the U.S., as joint controllers for the personal data of drivers in the European Economic Area (EEA). The regulator established that Uber was in breach of the GDPR from August 6, 2021 - the date Uber removed SCCs from its internal data sharing agreement - until November 27, 2023, when it certified under the new EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework.

Uber contended that Chapter V of the GDPR should not apply, arguing that because its U.S. entity (UTI) was already subject to the GDPR under Article 3, the data was sufficiently protected. The AP rejected this, clarifying that Chapter V is complementary to Article 3 and its safeguards are essential to protect data from foreign legal frameworks that could undermine the GDPR.

Uber also argued that the data flows did not constitute a "transfer" (and that the concept of a "transfer" is not clearly defined in the GDPR) because drivers directly entered their information into the U.S.-based platform. The AP dismissed this, identifying UBV as the "exporter" because it establishes the contractual relationship with EEA drivers and defines the terms for data collection, leaving drivers with no alternative but to send their data to UTI's U.S. servers.

Finally, Uber claimed the transfers were permissible under Article 49 GDPR exceptions for contractual necessity. The AP concluded these exceptions were not applicable because the data transfers were systematic, repetitive, and continuous, not "incidental" as required by the regulation. Furthermore, the AP found the transfers were not objectively "necessary," as Uber could have used less intrusive alternatives, such as processing the data on servers within the EU.

### SPECIFIC EXAMPLES

Driver App Usage

Personal data from drivers in the EEA, collected through the driver app, was directly stored on UTI's servers in the U.S.. This included not only account and location data but also sensitive information such as identity documents, health data, and criminal records, depending on local requirements.

GDPR Rights Requests

When an EEA driver exercised their GDPR rights (e.g., an access request), a structural exchange of personal data occurred between UBV in the Netherlands and UTI in the U.S.. UBV employees in the EEA would access UTI's U.S.-based systems to handle these requests, resulting in data flowing from the U.S. to the EEA and, in some cases, back to the U.S..

---

## fines and Penalties

The AP imposed a single administrative fine of €290,000,000 on Uber B.V. and Uber Technologies Inc. jointly. The regulator classified the infringement's severity as "high" based on several factors:

* Nature and Duration: The violation was systematic and continued for over two years.
* Scale: A large number of drivers across the EU were affected.
* Data Sensitivity: The transferred data included special category data, such as health and criminal records, which require a higher level of protection.

---

## Key quotes

* "The AP is of the opinion that Uber violated Article 44 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), because Uber allowed transfers of personal data to take place to the United States while no appropriate safeguards were provided as stipulated in Chapter V of the GDPR."
* "The AP has established that the intended interest of Article 44 GDPR, namely the continuity of the high level of protection of the GDPR in the transfer of personal data to third countries, was not guaranteed by Uber."

### Uber Faces €290 Million Fine for GDPR Violation in Data Transfer to US

**ComplexDiscovery Staff**

In a significant ruling, the Dutch Data Protection Authority (DPA) has imposed a €290 million fine on Uber for improperly transferring European driver data to the United States. The penalty is among the largest issued under the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), underscoring the stringent requirements of data protection laws within the EU.

The DPA’s investigation stemmed from a complaint filed by over 170 French Uber drivers to the human rights organization Ligue des droits de l’Homme, which subsequently escalated the complaint to the French Data Protection Authority (CNIL). Given that Uber’s European headquarters is located in the Netherlands, the Dutch DPA took the lead in the investigation. The findings revealed that from August 2021 to November 2023, Uber transferred sensitive information, including account details, taxi licenses, location data, photos, payment details, identity documents, and criminal or medical records, to servers in the United States without employing proper safeguards.

Aleid Wolfsen, chairman of the Dutch DPA, emphasized the significance of this violation, stating, “In Europe, the GDPR protects people’s fundamental rights by requiring companies and governments to handle personal data with care. Uber did not meet the requirements of the GDPR to ensure the level of protection to the data with regard to transfers to the US. That is very serious.” This failure to implement adequate protection tools was exacerbated by Uber’s decision to halt the use of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) in August 2021, further compromising the data security of its European drivers.

This is not Uber’s first encounter with GDPR penalties. Previously, the Dutch DPA fined Uber €600,000 in 2018 for failing to report a data breach in a timely manner and €10 million in 2023 for privacy infringements. In these instances, Uber has consistently opted to challenge the rulings, and it has already indicated its intention to appeal the latest fine.

The GDPR, enacted in 2016, sets forth rigorous guidelines for managing and sharing personal data. Violations of these regulations have led to significant financial penalties for numerous tech companies. Meta, for example, faced a $1.3 billion fine in 2023 for similar violations concerning inadequate data transfer protections.

The Dutch DPA’s actions highlight the necessity for companies to rigorously adhere to GDPR guidelines, especially when handling data transfers outside the EU. Such stringent measures are essential to safeguard personal data and uphold individuals’ rights. The cross-border collaboration among European DPAs, in this case, illustrates the collective effort to enforce GDPR compliance and protect data privacy across the EU.

As the digital landscape evolves, regulatory bodies remain vigilant in ensuring that companies like Uber align their data protection practices with established legal frameworks. The repercussions of failing to do so are a stark reminder of the importance of compliant data handling in an interconnected world.

args.summary:
The Dutch Data Protection Authority (DPA) has imposed a €290 million fine on Uber for improperly transferring European driver data to the United States, marking one of the largest penalties issued under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The investigation originated from a complaint filed by over 170 French Uber drivers to the human rights organization Ligue des droits de l'Homme, which escalated the matter to the French Data Protection Authority (CNIL). Since Uber's European headquarters is located in the Netherlands, the Dutch DPA led the investigation.

The findings revealed that from August 2021 to November 2023, Uber transferred sensitive information—including account details, taxi licenses, location data, photos, payment details, identity documents, and criminal or medical records—to servers in the United States without employing proper safeguards. The situation was exacerbated by Uber's decision to halt the use of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) in August 2021.

This is not Uber's first GDPR-related penalty. The Dutch DPA previously fined Uber €600,000 in 2018 for failing to report a data breach in a timely manner and €10 million in 2023 for privacy infringements. Uber has indicated its intention to appeal the latest fine. The case follows a similar precedent: Meta faced a $1.3 billion fine in 2023 for inadequate data transfer protections. Aleid Wolfsen, chairman of the Dutch DPA, emphasized the seriousness of the violation, noting that Uber failed to meet GDPR requirements for protecting data transferred to the US. The case highlights the increasing scrutiny on how multinational corporations manage and protect personal data across borders, and underscores the importance of cross-border collaboration among European DPAs in enforcing GDPR compliance.
args.key_excerpts: "In Europe, the GDPR protects people's fundamental rights by requiring companies and governments to handle personal data with care. Uber did not meet the requirements of the GDPR to ensure the level of protection to the data with regard to transfers to the US. That is very serious." — Aleid Wolfsen, chairman of the Dutch DPA, "The penalty is among the largest issued under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), underscoring the stringent requirements of data protection laws within the EU.", "This failure to implement adequate protection tools was exacerbated by Uber's decision to halt the use of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) in August 2021, further compromising the data security of its European drivers.", "Meta, for example, faced a $1.3 billion fine in 2023 for similar violations concerning inadequate data transfer protections."

## English Summary

### Facts

In September 2018, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) launched two inquiries into data processing activities of Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, here the controller.

In July 2017, Meta implemented a so-called “View-as” function on Facebook which allowed users to see their own Facebook page as it would appear to another user. The function included a video upload feature which created so-called “user tokens”. User tokens are coded IDs which are used to verify users and can control access to platform features as well as personal data. Users could therefore use these tokens to gain access to other accounts.

Between the 14 and 18 September 2018, third parties caused a major data breach by using the tokens to log on as other Facebook account holders. The data breach impacted approximately 29,000,000 Facebook users globally of which 3,000,000 were based in the EU/EEA.

Meta employees became aware of the data breach through an unusual increase in video uploads and removed the function shortly after.

### Holding

Decision one: Documentation concerning the data breach

The DPC found that Meta had violated [Article 33(3) GDPR](https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=Article_33_GDPR#3 "Article 33 GDPR") for failing to include necessary information in their data breach report. For this violation, the DPC issued a reprimand and set an administrative fine of €8,000,000.

Further, the DPC found a violation of [Article 33(5) GDPR](https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=Article_33_GDPR#5 "Article 33 GDPR") as Meta had failed to appropriately document facts of the breach and remedial steps taken. For obstructing the supervisory authorities ability to verify compliance, the DPC issued a reprimand and set and administrative of €3,000,000.

Decision two: Privacy by design

The DPC found that Meta had violated [Article 25(1) GDPR](https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=Article_25_GDPR#1 "Article 25 GDPR") for failing to embed data protection principles into the design of the feature. For this the DPC issued a reprimand and an set an administrative fine of €130,000,000.

Additionally, the DPC found that Meta had violated [Article 25(2) GDPR](https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=Article_25_GDPR#2 "Article 25 GDPR") for failing to ensure that by default only necessary personal data was processed. For this the DPC issued a reprimand and set an administrative fine of €110,000,000.

# Google Fined €325 Million by France Over Gmail Ads and Cookie Violations

France’s data protection watchdog CNIL has imposed a €325 million fine on Google for violating European privacy laws by displaying advertising content in Gmail without valid user consent and by failing to comply with cookie consent regulations.

![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/3dfdda1c1436ad8ca7e1ff4efc7f6b704bee416b876f0758b0cb53c10990cb5d?s=40&d=mm&r=g)

**Editor** Editor

Share this article:

![](https://worldef.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Adsiz-tasarim-2025-09-05T122151.214.jpg)

September 5, 2025

France’s data protection watchdog CNIL has imposed a €325 million fine on [Google](https://news.worldef.com/2025/08/14/google-launches-commerce-media-suite-to-boost-festive-season-sales/) for violating European privacy laws by displaying advertising content in Gmail without valid user consent and by failing to comply with cookie consent regulations. The decision, announced in early September 2025, highlights the growing scrutiny faced by major tech platforms over how they handle personal data in the European Union.

This is one of CNIL’s largest fines to date and underscores the regulator’s ongoing efforts to enforce the ePrivacy Directive and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) against even the most powerful digital companies.

#### Gmail Ads Without Consent

The CNIL investigation centered around Gmail’s “Promotions” and [“Social”](https://news.worldef.com/2025/08/04/new-social-media-advertiser-permit-system-introduced-in-the-uae/) tabs, where Google displayed promotional content designed to resemble ordinary emails. According to CNIL, these advertising messages were not only unsolicited but also formatted to appear indistinguishable from user-generated emails. This lack of transparency created confusion and undermined users’ control over their inboxes.

More importantly, these ads were delivered without users giving prior, informed consent a fundamental requirement under EU privacy law. CNIL concluded that Google had failed to obtain valid legal basis to process user data for targeted advertising within Gmail, particularly for newly created accounts. An estimated 50 to 60 million users were affected by the practice (Euractiv).

#### Cookie Policy Violations

In addition to the issue with Gmail ads, CNIL found that Google’s cookie banner and data collection practices did not meet EU standards. During the account registration process, users were presented with options that nudged them toward accepting personalized ad tracking. While there was a theoretical option to refuse consent, CNIL said that the user interface was designed in a way that made refusal difficult or unclear, thus invalidating any supposed consent ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/france-hits-google-with-381-million-fine-consumer-protection-failures-2025-09-03?utm_source=chatgpt.com)).

Moreover, cookies related to personalized advertising were allegedly placed on users’ devices before meaningful consent had been obtained. This practice directly contradicts the ePrivacy Directive, which requires explicit opt-in consent for non-essential cookies.

#### Breakdown of the Penalty

The €325 million fine has been split across two Google entities: €200 million was levied against Google LLC, the U.S.-based parent company, and €125 million against Google Ireland Limited, which handles most of Google’s European operations. This structure reflects how Google operates across borders and the scope of responsibility for each legal entity.

In addition to the fine, CNIL has issued a legally binding order that mandates Google to bring its Gmail advertising practices into full compliance within six months. If the company fails to meet this deadline, it will be subject to a further fine of €100,000 for each day of non-compliance ([Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/tech/french-watchdog-fines-google-shein-record-553-9-million-over-cookies-29da3100?utm_source=chatgpt.com)).

#### CNIL’s Statement and Legal Basis

In its official statement, CNIL emphasized that unsolicited advertising via email, particularly when disguised to look like ordinary emails, constitutes a form of spam. According to European privacy law, such communication requires prior, freely given, and informed consent.

The authority also clarified that its action is based not only on GDPR but also on the ePrivacy Directive, which governs electronic communications and sets strict rules on marketing via email, messaging platforms, and cookies.

“Users must be able to clearly distinguish between private correspondence and advertising. Companies cannot bypass consent requirements by embedding ads in a service that resembles personal communication,” CNIL stated in its press release.

#### Google’s Response

Google responded to the fine by expressing disappointment and defending its advertising practices. A spokesperson for the company stated:

“We provide users with clear information and simple controls for ad personalization, and we’ve made improvements over time to increase transparency and choice. We will review the CNIL’s decision carefully and continue working constructively with regulators across Europe.”

Google also reiterated that its Gmail ads are not based on the content of individual users’ emails and that the platform offers settings that allow users to opt out of personalized ads. However, CNIL argued that the way those settings are presented does not meet the criteria for freely given and informed consent under GDPR.

#### Role of Privacy Advocates

This case was triggered by a complaint filed by NOYB (None of Your Business), the Austrian-based privacy rights organization founded by activist and lawyer Max Schrems. NOYB has been at the forefront of several high-profile privacy cases across Europe and has filed numerous complaints against Google, Meta, [Amazon,](https://news.worldef.com/2025/09/03/amazon-launches-ai-powered-lens-live/) and other major digital platforms.

In a statement following the CNIL ruling, NOYB said the decision was a significant win for users and a step toward eliminating “email spam disguised as legitimate content.” The organization noted that Google’s Gmail promotions had become “a new form of commercial intrusion that users never agreed to” ([NOYB](https://noyb.eu/en/noyb-win-french-dpa-fines-google-eu325-million-spam-emails-gmail?utm_source=chatgpt.com)).

#### Broader Regulatory Context

This is not the first time Google has faced legal action over privacy issues in Europe. In previous years, the company has received several fines from EU data protection authorities related to advertising personalization, location tracking, and cookie consent. The latest fine adds to growing pressure on Google to overhaul its consent mechanisms and data processing policies in line with EU standards.

CNIL has also issued major fines to other companies in recent months, including a €176 million fine to fast fashion retailer Shein for similar cookie consent violations ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/france-fines-shein-176-million-over-cookies-2025-09-03?utm_source=chatgpt.com)).

Legal experts suggest that CNIL’s ruling against Google may set a precedent for how data protection authorities across the EU handle similar cases in the future, particularly as the European Commission continues pushing for stronger enforcement of digital regulations under the upcoming Digital Services Act (DSA) and Digital Markets Act (DMA).

#### Why This Matters

The case raises essential questions about the boundaries of user consent in digital services. As online platforms increasingly rely on behavioral data for monetization, regulators are drawing clearer lines around what constitutes informed, voluntary agreement and what counts as manipulation.

Google’s Gmail, a service used by over 1.5 billion people globally, functions as a core communication tool. When advertising begins to blur with personal communication, the stakes for privacy and transparency grow significantly.

This ruling from CNIL demonstrates that regulatory bodies are not only willing to go after data breaches or cyberattacks, but also increasingly focused on the subtle ways companies may exploit user attention and consent for profit.
