# Spanish Airport Operator Aena Hit With €10M Fine Over Biometric Boarding

November 28, 2025

Spain’s data protection authority, the Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD), has fined airport operator Aena just over €10 million for deploying facial recognition systems at eight airports without carrying out a valid data protection impact assessment (DPIA). The decision, dated November 6 and [reported this week](https://elpais.com/economia/2025-11-25/aena-se-revuelve-ante-los-10-millones-de-multa-de-la-agencia-de-proteccion-de-datos-por-la-identificacion-biometrica-en-los-aeropuertos.html), finds that Aena’s biometric boarding programme amounted to "high-risk" processing and that the company failed to demonstrate the necessity, proportionality and safeguards required under Article 35 of the GDPR.

According to Spanish and international press reports, the systems were used to control access to certain zones and to support biometric boarding at major hubs including Madrid-Barajas and Barcelona-El Prat, as well as several other tourist-heavy airports. The AEPD has ordered the temporary suspension of all biometric data processing linked to these systems, including facial recognition used for passenger identification, until an adequate DPIA is completed and any non-compliant processing is brought into line with EU data protection rules.

Aena has [said it will appeal the fine](https://efe.com/ciencia-y-tecnologia/2025-11-25/aena-multa-proteccion-datos/), arguing that passengers who enrolled in the programme did so voluntarily and with informed consent, and that no data breaches or security incidents have occurred. The company maintains that the biometric boarding trials were intended to improve passenger experience and reduce congestion at boarding gates.

However, the AEPD’s decision focuses less on consent and more on structural compliance failures, including the choice of a one-to-many (1:N) facial recognition architecture and the lack of an adequate impact assessment before deployment. For airlines, airport operators and biometric vendors operating in the EU, the case is a clear warning that biometric pilots and "innovation" projects are subject to the same GDPR requirements as full-scale rollouts.

The case follows [Italy’s suspension of facial recognition boarding at Milan’s Linate Airport](https://idtechwire.com/italian-watchdog-suspends-facial-recognition-boarding-at-milan-airport/) earlier this year, also citing GDPR violations, and underscores growing regulatory scrutiny of [airport biometric systems across Europe](https://idtechwire.com/sita-report-airports-and-airlines-accelerate-biometric-adoption/). Robust DPIAs, clear legal bases and careful evaluation of system design choices, particularly one-to-many facial recognition, will be essential to withstand regulatory scrutiny.

In its statement, Aena insisted that its biometric programme has guaranteed the privacy and security of users at all times. The company has stressed that there has been no data breach affecting users of the various biometric programmes deployed across the airport network in Spain, nor a breach of any third-party data.

"The security of this data has not been at risk at any time," asserts the airport operator.

Furthermore, Aena reiterates that the processing of biometric data was carried out after obtaining the informed and voluntary consent of passengers and that such data has been subject to the retention, blocking and deletion procedures set out in the current regulations.

The airport operator concludes that it will continue to work on streamlining passenger documentation processes in order to restart the biometric boarding programme "as soon as possible".

### 10-million-euro fine

The AEPD has fined Aena 10,043,002 euros for failing to comply with article 35 of Spain's general data protection regulations (GDPR) in the implementation of its facial recognition system at its airports.

The resolution imposing the fine states that Aena failed to conduct a valid data protection impact assessment prior to the processing, nor did it justify the necessity and proportionality of using biometric data for passenger identification.

The system, designed to expedite passenger transit and improve security, processed special category biometric data, such as facial patterns, along with other personal data.

The AEPD determined that the processing did not comply with the principles of necessity and proportionality, as less intrusive alternatives existed to achieve the same objectives. In addition, deficiencies were identified in the risk management and security measures adopted.

The fine includes the temporary suspension of biometric data processing until Aena carries out a proper impact assessment. The resolution will also be published in the official state gazette (BOE), given that the fine exceeds one million euros.

A DPA fined an airport managing company €10,043,002 for deploying a facial recognition system without an adequate Data Protection Impact Assessment in violation of [Article 35 GDPR](https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=Article_35_GDPR "Article 35 GDPR").

## English Summary

### Facts

The Spanish DPA investigated AENA (the controller) after a complaint from a data subject, both on their own behalf and on behalf of the Fundación Éticas Data Society, regarding a facial recognition pilot project at Barcelona-El Prat Airport. The data subject claimed that the controller violated the GDPR by processing biometric data for passenger identification and airport security.

The controller replied. It stated that the pilot project validated passenger identity by comparing images taken at registration with identification documents and boarding passes. The controller said the system improved security and passenger experience, was voluntary, and did not restrict fundamental rights, as passengers could opt out and board by traditional methods.

Additionally, the controller provided a prior data protection impact assessment (DPIA) and confirmed that no sensitive data, such as race or religion, was inferred. The company noted that all biometric pilot projects from 2019 to 2022 had been completed, and the personal data collected had been deleted.

The DPA admitted the complaint and initiated preliminary investigations. AENA submitted detailed documentation, including the DPIA, risk analyses, consent mechanisms, system architecture, security measures, and agreements with partner companies. The report confirmed that AENA implemented the biometric system incrementally at several airports and ensured that participation was voluntary. The DPIA documented the purposes, legal bases, necessity, proportionality, retention periods, risk mitigation measures, and security protocols.

### Holding

The Spanish DPA found that the controller violated [Article 35 GDPR](https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=Article_35_GDPR "Article 35 GDPR") because it failed to carry out an adequate DPIA. The DPA held that the controller did not comply with the requirements of [Article 35(7)(b) GDPR](https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=Article_35_GDPR#7b "Article 35 GDPR") and the principle of data minimisation under [Article 5(1)(c) GDPR](https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=Article_5_GDPR#1c "Article 5 GDPR").

Although the controller described benefits for passengers, such as faster boarding and reduced congestion, and for the airport, such as improved security, it did not identify or evaluate the disadvantages, risks, or less invasive alternatives to biometric processing.

The DPA noted that the biometric system posed a high risk due to the use of special categories of data, biometric identifiers, and new technologies. The system also involved storing more personal data than the previous manual identity verification system, including biometric facial patterns and other information from passengers’ identification documents and boarding passes, which increased risks substantially. The DPIA failed to justify the necessity or proportionality of the processing, even though less invasive alternatives existed such as traditional ID checks.

Taking into account the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, as well as the number of data subjects affected, the type of personal data processed, and the controller’s turnover of €5,021,501,000 in 2024, the DPA imposed a fine of €10,043,002. The DPA also imposed a temporary suspension of all biometric data processing, including the facial recognition system, until the controller completes a compliant DPIA under Article 35 GDPR.

args.summary:
This is a GDPRhub case page documenting a Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) decision in case EXP202304532 against AENA, the airport managing company in Spain. The case concerns a facial recognition pilot project at Barcelona-El Prat Airport (and other Spanish airports) that the AEPD found violated the GDPR.

**Facts:** The complaint was filed on March 22, 2023 by a data subject (A.A.A.) both on their own behalf and on behalf of the Fundación Éticas Data Society. The complaint concerned AENA's biometric facial recognition system implemented at Barcelona-El Prat Airport for passenger identification, security checks, boarding, and self-bag drop. AENA argued the system improved security and passenger experience, was voluntary (passengers could opt out and use traditional boarding), and that a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) had been conducted. AENA confirmed that all biometric pilot projects from 2019-2022 were completed by June 2022 and personal data had been deleted. AENA also noted it had suspended the gradual implementation of the system in May 2024 following the issuance of EDPB Opinion 11/2024 on facial recognition at airports.

**Key Procedural Timeline:**
- March 22, 2023: Complaint filed with AEPD
- May 12, 2023: AENA's DPO responded to the complaint transfer
- September 4, 2023 - June 14, 2024: Multiple information requests and responses from AENA
- November 8, 2024: AEPD initiated sanction proceedings against AENA
- December 12, 2024: AENA submitted allegations

**Holding:** The Spanish DPA found AENA violated Article 35 GDPR because it failed to carry out an adequate DPIA. The DPA held that AENA did not comply with Article 35(7)(b) GDPR (regarding the assessment of risks) and the principle of data minimisation under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. Although AENA described benefits (faster boarding, reduced congestion, improved security), it did not identify or evaluate disadvantages, risks, or less invasive alternatives to biometric processing. The DPIA failed to justify the necessity or proportionality of the processing, especially since less invasive alternatives (traditional ID checks) existed. The system also posed a high risk due to the use of special category data (biometric data) and new technologies, and involved storing more personal data than the previous manual identity verification system.

**Fine and Measures:** AENA was fined €10,043,002. The fine took into account the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, the number of data subjects affected, and AENA's turnover of €5,021,501,000 in 2024 (though an earlier certificate noted turnover of €4,386,767,000 in 2023, with 8,301 employees). The DPA also imposed a temporary suspension of all biometric data processing, including the facial recognition system, until AENA completes a compliant DPIA under Article 35 GDPR.

The decision was made under the AEPD, with national case number EXP202304532, originally in Spanish. The original source is the AEPD document ps-00431-2024.pdf.
args.key_excerpts: "A DPA fined an airport managing company €10,043,002 for deploying a facial recognition system without an adequate Data Protection Impact Assessment in violation of Article 35 GDPR."

# Don’t Forget the EU: Italy Issued First GenAI Fine of €15 Million Alleging GDPR Violations

At the end of 2024 the Italian Data Protection Authority issued a 15 million euro fine in the first generative AI-related case brought under GDPR. [According](https://www.garanteprivacy.it/home/docweb/-/docweb-display/docweb/10085432#english) to Garante (the Italian authority), OpenAI trained ChatGPT with users’ personal data without first identifying a proper legal basis for the activity, as required under GDPR. The Order also alleges that OpenAI failed to notify Garante about a data breach the company experienced in March 2023. Additionally, the Order states that OpenAI did not provide proper age verification mechanisms for users under age 13.

In addition to the fine, OpenAI must also conduct a six-month public education campaign on how ChatGPT works and how data is used to train AI products. The campaign must also provide individuals with information about their rights and how to exercise their rights. OpenAI intends to appeal the decision.

This decision follows March 2023 [temporary ban](https://gpdp.it/web/guest/home/docweb/-/docweb-display/docweb/9870847) of ChatGPT in Italy. And in July 2023, the FTC issued a [Civil Investigative Demand](https://www.washingtonpost.com/documents/67a7081c-c770-4f05-a39e-9d02117e50e8.pdf?itid=lk_inline_manual_4) to OpenAI.

**Putting it into Practice: While it is unclear the extent to which AI will receive the same type of scrutiny in the US that it did under the prior administration, this decision is a reminder that the EU regulators are keeping a close eye on AI activities, especially when personal data is used to train the tool. For an ongoing update of executive actions that may impact AI (and much more), check out this [tool](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1C4m_Gzy27HsemsR4bocDUAjl36OumcYh9I1oPnw9pYg/edit?gid=2034954957#gid=2034954957) created by our partner, Jon Meyer.**

Italy's data protection authority has [fined](https://www.garanteprivacy.it/home/docweb/-/docweb-display/docweb/10085432#english) ChatGPT maker OpenAI a fine of €15 million ($15.66 million) over how the generative artificial intelligence application handles personal data.

The fine comes nearly a year after the Garante [found](https://thehackernews.com/2024/01/italian-data-protection-watchdog.html) that ChatGPT processed users' information to train its service in violation of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

The authority said OpenAI did not notify it of a [security breach](https://thehackernews.com/2023/03/openai-reveals-redis-bug-behind-chatgpt.html) that took place in March 2023, and that it processed the personal information of users to train ChatGPT without having an adequate legal basis to do so. It also accused the company of going against the principle of transparency and related information obligations toward users.

[![Cybersecurity](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mP8Xw8AAoMBgDTD2qgAAAAASUVORK5CYII=)](https://thehackernews.uk/zero-trust-ai-claude-m)

"Furthermore, OpenAI has not provided for mechanisms for age verification, which could lead to the risk of exposing children under 13 to inappropriate responses with respect to their degree of development and self-awareness," the Garante said.

Besides levying a €15 million fine, the company has been ordered to carry out a six-month-long communication campaign on radio, television, newspapers, and the internet to promote public understanding of how ChatGPT works.

This specifically includes the nature of data collected, both user and non-user information, for the purpose of training its models, and the rights that users can exercise to object, rectify, or delete that data.

"Through this communication campaign, users and non-users of ChatGPT will have to be made aware of how to oppose generative artificial intelligence being trained with their personal data and thus be effectively enabled to exercise their rights under the GDPR," the Garante added.

Italy was the first country to impose a [temporary ban](https://thehackernews.com/2023/04/italian-watchdog-bans-openais-chatgpt.html) on ChatGPT in late March 2023, citing data protection concerns. Nearly a month later, access to ChatGPT was [reinstated](https://thehackernews.com/2023/04/chatgpt-is-back-in-italy-after.html) after the company addressed the issues raised by the Garante.

In a [statement](https://apnews.com/article/italy-privacy-authority-openai-chatgpt-fine-6760575ae7a29a1dd22cc666f49e605f) shared with the Associated Press, OpenAI called the decision disproportionate and that it intends to appeal, stating the fine is nearly 20 times the revenue it made in Italy during the time period. It further said it's committed to offering beneficial artificial intelligence that abides by users' privacy rights.

The ruling also follows an opinion from the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) that an AI model that unlawfully processes personal data but is subsequently anonymized prior to deployment does not constitute a violation of GDPR.

"If it can be demonstrated that the subsequent operation of the AI model does not entail the processing of personal data, the EDPB considers that the GDPR would not apply," the Board [said](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2024/edpb-opinion-ai-models-gdpr-principles-support-responsible-ai_en). "Hence, the unlawfulness of the initial processing should not impact the subsequent operation of the model."

"Further, the EDPB considers that, when controllers subsequently process personal data collected during the deployment phase, after the model has been anonymised, the GDPR would apply in relation to these processing operations."

Earlier this month, the Board also published guidelines on handling data transfers outside non-European countries in a manner that complies with GDPR. The guidelines are subject to public consultation until January 27, 2025.

"Judgements or decisions from third countries authorities cannot automatically be recognised or enforced in Europe," it [said](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2024/edpb-clarifies-rules-data-sharing-third-country-authorities-and-approves-eu-data_en). "If an organisation replies to a request for personal data from a third country authority, this data flow constitutes a transfer and the GDPR applies."

<webpage_content>
[![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fedge.sitecorecloud.io%2Flewissilkin1267-lewissilkinc0b3-production2ebf-9a4c%2Fmedia%2FProject%2FLewis-Silkin%2FLewis-Silkin%2Fimages%2Fmisc%2Flewis-silkin-logo-rgb-black-text.png%3Fh%3D264%26iar%3D0%26w%3D1180&w=640&q=75)](https://www.lewissilkin.com/)

Welcome to Lewis Silkin  
United Kingdom



**Summary**

Once again, OpenAI finds itself under intense scrutiny from the Italian data protection authority, Garante Per La Protezione Dei Dati Personali (**Garante**), after its investigation revealed various data protection violations in relation to its management of the company's flagship AI tool, ChatGPT. The violations included training ChatGPT "*without having an adequate legal basis*" and not complying with "*information obligations towards users*". Besides levying a [€15 million fine](https://www.garanteprivacy.it/home/docweb/-/docweb-display/docweb/10085432#english), OpenAI will also have to conduct an information campaign for a six month period across Italian media platforms. This decision is one of the most significant actions taken against the tech powerhouse, and underscores the growing demand for accountability and transparency with data processing in artificial intelligence (**AI**) systems.

**The origins of the investigation**

The Garante's probe into OpenAI began in [March 2023](https://www.garanteprivacy.it/web/guest/home/docweb/-/docweb-display/docweb/9870832), with a particular focus on ChatGPT, amid growing concerns about its collection and processing of personal data. The investigation quickly escalated, with the Garante taking an unprecedented move imposing an "*immediate temporary limitation*" on the use of ChatGPT, citing various privacy violations including the:

* "*mass collection and storage of personal data for the purpose of 'training' the algorithms*";
* failure to report "*a bug in an open source library*" exposing users conversation history; and
* lack of appropriate age verification mechanisms exposing minors to "*absolutely unsuitable answers compared to their degree of development and awareness*".

However, the restriction proved short-lived. Within less than a month, the ban was lifted and the use of ChatGPT was reinstated after OpenAI agreed to take corrective measures to meet data protection obligations. These included:

* clarifying the explanation of "*the activities of collection and processing*" of user data "*for the purpose of algorithm training, the manner of processing, the logic behind the processing necessary for the operation of the service, the rights of data subjects, and any other information required...*";
* changing the legal basis for processing users' personal data to "consent or legitimate interest" to comply with the "*principle of accountability*"; and
* introducing age verification mechanisms for excluding access to the service for users under 13 years.

**Unveiling ongoing privacy breaches**

Despite OpenAI's efforts to address initial privacy concerns, the Garante continued with a wide scope review into ChatGPT which concluded with their decision on 20 December 2024.  From their investigation, the Garante noted numerous data protection violations including:

* the absence of an "*appropriate legal basis*" for processing personal data used to train ChatGPT;
* failure to fulfil transparency obligations, as required under Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation (**GDPR**)), to its users; and
* lack of sufficient age verification measures to protect minors.

According to the Garante, OpenAI had processed user data "*to train ChatGPT without first identifying an adequate legal basis*", directly violating the GDPR's transparency principle and its obligation to inform users. Specifically, they determined the processing of personal data had occurred before ChatGPT's public release on 30 November 2022. In their opinion, "*at least on that date*", if not earlier, OpenAI was under an obligation to have identified a legal basis, the absence of which meant there was a violation as there was no legal basis "*prior to the start of processing*".

But that's not all. The Garante also rejected OpenAI's attempts to defend its actions by relying on the data protection impact assessment (**DPIA**) and legitimate interest assessment (**LIA**), both of which failed to convince the authority. According to the Garante, the DPIA and LIA, produced on 19 May and 20 November 2023 respectively, were not "*decisive*" in establishing that a legal basis for processing existed prior to the launch of the service, making it "*impossible*" for data subjects "*to exercise their rights*" directly violating the "*principle of accountability*". In particular:

* the DPIA, which pointed to "*legitimate interests*" as the basis for processing, failed to evidence a relevant adequacy assessment took place before 30 November 2022; and
* the LIA was produced "*only at the express request*" of the Garante and did not provide evidence that "*the identification of one of the legal bases took place before 30 March 2023*".

The Garante's ruling underscored a fundamental issue – OpenAI had lacked the necessary legal safeguards from the outset. In reaching its decision, the Garante also cited the European Data Protection Board's recent [opinion](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2024/edpb-opinion-ai-models-gdpr-principles-support-responsible-ai_en), issued just days earlier, regarding the lawful use of personal data for the "*design, development and deployment*" of AI systems.

The investigation also uncovered OpenAI had failed to comply with the requirement to implement age verification mechanisms, the absence of which placed minors under the age of 13 years at risk of being exposed to inappropriate AI generated content.

Adding to the weight of its final decision, the Garante also faulted OpenAI for failing to inform the Garante, as required by Article 33 of the GDPR, of a breach it experienced on [20 March 2023](https://openai.com/index/march-20-chatgpt-outage/). The breach, triggered by an internal security bug rather than an external attack, exposed personal data – specifically chat histories and payment information of ChatGPT Plus subscribers who were active during "*a specific nine-hour window*". This lapse in security compromised the confidentiality of data subjects. The Garante noted that OpenAI should have notified "*all European data protection authorities whose data subjects had been involved in the data breach. Given that the investigation documents showed that the event affected 440 Italian users, OpenAI should have notified the data breach directly to the Authority*". Failure to do so further undermined the trust in the company's commitment to its transparency obligations.

**Imposing corrective measures and financial penalties**

OpenAI have found itself facing a hefty penalty after the series of actions collectively amounted to several data protection violations. The Garante has not held back, imposing a €15 million fine equivalent to approximately 1.58% of the "*total annual worldwide turnover for the 2023 financial year*". The total amount was determined based on the following proportions:

* €9,000,000 for violations related to processing personal data unlawfully;
* €320,000 for the failure to report a personal data breach to the Garante; and
* €5,680,000.00 for the failure to comply with corrective measures imposed by the Garante in 2023.

In determining the fine, the Garante concluded that the calculation represents an "*effective, proportionate and dissuasive*" sanction. This approach not only mirrors the gravity of violations but also sends a crucial reminder to organisations to prioritise privacy rights within their AI systems.

The Garante have also invoked its authority granted by Article 166, paragraph 7 of the Privacy Code, instructing OpenAI to conduct a six month "*institutional communication campaign*" across media outlets including TV networks, radio stations, and newspapers. The aim of the campaign is to "*promote a public understanding and awareness of the functioning of ChatGPT*", particularly with the "*collection of user and non-user data*" for the purpose of training AI systems, and to outline rights "*exercisable by data subjects*" including the right to object, rectify and delete their personal data.

This dual action of financial penalty and public education serves as a stark reminder of the growing regulatory focus on the lawful development and deployment of AI systems.

**OpenAI's response: pushback and cooperation**

Unsurprisingly, OpenAI have expressed their intention to appeal the Garante's ruling, labelling it as "*disproportionate*". In a public statement the company emphasised its collaborative efforts with privacy regulators, particularly following the 2023 temporary ban – "*when the Garante ordered us to stop offering ChatGPT in Italy in 2023, we worked with them to reinstate it a month later... they've since recognized our industry-leading approach to protecting privacy in AI, yet this fine is nearly 20 times the revenue we made in Italy during the relevant period*".

Despite this, OpenAI have reaffirmed their commitment to working with privacy authorities to ensure they offer "*beneficial AI that respects privacy rights*".

**A broader perspective on AI accountability**

The Garante's decision marks a significant stride in AI regulation, showcasing an assertive approach to enforcing GDPR provisions including, specifying the legal basis for processing, promoting user privacy, developing transparent practices to ensure accountability, and safeguarding the rights of data subjects. It also sends a clear message to the global AI community – *that is* – compliance with data protection laws is non-negotiable.

Therefore, AI developers should ensure they embed privacy-by-design principles at the core of AI systems to support the responsible development and deployment of AI models. Companies are encouraged to:

* **Ensure GDPR Compliance**: Implement or develop AI systems that comply with the provisions of the GDPR.
* **Adopt a Privacy First Approach**: Protect personal data by default by incorporating a privacy-by-design approach within AI systems.
* **Establish a Legal Basis**: Carefully assess, define and document the legal basis for processing personal data. Remember the legal basis must be established prior to processing and cannot be retrospectively applied.
* **Transparency and Accountability**: Update privacy policies with detailed and transparent information about the use of personal data within AI systems. Provide users with clear guidance and mechanisms on how to exercise their rights, including objecting to data processing for training purposes and requesting data deletion. Transparency builds trust.
* **DPIAs**: Complete a DPIA prior to deployment of the AI system and at each stage of the AI life cycle. Stay proactive, not reactive, when it comes to privacy risks.
* **Review and Update**: Review organisational practices and update technical documentation to ensure compliance with data protection practices and evolving standards. This will not only meet the minimum requirements but will actively build a data protection strategy into AI systems.

**A global wake-up call**

The fine against OpenAI isn't just a penalty but may be the beginning of a new era of accountability in the world of AI. What is clear is that a legal basis must exist prior to processing, as AI systems must not come at the expense of user privacy.

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into daily life, regulators will need to collaborate to strike a balance between innovation and the protection of fundamental rights. OpenAI's challenges in Italy are likely just the beginning, as the global conversation around responsible AI intensifies.

This article from Lewis Silkin law firm discusses the Italian data protection authority (Garante) fining OpenAI €15 million for GDPR violations related to ChatGPT. The investigation, which began in March 2023, found that OpenAI trained ChatGPT without an adequate legal basis, failed to meet transparency obligations toward users, and lacked sufficient age verification mechanisms. The Garante's investigation originated in March 2023 when it temporarily banned ChatGPT in Italy over concerns about mass collection of personal data for algorithm training, a bug exposing user conversation histories, and inadequate age verification. The ban was lifted within a month after OpenAI agreed to corrective measures, including clarifying data processing practices, changing its legal basis to consent or legitimate interest, and introducing age verification for users under 13.

The final decision on December 20, 2024 found multiple violations: OpenAI processed personal data to train ChatGPT without identifying an adequate legal basis prior to the service's public launch on November 30, 2022; its DPIA and LIA (produced in May and November 2023) were not decisive in establishing a prior legal basis; it failed to implement adequate age verification; and it failed to notify the Garante of a March 20, 2023 data breach (as required by Article 33 of GDPR) that exposed chat histories and payment information of ChatGPT Plus subscribers during a nine-hour window, affecting 440 Italian users.

The €15 million fine (approximately 1.58% of OpenAI's 2023 annual worldwide turnover) was broken down as: €9 million for unlawful data processing, €320,000 for failing to report the data breach, and €5,680,000 for failing to comply with corrective measures imposed in 2023. OpenAI was also ordered to conduct a six-month institutional communication campaign across Italian media to promote public awareness of how ChatGPT functions, data collection practices, and data subject rights.

OpenAI has expressed intent to appeal the ruling, calling the fine "disproportionate," noting it is nearly 20 times the revenue the company made in Italy during the relevant period, while reaffirming its commitment to working with privacy authorities. The article concludes with practical recommendations for AI developers, including ensuring GDPR compliance, adopting privacy-by-design principles, establishing legal bases before processing (which cannot be applied retrospectively), maintaining transparency and accountability, completing DPIAs before deployment, and regularly reviewing and updating compliance practices. The article frames this decision as a significant step in AI regulation and a global wake-up call for accountability in AI development.

# Generative AI and GDPR Enforcement in Europe: A Lot of Noise, One Fine, Zero Survivors

* Posted on

[Theodore Christakis](https://www.crossborderdataforum.org/author/theodore-christakis/ "Theodore Christakis")

On March 18, 2026, as reported by Matthew Newman at [MLex](https://mlexwatch.com/), the Court of Rome annulled Decision No. 755, issued on November 2, 2024, by Italy’s data protection authority (the Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali), which had imposed a €15 million fine on OpenAI for multiple GDPR violations linked to the management of its ChatGPT service. The decision had already been suspended by the same court on March 21, 2025, and subsequently [removed from the Garante’s own website](https://www.garanteprivacy.it/home/docweb/-/docweb-display/docweb/10085432#english). Yesterday’s ruling now overturns the substance of the authority’s decision.

This was not just any enforcement decision. It was the only final GDPR enforcement action ever adopted in Europe concerning the period of the launch of generative AI to the public.

**A short history of regulatory hype**

When the Garante imposed the fine in late 2024, the news landed with considerable force. My own [LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/theodore-christakis-9ab5a6260_chatgpt-gets-a-christmas-present-from-italy-activity-7275827704145313792-9PgQ) at the time, titled “ChatGPT Gets a Christmas Present from Italy: Europe’s First GDPR Fine for Generative AI”, reached over 64,000 impressions. The data protection community was buzzing.

And for good reason. The Garante had found that OpenAI processed personal data for training ChatGPT without an adequate legal basis, violated GDPR transparency and information obligations, failed to properly notify the authority of a March 2023 data breach, and lacked age verification mechanisms for minors. In addition to the fine, the Garante exercised for the first time powers under Article 166(7) of the Italian Data Protection Code, ordering OpenAI to conduct a six-month public awareness campaign across radio, television, print and online media.

The regulatory momentum at the time appeared unstoppable. In the spring of 2023, data protection authorities across Europe had opened investigations into ChatGPT in rapid succession: [Spain’s AEPD](https://www.euronews.com/next/2023/04/14/spain-opens-an-investigation-into-openais-chatgpt-over-a-potential-data-breach.), [Poland’s UODO](https://techcrunch.com/2023/09/21/poland-chatgpt-gdpr-complaint-probe/) (following a complaint by security researcher Lukasz Olejnik about hallucinated biographical data), France’s CNIL (which received [at least five complaints](https://www.cnil.fr/en/artificial-intelligence-action-plan-cnil)), and several [German state data protection authorities](https://www.thelocal.de/20230425/germany-launches-data-protection-inquiry-over-chatgpt). Later, in April 2024, noyb filed a [complaint](https://noyb.eu/en/chatgpt-provides-false-information-about-people-and-openai-cant-correct-it) in Austria about data accuracy. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) established a dedicated [ChatGPT Taskforce in April 2023](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2023/edpb-resolves-dispute-transfers-meta-and-creates-task-force-chat-gpt_en) to coordinate enforcement across the bloc. I recall a call shortly after the Italian fine during which the representative of a DPA in another EU Member State confidently announced that “their own decision concerning OpenAI was ready and should be published imminently”.

**What followed: nothing**

Since then, not a single other European DPA has published a final enforcement decision concerning GDPR violations linked to the launch period of ChatGPT (November 2022 to March 2023).

The EDPB Taskforce published its [report](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/other/report-work-undertaken-chatgpt-taskforce_en) in May 2024, but it contained only “preliminary views” and expressly noted that investigations were “still ongoing”. Meanwhile, in February 2024, OpenAI established OpenAI Ireland Limited, triggering the GDPR’s one-stop-shop mechanism. A footnote in the Taskforce report itself acknowledged that for infringements of a “continuing or continuous nature”, pending proceedings “should be transferred” to the lead DPA, which would now be the Irish Data Protection Commission. This procedural development may well have absorbed or frozen several national investigations.

But the end result is the same: Europe’s regulatory response to the most consequential AI deployment in its history produced a single enforcement decision. And that decision has now been annulled.

**Proportionality concerns then and now**

At the time of the Garante’s decision, I had [raised questions](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/theodore-christakis-9ab5a6260_chatgpt-gets-a-christmas-present-from-italy-activity-7275827704145313792-9PgQ) about the proportionality of the fine. €15 million was almost as much as the €20 million penalty imposed on Clearview AI, a company widely criticized for mass biometric surveillance.

That said, the underlying findings of GDPR non-compliance were difficult to contest on the merits. When ChatGPT was launched to the European public, there was a clear disregard for basic data protection requirements: no adequate legal basis had been identified, transparency obligations were not met, and no age verification was in place. These were not marginal infractions.

Crucially, the full reasoning of the Court of Rome has not yet been published. The Garante itself received the ruling (Judgment no. 4153/2026, R.G. 4785/2025) on the morning of March 19, but, as the reasoning has not yet been made available, the Authority was not in a position, at this stage, to provide comments or to assess whether to lodge an appeal. This is an important clarification: the annulment may not be the end of the story, and a Garante appeal remains a real possibility.

In the meantime, the key questions remain open. Did the Court challenge the proportionality of the sanction? Or did it call into question the Garante’s findings of GDPR violations themselves? Could a new Garante decision follow on the basis of the Court’s instructions? Matthew Newman’s article in MLex does not offer an answer on these points, and I would welcome any clarification from him, from Italian colleagues, or from anyone with access to the decision.

**The widening gap between guidance and formal enforcement**

Regardless of the specific reasoning of the Court of Rome, the broader picture is interesting. The initial regulatory intensity surrounding ChatGPT’s launch in Europe has given way to an extended period of inaction. No other DPA in Europe has issued a decision. The only decision that was issued has been annulled.

Meanwhile, data protection authorities across Europe have invested, and continue to invest, considerable energy in producing guidance documents on web scraping and the training of large language models with publicly available data. Wenlong Li, Yueming Zhang, Qingqing Zheng, and Aolan Li have recently and usefully mapped this phenomenon in a comparative study published in the *International Data Privacy Law* journal, documenting how the legal basis for AI training is framed in data protection guidelines and regulatory interventions across multiple jurisdictions ([*How the Legal Basis for AI Training is Framed in Data Protection Guidelines and Interventions: Comparative Perspectives and the Prospect of Global Convergence*](https://doi.org/10.1093/idpl/ipaf032), IDPL 2026). With the notable exception of the [Garante’s own continuing ban on DeepSeek in Italy](https://ai-regulation.com/deepseek-one-year-later-regulatory-storm-global-surge/), the gap between the proliferation of such guidances and the near-total absence of formal enforcement is becoming increasingly visible.

**The other side of the coin: regulatory engagement that worked**

This assessment would be incomplete, however, without acknowledging what DPA interventions have actually achieved in practice, even in the absence of final sanctions.

The Garante’s 2023 temporary ban on ChatGPT in Italy may not have produced a lasting fine, but its immediate operational impact was considerable. Within weeks, OpenAI implemented a privacy notice, introduced an opt-out mechanism for training data, and deployed an age verification system. These were concrete changes to a product used by hundreds of millions, and they were adopted not because of a fine but because a regulator forced the issue. The investigations opened across Europe in 2023, and the EDPB Taskforce’s work, undoubtedly contributed to the broader pressure that led OpenAI, and other major AI companies, to establish a European presence, appoint a DPO, and publish a dedicated EEA privacy policy. None of that would have happened on a voluntary basis.

More recently, the Irish DPC has demonstrated that regulatory engagement short of formal sanctions can yield significant results. In June 2024, following intensive engagement, the DPC [secured Meta’s agreement to pause](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/latest-news/dpcs-engagement-meta-ai) its plans to train large language models using public content shared by adults on Facebook and Instagram across the EU/EEA. The pause lasted nearly a year, during which the DPC sought a formal EDPB Opinion and Meta substantially revised its approach, implementing enhanced transparency notices, improved objection mechanisms, and technical safeguards including data de-identification and output filtering. When Meta [eventually resumed training in May 2025](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/latest-news/dpc-statement-meta-ai), it did so under conditions that bore little resemblance to its original proposal.

This process also prompted the DPC to request, and the EDPB to adopt in December 2024, [Opinion 28/2024 on the data protection aspects of AI model training and deployment](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2024-12/edpb_opinion_202428_ai-models_en.pdf), providing the first Europe-wide framework on the subject.

The DPC also took [unprecedented legal action against X](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/dpc-welcomes-xs-agreement-suspend-its-processing-personal-data-purpose-training-ai-tool-grok) in August 2024, bringing an urgent application before the Irish High Court to halt the use of EU users’ public posts for training xAI’s Grok chatbot. X [agreed to permanently suspend](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-welcomes-conclusion-proceedings-relating-xs-ai-tool-grok) the processing, and the proceedings were concluded on that basis in September 2024. It was the first time any lead supervisory authority had used such powers in the AI context.

These interventions matter. They demonstrate that DPA action, even when it does not result in a fine, can reshape how AI companies operate in Europe. The [Garante’s DeepSeek ban](https://ai-regulation.com/deepseek-one-year-later-regulatory-storm-global-surge/) remains the most visible illustration of this: a Chinese AI service effectively excluded from the Italian market for failure to engage with GDPR requirements.

But there is a difference between regulatory engagement that improves specific practices and the kind of formal enforcement that establishes legal precedent and signals to the broader market what the rules actually are. On the latter front, the record remains thin.

**A changed world?**

The timing could hardly be more symbolic. Just days before the Court of Rome annulled the Garante’s ChatGPT fine, the [Luxembourg Administrative Court annulled the €746 million GDPR fine](https://cnpd.public.lu/en/actualites/national/2026/03/arret-ca-amazon-cnpd.html) that had been imposed on Amazon in 2021 for targeted advertising practices without proper consent. In that case, the court largely upheld the substance of the GDPR violations but found that the regulator had failed to properly assess fault and proportionality before imposing its sanction. In the space of a single week, two of the most high-profile GDPR fines ever imposed in Europe have been struck down by national courts. The Luxembourg CNPD has been invited to reassess its case, and the Garante’s story may not be over either. But the signal is hard to miss.

The landscape has shifted in ways that would have been difficult to imagine two years ago. From the regulatory hype of 2023 and 2024, the EU data protection system seems to have moved into a posture of cautious observation when it comes to formal enforcement. Whether this reflects genuine procedural constraints, the complexity of applying legacy data protection rules to novel AI systems, or something else is an open question.

The Garante may yet appeal the Court of Rome’s judgment, and the full reasoning of the ruling could change the picture considerably.

Still, it is difficult not to wonder whether the current “don’t regulate, don’t harm innovation” frenzy sweeping across both sides of the Atlantic has quietly reached the corridors of Europe’s data protection authorities as well.

--- SOURCE 1: GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2025 ---
URL: https://cms.law/en/media/international/files/publications/publications/gdpr-enforcement-tracker-report-may-2025?v=8

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2025 (6th Edition), published by the CMS Data Protection Group, provides a comprehensive analysis of GDPR fines imposed by European Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) from 2018 to the editorial deadline of 1 March 2025. Key findings include:

- A total of 2,245 fines were issued and recorded in the Enforcement Tracker (with complete information), up 159 from the 2024 report; the database includes 2,560 total cases when limited-information cases are counted.
- Total fines exceeded the five-billion mark for the first time, reaching approximately EUR 5.65 billion (up EUR 1.17 billion from 2024). The average fine across 2018-2024 was about EUR 2.36 million.
- The highest GDPR fine to date is EUR 1.2 billion imposed by the Irish DPA in May 2023 for violations of international data transfer regulations (against Meta). This was followed by a EUR 746 million fine from Luxembourg (July 2021), seven Irish fines ranging from EUR 225-405 million, and a EUR 290 million fine from the Netherlands (July 2024).
- Top violation types by number of fines and average amounts: "insufficient legal basis for data processing" (669 fines, avg EUR 2.9M), "non-compliance with general data processing principles" (644 fines, avg EUR 3.8M), and "insufficient technical and organisational measures for information security" (418 fines, avg EUR 2.0M).
- Spain leads the list of fines by number for the sixth consecutive year (followed by Italy and Romania); Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands lead in average and total fine amounts due to record fines against big tech.
- The first GDPR fine was recorded in Portugal in July 2018 (EUR 400,000 against a public hospital). Enforcement ramped up between 2019 and mid-2021, with big tech sanctions in 2022 and the first billion-euro fine in 2023. The current period shows a "business as usual" approach with limited landmark cases.

Sector insights: The media, telecoms and broadcasting sector accounts for 70% of fines and has the highest sector exposure for the fourth consecutive year. The finance, insurance and consulting sector saw significant fine increases with four fines exceeding EUR 1 million (including against Clearview AI, which accumulated over EUR 100 million in fines across multiple EU countries). Other sectors covered include healthcare, accommodation/hospitality, industry and commerce, real estate, transportation/energy, public sector/education, individuals/private associations, and employment (including a record EUR 290 million Dutch employment fine).

Key takeaways: GDPR enforcement remains heavily influenced by national laws and practices, creating significant variation across Member States. CJEU rulings (including C-683/21, C-807/21, C-154/21, C-487/21, C-579/21) are increasingly clarifying the scope of GDPR provisions, including data subject access rights and DPA fining powers. The EDPB's 2024-2027 strategy focuses on harmonizing enforcement and addressing new technologies like AI. Non-financial sanctions (e.g., temporary restrictions, like the Italian ban on generative AI) may become more important. Class actions and representative actions by consumer associations are expected to increase following the Representative Actions Directive (EU 2020/1828).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Up to March 2025, a total number of 2,245 fines (+159 in comparison to the 2024 ET Report) were issued and recorded in the Enforcement Tracker... Total fines exceeded the five-billion mark for the first time and amount to around EUR 5.65 billion."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Avoiding GDPR fines in 2025: Enforcement trends and tips ---
URL: https://www.scrut.io/hub/gdpr/gdpr-fines-penalties-us-eu-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Scrut.io provides a comprehensive guide to GDPR fines and penalties in the US and EU, updated as of November 2025. It outlines the two-tiered GDPR fine structure established under Article 83: Tier 1 fines (up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover) for less severe violations like failing to report a data breach within 72 hours, not appointing a DPO when required, or neglecting DPIAs; and Tier 2 fines (up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover) for serious violations like processing data without a valid legal basis, failing to meet consent conditions, violating data subject rights, or unlawful cross-border transfers.

Key enforcement statistics: Since May 2018 to August 2025, over 2,800 GDPR fines totaling over €6.2 billion have been issued, with over 60% (€3.8 billion) imposed since January 2023 alone. The top three countries by number of fines are Spain (107), Romania (61), and Italy (41). The top countries by fine amounts are Ireland (€1.18 billion), Germany (€45.9 million), and Italy (€32.4 million). From 2024–2025, enforcement intensified with record-breaking fines, the first €1.2 billion fine (Meta in May 2023), expansion beyond tech into finance and energy, personal accountability for executives, and growing attention on AI and cloud services.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On August 26, 2024, the Dutch Data Protection Authority (Dutch DPA) fined Uber Technologies, Inc. and Uber B.V. €290 million for violating the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The fine stems from Uber's failure to implement appropriate safeguards for transferring EEA-based drivers' personal data to the United States over a 27-month period, during which Uber removed Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) from its data-sharing agreements between EEA and U.S. entities.

The investigation originated from complaints by drivers to the French data protection authority and was transferred to the Dutch DPA since Uber's European headquarters are in the Netherlands. Uber's personal data transfers included special category and criminal record data, and were directed to Uber's centralized IT infrastructure in the United States.

Key findings of the Decision:
- **Adequate safeguards required for intra-group transfers**: Uber argued both its U.S. and EEA entities were subject to GDPR under Article 3 as joint controllers, making Chapter V compliance unnecessary. The Dutch DPA rejected this, stating the data transfer requirements in Chapter V place a direct obligation on parties processing personal data in third countries. The DPA also determined an "onward transfer" occurred from Uber EEA (data exporter) to Uber U.S. (data importer), even though drivers entered data directly into the Uber platform.
- **Article 49 derogations limited**: Uber argued the transfers were lawful under Article 49 as necessary for contract performance. The DPA rejected this, finding the transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing rather than incidental, and that contract existence alone does not constitute "necessity." The DPA was unconvinced that centralized U.S. processing was crucial to Uber's services, suggesting efficiency motives were insufficient.
- **Fine proportionality**: The DPA considered the violation serious, given the sensitive nature of drivers' personal data (including criminal data) and the 27-month duration. The fine was evaluated under the maximum parameters (higher of €20 million or 4% annual turnover). The DPA determined Uber "could have known" the transfer would require additional safeguards based on GDPR, CJEU case law, and prior regulator decisions.

The Dutch DPA coordinated its decision with other EU data protection authorities, meaning similar determinations could follow. Uber is expected to appeal. The Decision's biggest takeaway is the added uncertainty to the international data transfer landscape, particularly casting doubt on whether companies can rely on European Commission Q&A guidance for compliance or penalty mitigation purposes. The article was authored by attorneys at Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP and published in The Computer & Internet Lawyer, Volume 42, Number 1, January 2025.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Into the Data Transfer Thicket: The Dutch Uber Decision and the ... ---
URL: https://europeanlawblog.eu/1xjmngct

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an opinion/analysis article from the European Law Blog (22 October 2024) by E J Kyriakides examining the Dutch DPA's enforcement decision against Uber and the legal relationship between GDPR Article 3 (territorial scope) and Chapter V (data transfer safeguards).

KEY ISSUE: The article addresses a lingering legal ambiguity: under what circumstances are GDPR data transfer safeguards required when a foreign firm is already subject to the GDPR. The classic transfer scenario involves a foreign company NOT governed by GDPR receiving EU data. But GDPR has extraterritorial effect (Article 3(2)), meaning foreign companies targeting the EU can also be subject to it.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:
- Article 3(1): Entities with an EU "establishment" are subject to GDPR
- Article 3(2): Entities without EU establishment are subject if they (a) offer goods/services to EU data subjects, or (b) monitor EU data subject behavior
- Chapter V (Articles 44-47) requires transfer safeguards including adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses (SCCs), binding corporate rules, etc.
- Under Schrems II, firms must independently assess whether transfer tools ensure "essentially equivalent" protection, potentially requiring supplementary measures
- Chapter V applies only to a "transfer" — a term the GDPR does not define

EDPB GUIDELINES (05/2021):
- Defined "transfer" as occurring when: (1) a controller/processor (exporter) is subject to GDPR; (2) the exporter discloses personal data to another controller/processor (importer); (3) the importer is in a third country (regardless of whether importer is subject to GDPR)
- Critically concluded NO transfer occurs when data is directly disclosed by an individual in the EU to a firm in a third country
- Companies subject to GDPR must still assess third country government access risks under other GDPR obligations (Articles 32, 33, 35)
- Not binding but highly authoritative

THE DUTCH DPA UBER DECISION (August 2024):
- Dutch DPA fined Uber €290 million — the largest fine ever from the Dutch DPA — for transferring French Uber drivers' data to the US without Chapter V safeguards
- Fine originated from an NGO (Ligue Des Droits De L'homme) complaint to the French CNIL
- Transfer involved Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) and Uber Technologies Inc (UTI, US parent)
- Uber relied on SCCs until August 2021, then determined SCCs were unnecessary because Article 3 directly applied to UTI's US processing; Uber had NO transfer mechanism from August 2021 until relying on the Data Privacy Framework in November 2023
- Two scenarios found to involve transfers: (1) EU drivers' data sent directly via Uber app to UTI for US storage; (2) data relating to GDPR rights requests where UBV and UTI collaborated
- Dutch DPA rejected Uber's defenses (direct collection, joint controllership, Article 49 derogations), holding transfers between joint controllers subject to GDPR in different countries are governed by Chapter V
- DPA departed from EDPB guidance by finding scenario one (direct collection from EU data subjects) constituted a "transfer," relying on the employment relationship between UBV and drivers and the asymmetry of power
- DPA argued Chapter V should be read broadly to counterbalance risks of diminished protection when data is processed abroad and difficulty enforcing against foreign entities
- DPA found Article 49(b-c) derogations inapplicable because transfers were ongoing, not "incidental" or "necessary"

ANALYSIS/NEXT STEPS:
- Uber is appealing; Dutch courts are likely to refer questions to the CJEU on the Article 3/Chapter V relationship
- The Dutch decision failed to articulate a clear legal standard for when direct collection by foreign providers subject to GDPR triggers Chapter V
- The article recommends that EU entities subject to GDPR under Article 3(2) in doubt apply Chapter V safeguards until the issue is settled
- European Commission has not yet issued SCCs for scenarios where the importer is subject to GDPR (current SCCs only apply when importer is NOT subject to GDPR)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The EDPB concluded that a transfer occurs when: 1) A controller or a processor ('exporter') is subject to the GDPR for the given processing; 2) The exporter discloses by transmission or otherwise makes personal data... available to another controller, joint controller or processor ('importer'); 3) The importer is in a third country, irrespective of whether or not this importer is subject to the GDPR for the given processing in accordance with Article 3"

1. **Article 3 GDPR and Chapter V can apply simultaneously**: The DPA rejected Uber's argument that the territorial scope (Article 3 GDPR) and Chapter V (international transfers) were mutually exclusive. 2. **The processing constituted a transfer**: Applying the EDPB Guidelines 05/2021's three cumulative criteria, the DPA found all criteria met. --- SOURCE 1: EU & Ireland: Meta’s legal basis for targeted ads found to breach GDPR | Privacy Matters ---
URL: https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/2023/01/eu-ireland-metas-legal-basis-for-targeted-ads-found-to-breach-gdpr

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a DLA Piper "Privacy Matters" blog post (authors: James Sullivan, John Magee & David Brazil) analyzing Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) decisions announced January 4, 2023, fining Meta €390 million for breaching GDPR by using 'contractual necessity' as the legal basis for processing millions of Europeans' personal data for targeted advertising on Facebook and Instagram.

**Key Background:**
- Prior to GDPR's effective date (May 25, 2018), Meta changed its Terms of Service to rely on 'contractual necessity' instead of consent as the lawful basis for processing user data for personalized advertising.
- Two EU complainants argued Meta was "forcing" users to consent by conditioning services on accepting updated Terms of Service.
- The DPC initially sided with Meta, concluding 'contractual necessity' was a valid legal basis for personalized ads, while also finding transparency violations (with proposed fines understood to be €28-36 million).

**The Dispute:**
- 10 DPAs from across Europe contested the DPC's draft decision, arguing personalized advertising was not necessary to perform the core contract with users.
- On December 5, 2022, the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued a binding determination partially reversing the DPC, finding Meta was NOT entitled to rely on 'contractual necessity.' The EDPB also ordered the DPC to conduct a new investigation into ALL of Facebook's and Instagram's data processing operations.
- The DPC's final decisions on December 31, 2022 incorporated the EDPB's ruling, and were announced January 4, 2023.

**Disagreements Among Regulators:**
The decisions reflect two growing divisions among European DPAs: (1) whether 'contractual necessity' is an appropriate GDPR legal basis for personalized advertising, and (2) whether the EDPB has legal authority to order DPAs to bring new investigations. The DPC characterized the EDPB's order as an "open-ended and speculative investigation" and overreach, and indicated it will bring an annulment action before the Court of Justice of the EU—the DPC's first legal challenge of the EDPB's directions.

**Next Steps & Implications:**
- Meta announced its intention to appeal both the substance and the fines, meaning the 'contractual necessity' issue will be litigated for years.
- The DPC required Meta to bring processing into compliance within three months, but Meta's appeal may allow it to continue its current approach pending appellate outcomes.
- The decisions did not prohibit personalized advertising; Meta could pivot to 'consent' or 'legitimate interest' as legal bases, though 'legitimate interest' gives users a right to object that could undermine personalized advertising at scale.
- A third DPC decision regarding Meta's WhatsApp service was due imminently, though that inquiry concerned processing for service improvement purposes.
- Commercial implications are significant: Meta's share price fell 6.2% on the day the EDPB's position was reported. The business model of providing personalized ads without an opt-out option is increasingly difficult to justify.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced on January 4, 2023, that it has fined Meta a total of €390 million after finding that the company's Facebook and Instagram platforms lacked proper legal grounds for processing millions of Europeans' personal data for targeted advertising."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 4 January 2023, Ireland's data protection authority (DPC) announced its final decision fining Meta Ireland €210 million for GDPR breaches regarding its Facebook services and €180 million for breaches regarding its Instagram services, totaling €390 million. The decisions center on the legal basis Meta used for processing personal data for personalised advertising.

Key events in the timeline:
- The DPC launched an investigation into Meta on 25 May 2018, following complaints about Facebook and Instagram. Meta had previously relied on user consent but shifted to the 'performance of a contract' legal basis after the GDPR took effect on 25 May 2018, arguing that processing personal data (including for personalised ads) was necessary to fulfil its contractual obligations under its terms of service.
- The DPC published a draft decision on 6 October 2021 proposing fines of up to €23 million for Instagram and €36 million for Facebook, finding that personalised advertising was a core element of Meta's services and that Meta had breached transparency obligations.
- Ten European supervisory authorities (including the Dutch DPA) disagreed with the DPC's draft, arguing personalised ads are not a core element of Meta's services. This triggered the European Consistency Mechanism, and the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued a binding decision on 5 December 2022.
- The EDPB upheld the DPC's position on transparency breaches but found that 'performance of a contract' was not a lawful basis for processing personal data for personalised advertising. The EDPB reasoned that: (1) Meta is not contractually obligated to offer personalised ads to users (the obligation exists with advertisers instead); (2) transparency requirements are indispensable to the contract basis; and (3) under Article 21(2)-(3) GDPR, users can object to direct marketing processing at any time without reason, meaning such processing is not "necessary" for the contract. The EDPB also ordered significantly increased fines.
- The DPC adopted the EDPB's binding decision on 31 December 2022, finding breaches of Article 6(1) GDPR from the GDPR's entry into force. Meta was given three months to bring its data processing into compliance.

Impact: The decisions strike at Meta's core business model, which relies on personalised advertising. Meta announced it would appeal, and the case may ultimately be referred to both the Irish Supreme Court and the CJEU. The decision also highlights significant disagreement between the DPC and other European supervisory authorities, with the DPC claiming the EDPB exceeded its powers. The ruling may affect other platforms relying on personalised ads, and preliminary questions on the 'legitimate interest' legal basis are pending before the CJEU (Case C-621/22). Meta is also facing revenue loss from Apple's iOS opt-out tracking feature.

SUMMARY:

The DPC ruled that Meta's legal basis for seeking user permission to collect data for personalized advertising is invalid under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and gave the company three months to bring its data processing operations into compliance.

The decisions stem from complaints filed by privacy rights group NOYB on May 25, 2018—the day the GDPR took effect. The DPC's findings reflect binding decisions by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) that Meta violated transparency obligations by not clearly outlining its legal basis for personal data processing and invalidating its "contract" legal basis for ad targeting. This is a legal analysis from Matheson LLP (dated 17/10/2023) regarding the Irish Data Protection Commission's (DPC) decision to fine TikTok €345 million for GDPR violations concerning children's data.

**Background:** The DPC conducted an own-volition inquiry into TikTok's processing of data of child users aged 13-17 (and children under 13) during the period 31 July 2020 to 31 December 2020. As TikTok's processing constituted "cross-border processing," the DPC acted as Lead Supervisory Authority under the one-stop-shop procedure (Article 60 GDPR). The CSAs of Italy and Berlin raised objections, which were referred to the EDPB for dispute resolution under Article 65 GDPR. The EDPB directed the DPC to include a finding on the fairness principle (Article 5(1)(a)) regarding "dark patterns" as proposed by Berlin, but did not direct a violation of Article 25(1) regarding age verification as requested by Italy.

**Key Findings (6 total):**
- **Finding 1 (Platform Settings):** TikTok made Child User accounts public by default, infringing data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c)) and data protection by design and by default (Articles 25(1) and 25(2)). Content was accessible to anyone on or off TikTok, to a "global extent."
- **Finding 2:** Public-by-default settings created severe risks to Child Users' rights and freedoms; TikTok failed to comply with Article 24(1) GDPR as controller.
- **Finding 3 (Family Pairing):** TikTok's "Family Pairing" setting allowed unverified non-Child Users (not necessarily parents/guardians) to pair with and control Child User accounts, including enabling direct messaging for users over 16, infringing Article 5(1)(f) and Article 25(1).
- **Finding 4 (Age Verification):** TikTok's DPIA failed to identify the specific risk of children under 13 accessing the platform, infringing Article 24(1), though no violation of Article 25(1) was found regarding age verification.
- **Finding 5 (Transparency):** TikTok's Privacy Policy and summary failed to inform Child Users that public accounts would be viewable by an indefinite number of people including non-registered users, and used vague terms like "may" and "third parties," breaching Articles 12(1) and 13(1)(e).
- **Finding 6 (Dark Patterns):** Following the EDPB's determination, TikTok was found to have used Registration and Video Posting Pop-Ups as "dark patterns" to nudge Child Users toward privacy-intrusive settings, infringing the fairness principle under Article 5(1)(a).

**Corrective Powers:** The DPC ordered TikTok to comply within 3 months, issued a reprimand, and imposed fines totaling €345 million: €100 million for Finding 1, €65 million for Finding 3, and €180 million for Finding 5.

**Implications:** The decision has broader implications for all EU/EEA organisations processing children's data. Organisations must: adopt privacy by design/by default; identify risks to children (including under-13 risk) in DPIAs; use clear and definitive language in privacy notices identifying recipients; and avoid dark patterns that nudge users toward privacy-intrusive settings. The DPC acknowledged TikTok's post-Relevant Period improvements as "mitigating value" but noted "it is not always possible to retrospectively correct a past lack of control."

# Biggest GDPR Fines of All Time: Top 50 Ranked [2026]

The EUR 1.2 billion fine against Meta Platforms Ireland remains the largest GDPR fine on record as of 2026, according to the CMS Enforcement Tracker Report and enforcementtracker.com. See the ranked top 10, the full top-50 range, and how the biggest fines are holding up on appeal.

[By PrivacyTerms.io](/authors/privacytermsio) ,  · 12 min read

![Biggest GDPR Fines of All Time: Top 50 Ranked [2026]](/_astro/biggest-gdpr-fines-all-time.BJNzFfK6_2vYFwd.webp)
