## EDPB Annual Report 2024 - Summary

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) published its 2024 Annual Report, titled "Protecting Personal Data in a Changing Landscape." The report covers the Board's activities throughout 2024, including its strategy, guidance, opinions, enforcement cooperation, and the work of its Secretariat.

### Key Highlights of 2024

**Strategy and Governance:**
- Adopted the new 2024-2027 Strategy in April 2024, structured around four pillars: (1) advancing harmonisation and promoting compliance, (2) reinforcing a common enforcement culture, (3) addressing technological challenges, and (4) enhancing the EDPB's global role
- Adopted the 2024-2025 Work Programme implementing the Strategy
- Zdravko Vukić (Croatia) elected as new EDPB Deputy Chair in June 2024
- Anu Talus served as Chair; Isabelle Vereecken as Head of Secretariat

**Consistency Opinions (28 total in 2024):**
- 20 opinions under Art. 64(1) GDPR (covering DPIA lists, codes of conduct, certification bodies, SCCs, BCRs, etc.) — bringing the total to 188 since 2018
- 8 opinions under Art. 64(2) GDPR on matters of general application, including:
  - **Opinion 04/2024** (Feb): Notion of "main establishment" of a controller — clarified that a place of central administration qualifies as main establishment only if it takes decisions on purposes/means of processing and has power to implement them; burden of proof falls on controllers
  - **Opinion 08/2024** (April): "Consent or Pay" models by large online platforms — concluded most current implementations are unlikely to meet GDPR's valid consent requirements; platforms should offer free alternatives without behavioural advertising, ensure transparency, and avoid excessive fees
  - **Opinion 11/2024** (May): Use of facial recognition at airports — only storage solutions with biometric data held by the individual or central storage with encryption key solely in the individual's hands were found compatible with data protection principles
  - **Opinion 22/2024** (Oct): Obligations regarding processors and sub-processors under Art. 28 GDPR — controllers must have identity information on all processors readily available; verification obligations apply regardless of risk level but extent varies by risk; controller retains ultimate decision on engaging sub-processors
  - **Opinion 28/2024** (Dec): Processing personal data to train AI models — confirmed legitimate interest can serve as legal basis under certain conditions, with a three-step test proposed; EDPB consulted the EU AI Office before adoption

**Statements on Legislative Developments (6 in 2024):**
Covered the child sexual abuse regulation proposal, the financial data access and payments package, DPA roles in the AI Act framework, GDPR procedural rules draft regulation, High-Level Group on Access to Data recommendations, and the Second Report on GDPR Application.

**Enforcement and Litigation:**
- No Art. 65 binding decisions issued in 2024 (first year since 2020)
- EDPB involved as main party in 13 cases before the CJEU (2 new in 2024), mostly annulment applications against binding decisions, plus 1 case as intervener
- Sharp increase in Art. 64(2) opinion requests

**New Roles and Cross-Regulatory Cooperation:**
- EDPB became a member of the DMA High-Level Group and the European Data Innovation Board (EDIB)
- Cooperated with the European Board for Digital Services (EBDS) and the EU AI Office
- New digital legislation (DMA, DSA, AI Act, Governance Act, Data Act) expanded DPA responsibilities — DPAs designated as Market Surveillance Authorities for certain high-risk AI systems under the AI Act

**Secretariat Operations:**
- Budget of €8.36 million (part of EDPS budget)
- Team of 395 professionals across five sectors (legal affairs, litigation/international affairs, IT, information/communications, administrative)
- Organised over 530 meetings in 2024 (up from 360+ in 2023)
- Managed over 4,200 IT assistance requests and queries (up from 3,400 in 2023)
- IMI system facilitated over 5,644 procedures; 907 support requests handled
- EDPB HUB content grew 64% (12,307 content pieces); user base exceeded 1,500 members (7% increase)

- Coordinated Supervision Committee (CSC) extended to Visa Information System (VIS); work on ETIAS supervision ongoing

- Data Protection Guide for Small Business made available in 18 languages
- Launched series of summaries of EDPB guidelines for non-experts
- Two stakeholder events held (AI models and "Consent or Pay")
- First meeting of EDPB with DPAs of countries with an adequacy decision (October 2024)

--- SOURCE 2: Fines / Penalties - General Data Protection Regulation ... ---
URL: https://gdpr-info.eu/issues/fines-penalties

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from gdpr-info.eu provides a comprehensive overview of fines and penalties under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). National authorities can or must assess fines for data protection violations, which are applied in addition to or instead of corrective powers such as orders to end violations, instructions to adjust data processing, and temporary or definitive limitations including bans on data processing. Processors may be subject to sanctions directly and/or in conjunction with the controller.

Fines must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive for each individual case. Authorities use a statutory catalogue of criteria when determining penalty levels, with aggravating factors including intentional infringement, failure to take mitigation measures for damage, and lack of collaboration with authorities. For especially severe violations under Art. 83(5) GDPR, fines can reach up to €20 million or, for an undertaking, up to 4% of total global turnover of the preceding fiscal year (whichever is higher). Less severe violations under Art. 83(4) GDPR carry fines of up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover (whichever is higher).

A key point is that the term "undertaking" is equivalent to its meaning under Art. 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). According to European Court of Justice case law, an undertaking encompasses every entity engaged in economic activity regardless of legal status or financing method. This means a whole corporate group can be treated as one undertaking, allowing total worldwide annual turnover to be used for calculating fines. Member States may also impose other penalties (often criminal) for violations not covered by Art. 83, which must also be effective, proportionate, and deterrent.

Violations can be revealed through proactive inspections by data protection authorities, employee or customer complaints, company self-denunciation, or press investigations. The page references the Enforcement Tracker for an overview of reported EU fines. It also links to relevant GDPR articles (Art. 58, 70, 83, 84), recitals (148-152), and external resources including the Article 29 Working Party's WP 253 guidelines on administrative fines, European Commission guidance, the Handbook on European data protection law, and expert analyses from JIPITEC, IAPP, and A&L Goodbody.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
For especially severe violations, listed in Art. 83(5) GDPR, the fine framework can be up to 20 million euros, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of their total global turnover of the preceding fiscal year, whichever is higher.

--- SOURCE 4: What are the GDPR Fines? - GDPR.eu - GDPR compliance ---
URL: https://gdpr.eu/fines

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from GDPR.eu explains the structure and assessment of GDPR fines under the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation. The GDPR establishes two tiers of administrative fines under Article 83:

**Tier 1 (Less severe):** Fines up to €10 million or 2% of the firm's worldwide annual revenue from the preceding financial year (whichever is higher). These apply to violations involving controllers and processors (Articles 8, 11, 25-39, 42, 43), certification bodies (Articles 42-43), and monitoring bodies (Article 41).

**Tier 2 (More serious):** Fines up to €20 million or 4% of the firm's worldwide annual revenue (whichever is higher). These apply to violations of basic processing principles (Articles 5, 6, 9), conditions for consent (Article 7), data subjects' rights (Articles 12-22), transfers of data to third countries (Articles 44-49), violations of member state laws adopted under Chapter IX, and non-compliance with supervisory authority orders.

Fines are administered by data protection regulators in each EU country. Regulators use 10 criteria to determine penalties: gravity and nature of the infringement, intention (intentional vs. negligent), mitigation efforts, precautionary measures, history of prior infringements, cooperation with authorities, data category affected, notification of the breach, certification/compliance with codes of conduct, and other aggravating/mitigating factors. If multiple violations occur in the same processing operation, only the most severe penalty is applied.

The article also highlights that data controllers remain fully liable for infringements caused by third-party processors unless they can demonstrate they were "not in any way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage." Article 82 additionally grants data subjects the right to seek compensation for material or non-material damage from GDPR infringements.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The less severe infringements could result in a fine of up to €10 million, or 2% of the firm's worldwide annual revenue from the preceding financial year, whichever amount is higher."

--- SOURCE 5: How GDPR Fines are Calculated when an EU Company is Found in Breach | AGPLAW ---
URL: https://www.agplaw.com/how-gdpr-fines-are-calculated-when-an-eu-company-is-found-in-breach

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a legal insight article published by AGPLAW (A.G. Paphitis & Co. LLC), a law firm based in Limassol, Cyprus with offices in London and Dubai, titled "How GDPR Fines are Calculated when an EU Company is Found in Breach" (dated 25 August 2025). The article explains the legal framework and practical methodology for calculating GDPR administrative fines in the European Union.

Key content:
- Legal basis: Article 83 GDPR establishes fines that must be "effective, proportionate and dissuasive," with two tiers of maximum fines: up to €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover (lower tier, for record-keeping failures or inadequate security), and up to €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover (higher tier, for unlawful processing, violating data subjects' rights, or cross-border transfer breaches).
- Article 83(2) lists mandatory criteria for setting fines: nature/gravity/duration of infringement, intentional vs. negligent character, mitigation efforts, degree of responsibility, past infringements, cooperation with authorities, categories of personal data affected, how the breach became known, and other aggravating/mitigating factors.
- The EDPB Guidelines 04/2022 (adopted 2023) provide a standardized 5-step methodology: (1) identify the infringement and tier, (2) assess gravity with indicative ranges (low 0-10%, medium 10-20%, high 20-100% of maximum), (3) adjust for aggravating/mitigating factors, (4) check against legal maximums, and (5) ensure effectiveness, proportionality, and deterrence.
- Turnover matters because the 2% or 4% thresholds apply to the entire corporate group's total worldwide annual turnover, preventing multinationals from sheltering in small subsidiaries.
- Real-world enforcement examples: Amazon Europe received a record €746 million fine from Luxembourg's CNPD (2021) for unlawful targeted-advertising processing; British Airways was initially threatened with £183 million by the UK ICO but reduced to £20 million after mitigation and COVID-19 impact; H&M was fined €35.3 million in Germany for systematic employee privacy monitoring.
- SMEs and non-profits benefit from proportionality — regulators may issue reprimands or reduce fines for low turnover, but seriousness matters more than size.
- Beyond fines, authorities can impose corrective orders, suspend/restrict processing, require data deletion, and data subjects can seek compensation; reputational damage is often costlier than fines.
- The article concludes that proactive GDPR compliance (privacy governance, training, security, incident management) is essential.

Recommended contacts listed are Angelos G. Paphitis (Managing Partner) and Andrea Hadjigeorgiou (Partner, Regulatory & Advisory). The article includes a disclaimer that it is for general informational purposes only and not formal legal advice.
</summary>

Google's spokesperson stated the company was reviewing the decision and had already begun reevaluating and redesigning its data-sharing practices with Lumen, while emphasizing its "long commitment to transparency" in managing content removal requests.

In addition to the fine, Google was ordered to change its practices to comply with GDPR, delete personal data subject to erasure requests that were communicated to Lumen, and urge Lumen to cease using and erase any personal data communicated without a valid legal basis. **GDPR Basics:** GDPR fines are administrative penalties imposed on organizations that violate data protection principles. Organizations are categorized as Controllers (entities deciding why/how data is processed, held primarily accountable) or Processors (organizations handling data on behalf of controllers, including cloud hosts, payroll processors, and analytics services—who can also be fined). SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Executive Summary of the sixth edition of the GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report ("ET Report") published by the CMS Data Protection Group in 2025, covering GDPR fines from 2018 to the editorial deadline of 1 March 2025.

KEY STATISTICS:
• Total of 2,245 fines with complete information (+159 vs. 2024 report), with 2,560 cases recorded overall when including limited-information cases
• Total fines exceeded EUR 5 billion for the first time, reaching approximately EUR 5.65 billion (+EUR 1.17 billion vs. 2024 report)
• Average fine across all countries for 2018-2024: approximately EUR 2.36 million (+EUR 0.22 million vs. 2024 report)
• The highest GDPR fine to date is EUR 1.2 billion imposed by the Irish DPA in May 2023 for violations of international data transfer regulations (ETid-1844) — the first fine in the billions
• Top ten fines include the Luxembourg fine (EUR 746 million, July 2021), seven Irish fines ranging from EUR 225 million to EUR 405 million, and a Netherlands fine (EUR 290 million, July 2024)

MOST COMMON VIOLATIONS:
1. Insufficient legal basis for data processing (669 fines, average EUR 2.9 million)
2. Non-compliance with general data processing principles (644 fines, average EUR 3.8 million)
3. Insufficient technical and organisational measures for information security (418 fines, average EUR 2.0 million)
4. Insufficient fulfilment of data subjects' rights (ranks fourth)

COUNTRY INSIGHTS:
• Spain leads in number of fines for the sixth consecutive year, followed by Italy and Romania
• Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands lead in average fine amounts and total fine amounts by country (reflecting big tech sanctions since 2021)
• First fine recorded in Portugal (EUR 400,000 against a public hospital, July 2018)
• Enforcement ramped up between 2019 and mid-2021; sanctions against big tech in 2022 and the first billion-euro fine in 2023 pushed total above EUR 4 billion; authorities now appear to be in a "business as usual" period

SECTOR INSIGHTS:
• Media, telecoms and broadcasting is the most fined sector (70% of all fines on companies), highest sector exposure for the fourth consecutive year
• Employment sector ranks second; a record employment fine of EUR 290 million was imposed by the Dutch DPA
• Finance, insurance and consulting saw four fines exceeding EUR 1 million during the reporting period
• Healthcare continues to be fined most often for lack of technical and organisational measures
• Clearview AI received fines from DPAs in France, Germany, Greece, Italy and the UK accumulating to more than EUR 100 million
• In the individuals/private associations sector, over 60% of fines were imposed by the Spanish DPA; nearly half of all fines were based on illegal video surveillance

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• GDPR fines remain heavily influenced by national laws and official practices across EU member states, with significant variation in interpretation and enforcement
• Recent CJEU rulings (C-154/21, C-487/21, C-579/21) have clarified and tightened data subjects' right of access under Art. 15 GDPR
• The CJEU was active in 2023, including landmark decisions in C-683/21 and C-807/21 on conditions for imposing fines
• New technologies, particularly AI, are increasing the likelihood of "risky" processing and potential violations

**GDPR Enforcement Structure:** Each EU member state has an independent Data Protection Authority (DPA) that investigates, issues warnings, bans unlawful processing, and imposes fines. Violations follow a two-tiered system under Article 83:
- **Tier 1 (Article 83(4))**: Fines up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (whichever greater) for first-time or less severe infringements, including lack of parental consent for children's data, failure to implement data protection by design, not maintaining records, failing to report breaches within 72 hours, and not appointing a DPO.
- **Tier 2 (Article 83(5))**: Fines up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for serious/repeated violations, including unlawful processing, processing without valid legal basis, invalid consent, processing special category data, violating data subject rights, and unlawful cross-border transfers.

Under Article 82, data subjects can claim compensation for material and non-material damage (the ECJ confirmed no minimum threshold), opening the door for mass litigation. A €10,000 Article 82 claim was cited as an example.

**Recent Enforcement Statistics:** From May 2018 to August 2025, regulators issued over 2,800 GDPR fines totaling over €6.2 billion, with more than 60% (€3.8 billion) imposed since January 2023. Top enforcement countries by number of fines: Spain (107), Romania (61), Italy (41). Top by fine amounts: Ireland (€1.18 billion), Germany (€45.9 million), Italy (€32.4 million). The media/telecommunications/broadcasting sector is most exposed (4th consecutive year). Top five reasons for fines: insufficient security measures (86 fines), non-compliance with processing principles (74), insufficient legal basis (73), insufficient cooperation with authorities (25), and failure to fulfill data subject rights (18).

**Largest Recent Fines:** TikTok (€530M, Ireland, May 2025, insufficient legal basis), LinkedIn (€310M, Ireland, Oct 2024), Meta Platforms Ireland (€251M and €91M, Dec 2024 and Sep 2024, insufficient security measures), and Vodafone GmbH (€45M, Germany, 2025).

Example: Clearview AI was fined €30.5 million by the Dutch DPA in 2024 and over €100 million total across seven fines since 2020. US companies must comply if they offer goods/services to EU/EEA residents or monitor their behavior.

**US vs EU Enforcement Comparison:** EU takes a proactive, rights-based approach treating privacy as a fundamental human right, with fines based on global turnover percentage (up to 4%). The US is reactive/complaint-based consumer protection, with fines per violation or per consumer. EU enforcers are national DPAs coordinated by EDPB; US enforcers are FTC and state AGs. The EU AI Act came into force August 1, 2024, with full applicability by August 2, 2027. URL: https://gdpr-info.eu/issues/fines-penalties

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from gdpr-info.eu provides a comprehensive overview of fines and penalties under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). National authorities can or must assess fines for data protection violations, which are applied in addition to or instead of corrective powers such as orders to end violations, instructions to adjust data processing, and temporary or definitive limitations including bans on data processing. Processors may be subject to sanctions directly and/or in conjunction with the controller.

Fines must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive for each individual case. Authorities use a statutory catalogue of criteria when determining penalty levels, with aggravating factors including intentional infringement, failure to take mitigation measures for damage, and lack of collaboration with authorities. For especially severe violations under Art. 83(5) GDPR, fines can reach up to €20 million or, for an undertaking, up to 4% of total global turnover of the preceding fiscal year (whichever is higher). Less severe violations under Art. 83(4) GDPR carry fines of up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover (whichever is higher).

A key point is that the term "undertaking" is equivalent to its meaning under Art. 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). According to European Court of Justice case law, an undertaking encompasses every entity engaged in economic activity regardless of legal status or financing method. This means a whole corporate group can be treated as one undertaking, allowing total worldwide annual turnover to be used for calculating fines. Member States may also impose other penalties (often criminal) for violations not covered by Art. 83, which must also be effective, proportionate, and deterrent.

Violations can be revealed through proactive inspections by data protection authorities, employee or customer complaints, company self-denunciation, or press investigations. The page references the Enforcement Tracker for an overview of reported EU fines. It also links to relevant GDPR articles (Art. 58, 70, 83, 84), recitals (148-152), and external resources including the Article 29 Working Party's WP 253 guidelines on administrative fines, European Commission guidance, the Handbook on European data protection law, and expert analyses from JIPITEC, IAPP, and A&L Goodbody.
</summary>

This publication from Simmons & Simmons (dated 24 April 2026) analyzes the Irish Data Protection Commission's (DPC) €530 million fine against TikTok for unlawful international data transfers to China, one of the most important post-Schrems II enforcement actions to date.

**The Decision:** TikTok was fined €485 million for unlawful data transfers to China and €45 million for transparency failures (lack of specific information in its privacy notice about such transfers), and was ordered to suspend the relevant transfers to China. **Key Findings:**
- TikTok stored EEA user data on servers in Singapore, the US, and Malaysia, but allowed ByteDance personnel in China to access that data remotely for core functions (content delivery, security, R&D, analytics, payments, support, and content moderation), constituting a "transfer" to China.
- TikTok relied on SCCs plus supplementary measures and had prepared TRAs with a leading Chinese law firm. Its central legal argument was based on the territoriality principle in Chinese law — that Chinese authorities could not lawfully compel access to data only accessed remotely and not stored domestically.
- The DPC rejected this argument, finding that TikTok failed to adequately assess Chinese law and practices, failed to assess the level of protection afforded to EEA users' data, and failed to verify/guarantee essentially equivalent protection. The supplementary measures (including encryption and "Project Clover," TikTok's €12 billion data security initiative) were deemed general security measures that did not address the risk of Chinese authorities accessing data under problematic laws.
- TikTok could not rely on GDPR Article 49 derogations (contractual necessity, compelling legitimate interests) since those apply only to occasional/non-repetitive transfers, whereas TikTok's transfers were systematic, repetitive, and continuous.

**Fine Factors (Article 83(2) GDPR):** The DPC weighed the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement (systematic transfers over years affecting a very large number of EEA users, including sensitive data), the highly negligent character (despite TRAs being carried out), TikTok's high degree of responsibility given the scale of processing, and the categories of data involved (daily life, location, private communications, financial data, user-generated content potentially revealing special category data). **Key Takeaways for Organisations:**
1. TRAs must be substantively robust — merely preparing a TRA is insufficient; they must include detailed analysis of local law measured against the European Essential Guarantees and form a defensible basis for conclusions about essentially equivalent protection.
2. Supplementary measures must meaningfully address specific risks (such as government access under destination-country laws); general security measures alone are insufficient.
3. Article 83(2) factors provide a useful framework for organisations' own risk management — large-scale, long-term, core-service transfers involving sensitive data should receive enhanced scrutiny.

**Practical Steps:** Organisations should revisit TRAs for transfers to non-adequate countries, redesign supplementary measures to address government access risks (strong encryption with key separation, pseudonymisation, data minimisation), and adopt a risk-based approach. The article promotes CtrlTransfer, Simmons & Simmons' tool providing jurisdiction-specific analysis mapped against the European Essential Guarantees, TRA templates, and objective country risk scoring.

URL: https://europeanlawblog.eu/1xjmngct

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an opinion/analysis article from the European Law Blog (22 October 2024) by E J Kyriakides examining the Dutch DPA's enforcement decision against Uber and the legal relationship between GDPR Article 3 (territorial scope) and Chapter V (data transfer safeguards).

KEY ISSUE: The article addresses a lingering legal ambiguity: under what circumstances are GDPR data transfer safeguards required when a foreign firm is already subject to the GDPR. The classic transfer scenario involves a foreign company NOT governed by GDPR receiving EU data. But GDPR has extraterritorial effect (Article 3(2)), meaning foreign companies targeting the EU can also be subject to it.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:
- Article 3(1): Entities with an EU "establishment" are subject to GDPR
- Article 3(2): Entities without EU establishment are subject if they (a) offer goods/services to EU data subjects, or (b) monitor EU data subject behavior
- Chapter V (Articles 44-47) requires transfer safeguards including adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses (SCCs), binding corporate rules, etc.
- Under Schrems II, firms must independently assess whether transfer tools ensure "essentially equivalent" protection, potentially requiring supplementary measures
- Chapter V applies only to a "transfer" — a term the GDPR does not define

EDPB GUIDELINES (05/2021):
- Defined "transfer" as occurring when: (1) a controller/processor (exporter) is subject to GDPR; (2) the exporter discloses personal data to another controller/processor (importer); (3) the importer is in a third country (regardless of whether importer is subject to GDPR)
- Critically concluded NO transfer occurs when data is directly disclosed by an individual in the EU to a firm in a third country
- Companies subject to GDPR must still assess third country government access risks under other GDPR obligations (Articles 32, 33, 35)
- Not binding but highly authoritative

THE DUTCH DPA UBER DECISION (August 2024):
- Dutch DPA fined Uber €290 million — the largest fine ever from the Dutch DPA — for transferring French Uber drivers' data to the US without Chapter V safeguards
- Fine originated from an NGO (Ligue Des Droits De L'homme) complaint to the French CNIL
- Transfer involved Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) and Uber Technologies Inc (UTI, US parent)
- Uber relied on SCCs until August 2021, then determined SCCs were unnecessary because Article 3 directly applied to UTI's US processing; Uber had NO transfer mechanism from August 2021 until relying on the Data Privacy Framework in November 2023
- Two scenarios found to involve transfers: (1) EU drivers' data sent directly via Uber app to UTI for US storage; (2) data relating to GDPR rights requests where UBV and UTI collaborated
- Dutch DPA rejected Uber's defenses (direct collection, joint controllership, Article 49 derogations), holding transfers between joint controllers subject to GDPR in different countries are governed by Chapter V
- DPA departed from EDPB guidance by finding scenario one (direct collection from EU data subjects) constituted a "transfer," relying on the employment relationship between UBV and drivers and the asymmetry of power
- DPA argued Chapter V should be read broadly to counterbalance risks of diminished protection when data is processed abroad and difficulty enforcing against foreign entities
- DPA found Article 49(b-c) derogations inapplicable because transfers were ongoing, not "incidental" or "necessary"

ANALYSIS/NEXT STEPS:
- Uber is appealing; Dutch courts are likely to refer questions to the CJEU on the Article 3/Chapter V relationship
- The Dutch decision failed to articulate a clear legal standard for when direct collection by foreign providers subject to GDPR triggers Chapter V
- The article recommends that EU entities subject to GDPR under Article 3(2) in doubt apply Chapter V safeguards until the issue is settled
- European Commission has not yet issued SCCs for scenarios where the importer is subject to GDPR (current SCCs only apply when importer is NOT subject to GDPR)
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This GDPRhub page documents the Dutch Data Protection Authority's (AP - Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens) decision to fine Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI) and Uber B.V. (UBV) €290,000,000 for violating Article 44 GDPR. The decision was issued on 22 July 2024 and published on 25 August 2024.

**Key Facts:**
- Uber B.V. (UBV), based in the Netherlands, is part of the Uber group and serves as the EEA representative. Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI), based in San Francisco, US, is the parent company and joint controller for Uber drivers' personal data.
- Uber used a centralized IT infrastructure with servers located in the US. EEA-based drivers' personal data was processed in the US in two situations: (1) data collected through the driver app and stored on US-based servers (including account, location, criminal and health data, identity documents, and taxi licenses), and (2) when drivers exercised their GDPR rights, UTI was responsible for making data available to UBV.
- Uber previously used the European Commission's Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) but removed them from their joint controllership agreement effective 6 August 2021, arguing SCCs could not be used when processing falls directly under GDPR scope.
- The complaint originated from the French human rights group Ligue des droits de l'Homme on behalf of 172 Uber drivers, filed with CNIL (French DPA) on 12 June 2020, and forwarded to the Dutch AP due to Uber's main establishment in the Netherlands.

**Key Holdings:**
1. **Article 3 GDPR and Chapter V can apply simultaneously**: The DPA rejected Uber's argument that the territorial scope (Article 3 GDPR) and Chapter V (international transfers) were mutually exclusive. Chapter V is complementary to Article 3, preventing circumvention of EU data protection law. The DPA also rejected the WTO agreement argument.
2. **The processing constituted a transfer**: Applying the EDPB Guidelines 05/2021's three cumulative criteria, the DPA found all criteria met. The DPA rejected Uber's argument that drivers themselves were the exporters, finding instead that UBV was the exporter because drivers have little influence over processing purposes and means (terms are pre-drafted and non-negotiable).
3. **No valid transfer mechanism**: From 6 August 2021 to 27 November 2023, Uber had no lawful transfer mechanism. The DPA rejected Uber's interpretation of the European Commission's FAQ statements regarding SCCs.
4. **Article 49 GDPR exceptions did not apply**: The transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing (not incidental per Recital 111). The transfers were not "necessary" for contract performance per C-252/21 (Meta Platforms), as there were practicable, less intrusive alternatives (e.g., processing on EU servers).

**Fine details:** The DPA imposed a €290,000,000 administrative fine on the joint controllers due to the seriousness of the violation. This is the third fine the Dutch DPA has issued against Uber: €600,000 in 2018 for a data breach notification violation, €10 million in 2023 for a nontransparent privacy policy (which Uber has appealed), and this €290 million fine.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from GDPR.eu explains the structure and assessment of GDPR fines under the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation. The GDPR establishes two tiers of administrative fines under Article 83:

**Tier 1 (Less severe):** Fines up to €10 million or 2% of the firm's worldwide annual revenue from the preceding financial year (whichever is higher). These apply to violations involving controllers and processors (Articles 8, 11, 25-39, 42, 43), certification bodies (Articles 42-43), and monitoring bodies (Article 41).

Fines are administered by data protection regulators in each EU country. Regulators use 10 criteria to determine penalties: gravity and nature of the infringement, intention (intentional vs. negligent), mitigation efforts, precautionary measures, history of prior infringements, cooperation with authorities, data category affected, notification of the breach, certification/compliance with codes of conduct, and other aggravating/mitigating factors. If multiple violations occur in the same processing operation, only the most severe penalty is applied.

The article also highlights that data controllers remain fully liable for infringements caused by third-party processors unless they can demonstrate they were "not in any way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage." Article 82 additionally grants data subjects the right to seek compensation for material or non-material damage from GDPR infringements.

--- SOURCE 20: Fines / Penalties - General Data Protection Regulation ... ---
URL: https://gdpr-info.eu/issues/fines-penalties

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from gdpr-info.eu provides a comprehensive overview of fines and penalties under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). National authorities can or must assess fines for data protection violations, which are applied in addition to or instead of corrective powers such as orders to end violations, instructions to adjust data processing, and temporary or definitive limitations including bans on data processing. Processors may be subject to sanctions directly and/or in conjunction with the controller.

Fines must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive for each individual case. Authorities use a statutory catalogue of criteria when determining penalty levels, with aggravating factors including intentional infringement, failure to take mitigation measures for damage, and lack of collaboration with authorities. For especially severe violations under Art. 83(5) GDPR, fines can reach up to €20 million or, for an undertaking, up to 4% of total global turnover of the preceding fiscal year (whichever is higher). Less severe violations under Art. 83(4) GDPR carry fines of up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover (whichever is higher).

A key point is that the term "undertaking" is equivalent to its meaning under Art. 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). According to European Court of Justice case law, an undertaking encompasses every entity engaged in economic activity regardless of legal status or financing method. This means a whole corporate group can be treated as one undertaking, allowing total worldwide annual turnover to be used for calculating fines. Member States may also impose other penalties (often criminal) for violations not covered by Art. 83, which must also be effective, proportionate, and deterrent.

Violations can be revealed through proactive inspections by data protection authorities, employee or customer complaints, company self-denunciation, or press investigations. The page references the Enforcement Tracker for an overview of reported EU fines. It also links to relevant GDPR articles (Art. 58, 70, 83, 84), recitals (148-152), and external resources including the Article 29 Working Party's WP 253 guidelines on administrative fines, European Commission guidance, the Handbook on European data protection law, and expert analyses from JIPITEC, IAPP, and A&L Goodbody.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 24: The Italian DPA's Fine Against Intesa Sanpaolo: Lessons for Access Management and Data Breach Handling ---
URL: https://www.dsn-group.com/privacy-notes/the-italian-dpas-fine-against-intesa-sanpaolo-lessons-for-access-management-and-data-breach-handling-2959622

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 26 March 2026, the Italian data protection authority (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, "Garante") fined Intesa Sanpaolo S.p.A. €31,800,000 — one of the largest fines the Garante has ever imposed — over a data breach involving unauthorized access to client banking data.

**What Happened:** Between 21 February 2022 and 24 April 2024, a bank employee accessed the banking data of 3,573 clients without professional justification, carrying out more than 6,637 consultations covering account details, transaction histories, credit card movements, and investment data. Affected clients included national politicians, public figures, Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), and ordinary customers. The bank notified the Garante on 17 July 2024 describing the breach as involving just 9 individuals; the true scale only emerged after press reports in early October 2024 prompted the Garante to open its own investigation.

**Key GDPR Violations Found:**
1. **Inadequate Security Measures and Access Management:** The bank allowed operators to query the entire client base "in full circularity," meaning any employee could access any client's data across all branches. While the Garante acknowledged this as a legitimate business choice, it required proportionate counterbalancing controls, which were inadequate. Specifically: no prior authorization required for accessing out-of-portfolio data, alerts configured to allow repeated accesses to go undetected, no enhanced controls for high-risk clients (PEPs), and no automatic escalation mechanism to supervisors. The central issue was the systemic design of access controls that failed to detect suspicious behavior for over two years.
2. **Failure to Notify the Breach Properly:** The initial notification understated the scope, was incomplete as to the breach perimeter, and Article 33 GDPR deadlines were not met. The bank downgraded the breach from high to medium risk, focusing on the internal actor rather than probability and severity of impact on data subjects — incompatible with EDPB Guidelines 9/2022.
3. **Failure to Notify Data Subjects:** Because the bank concluded the breach posed no high risk, it did not notify affected clients directly under Article 34 GDPR. The Garante held that notification is a preventive protection measure and waiting for evidence of actual harm inverts that logic. The bank eventually notified clients only after the Garante issued a specific order in November 2024.

**Fine Calculation:** Aggravating factors included ~3,500 individuals involved, financial nature of data, breach duration of over two years, incomplete and delayed notifications, and prior enforcement decisions against the bank. Mitigating factors included cooperation with the authority and corrective action (enhanced ex-ante and ex-post monitoring, new escalation procedures, dynamic data masking).

**Key Takeaways:** A broad access model is not unlawful in itself but requires proportionate compensating controls; high-risk individuals need enhanced protections. When breach scope is unclear, use the phased notification mechanism under Article 33 GDPR but do not use uncertainty to understate known facts. Risk assessment must be objective and impact-focused. If any realistic possibility of high risk exists, notify data subjects without undue delay. The decision matters beyond banking — any organization giving staff broad access to personal data (HR systems, CRMs, healthcare records, customer portals) faces equivalent risks. The article also emphasizes involving the DPO at the design stage, during incidents, and before breach notifications go out, as a genuine risk management tool.
</summary>

URL: https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2024/11/insights-finance-dpc-irish-data-protection-commission-fines-linkedin

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On October 24, 2024, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced a EUR 310 million fine against LinkedIn Ireland for GDPR violations related to the platform's use of member personal data for behavioural analysis and targeted advertising. The DPC found that LinkedIn lacked a valid lawful basis for these processing activities. The inquiry stemmed from an August 2018 complaint filed with the French data protection regulator by the non-profit organization La Quadrature Du Net.

The DPC concluded that LinkedIn failed to meet the thresholds for each of the three lawful bases it sought to rely on under Article 6(1) of the GDPR:
- Consent (used for third-party data): The consent was not freely given, sufficiently informed, specific, and unambiguous.
- Legitimate interests (used for first-party data for behavioural analysis/targeted advertising and third-party data for analytics): The rights and freedoms of members outweighed LinkedIn's commercial interests.
- Contractual necessity: The DPC found LinkedIn could not rely on this basis either.

LinkedIn was also found to have breached GDPR transparency obligations by failing to provide clear information to users about its reliance on these lawful bases, and violated the principle of fairness in data processing (which requires data handling that is not detrimental, discriminatory, unexpected, or misleading).

The DPC has not yet released the full text of its decision. The fine was accompanied by a reprimand and an order for LinkedIn to bring its data processing into compliance within three months. It is unclear whether LinkedIn will appeal. The article notes that the decision may follow similar reasoning to the CJEU's ruling in Meta Platforms and Others v German Federal Cartel Office regarding lawful bases for personalized advertising on social networks. The article was authored by Goodwin attorneys Gretchen Scott and Curtis McCluskey.
</summary>

This article from Keepabl (a GDPR compliance software company) discusses the €91 million GDPR fine imposed by Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) on Meta on 27 September 2024, for storing user passwords in plain text. Background: On 21 March 2019, Meta admitted in a blog post that it had stored passwords for hundreds of millions of users (including Facebook and Instagram) in plain text, discovered during a routine security review in January 2019. Meta fixed the issue and proactively notified users and the public, with no evidence of external exposure or internal abuse.

The article explains best practices for password storage — namely salting and hashing passwords (as recommended by NIST, NCSC, and OWASP) — and explains how hashing is a one-way conversion of passwords into fixed-length unreadable formats, how brute force and rainbow table attacks work, and how salts (unique random strings per user) mitigate these attacks.

The author draws out 7 key lessons:
1. Check your organization doesn't store passwords in plain text.
2. Ensure good security and privacy policies, training, internal reviews, and documentation of non-conformity.
3. At minimum, salt and hash passwords.
4. Have good monitoring and logging on your tech stack to quickly ascertain whether unauthorized access occurred.
5. Have a robust risk assessment policy and procedure.
6. Don't rely on a single point of failure — use multiple layers of security (firewalls, least privilege access, MFA, monitoring, logging, alerting, salted/hashed passwords).
7. Document breaches thoroughly, including all information GDPR requires.

The article also analyzes whether notification was actually necessary under Art 33(1), since Meta's blog stated passwords were never exposed externally or improperly accessed, and the DPC agreed passwords were not made available to external parties. It discusses the DPC's reasoning on what constituted a personal data breach (internal unauthorized access to plain text passwords) and notes the full decision is not yet published.

A comparison is made to the 2019 Monzo case in the UK, where encrypted PINs were visible in plain text to some engineers but resulted in no fine or enforcement action from the UK ICO. Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands lead in average and total fine amounts (reflecting big tech sanctions since 2021). Spain leads in number of fines for the sixth consecutive year (nearly 1,000 fines), followed by Italy and Romania; top enforcement countries by number of fines: Spain (107), Romania (61), Italy (41); top by fine amounts: Ireland (€1.18 billion), Germany (€45.9 million), Italy (€32.4 million). Notably, only ~20 million euros (0.5%) of Ireland's fines have actually been collected, as most are under appeal — though companies typically implement corrective orders. [1][2][3][6][10]

**Most common violations (CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report, May 2025).** (1) Insufficient legal basis for data processing (669 fines, average €2.9 million); (2) Non-compliance with general data processing principles (644 fines, average €3.8 million); (3) Insufficient technical and organisational measures for information security (418 fines, average €2.0 million); (4) Insufficient fulfilment of data subjects' rights (ranks fourth). Scrut.io (top five reasons as of 2025): insufficient security measures (86 fines), non-compliance with processing principles (74), insufficient legal basis (73), insufficient cooperation with authorities (25), and failure to fulfill data subject rights (18). The media/telecommunications/broadcasting sector is the most fined (70% of all fines on companies), highest sector exposure for the fourth consecutive year. [2][3]

**Fine structure under Article 83 GDPR.** Two tiers: Tier 1 (Art. 83(4)) up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (whichever greater) for less severe infringements (e.g., lack of parental consent for children's data, failure to implement data protection by design, not maintaining records, failing to report breaches within 72 hours, not appointing a DPO). Tier 2 (Art. 83(5)) up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for serious/repeated violations (e.g., unlawful processing, processing without valid legal basis, invalid consent, processing special category data, violating data subject rights, unlawful cross-border transfers). The term "undertaking" is equivalent to its meaning under Art. 101 and 102 TFEU — a whole corporate group can be treated as one undertaking, allowing total worldwide annual turnover to be used for calculating fines. Under Article 82, data subjects can claim compensation for material and non-material damage (ECJ confirmed no minimum threshold), opening the door for mass litigation. [7][8][3][9][52]

**Fine-calculation criteria.** Authorities use a statutory catalogue: gravity and nature of the infringement, intention (intentional vs. negligent), mitigation efforts, precautionary/security measures, history of prior infringements (recidivism as a penalty multiplier), cooperation with authorities, data category affected, proactive notification of breach, certification/codes of conduct, and other aggravating/mitigating factors. If multiple violations are found in the same processing operation, only the most severe is penalized (Art. 83(3)). [8][52][9]

**Key structural/contextual developments.** (a) Big tech and social media companies continue to be primary targets: the Irish DPC fined LinkedIn €310 million and Meta €251 million in 2024, while the Dutch DPA fined Uber €290 million for third-country data transfers. (b) Enforcement expanded into other sectors: financial services (Spanish DPA fined a large bank €6.2 million for inadequate security; Italian Garante fined Intesa Sanpaolo €49.4M across two fines) and energy (Italian Garante fined Enel Energia €79.1 million; a utility provider €5 million for outdated customer data). (c) The dawn of personal liability: the Dutch DPA is investigating whether it can hold Clearview AI directors personally liable following a €30.5 million fine. (d) Clearview AI received fines from DPAs in France, Germany, Greece, Italy and the UK accumulating to more than €100 million (seven fines since 2020). (e) Growing AI enforcement — the EU AI Act came into force August 1, 2024, with full applicability for high-risk systems by August 2, 2026, with penalties up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover. (f) The EDPB's 2024–2027 strategy focuses on "reinforcing a common enforcement culture and effective cooperation"; its Coordinated Enforcement Framework ran a 2024 sweep on "right to access" and a 2025 sweep on "right to erasure." (g) Non-fine sanctions (corrective measures) and class/representative actions (under the Representative Actions Directive (EU) 2020/1828) are expected to increase. (h) Eight of the 10 highest GDPR fines were imposed on US-based companies (Meta, Amazon, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Uber), totaling €3.9 billion (nearly 63% of all fines). (i) Recent CJEU rulings (C-154/21, C-487/21, C-579/21) have clarified and tightened data subjects' right of access under Art. 15 GDPR; the CJEU was also active in 2023, including landmark decisions in C-683/21 and C-807/21 on conditions for imposing fines. [1][2][3][10][6][8][53]

**Notable annulments/procedural outcomes affecting the record.** The €746 million Amazon fine (Luxembourg CNPD, July 2021) was annulled by a Luxembourg court in March 2026 on procedural grounds (failure to assess fault and proportionality), though the underlying violations were upheld. The Italian Garante's €15 million OpenAI fine (Decision No. 755) was annulled by the Court of Rome on March 18, 2026 (Judgment no. 4153/2026); this was the only final GDPR enforcement action in Europe concerning the launch period of generative AI. Two of Europe's most high-profile GDPR fines were thus struck down within a single week in March 2026. [6][78][25][15]

## 2. PRIORITIZED COMPLIANCE GAPS (WITH CASES AND PREVENTIVE CONTROLS)

### GAP 1: UNLAWFUL CROSS-BORDER TRANSFERS OF PERSONAL DATA TO THIRD COUNTRIES WITHOUT APPROPRIATE SAFEGUARDS

This is the highest-risk category, producing the three largest fines of the 2023–2026 period (TikTok €530M, Uber €290M, and the record Meta €1.2B in May 2023) and the largest fine ever imposed (Meta €1.2B, Irish DPC, May 2023, for violation of regulations on international data transfers — the first fine in the billions). Cross-border transfers are the highest-risk scenario: three of the five largest fines of the period (TikTok, LinkedIn, Uber) involved data transfers outside the EU. The enforcement basis is Article 44–49 GDPR (Chapter V), requiring adequacy decisions, Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) with supplementary measures, Binding Corporate Rules, or valid Article 49 derogations; under Schrems II, firms must independently assess whether transfer tools ensure "essentially equivalent" protection. [2][4][5][3]

**Case 1: TikTok — €530 million (Irish DPC, 2 May 2025).** TikTok Technology Limited was fined a total of €530 million: €485 million for violating Article 46(1) GDPR (unlawful transfers of EEA user data to China) and €45 million for violating Article 13(1)(f) GDPR (transparency failure — the October 2021 EEA Privacy Policy failed to identify China and other third countries as transfer destinations; the policy did not name third countries or explain that processing included remote access to data stored in Singapore and the US by personnel in China; the updated December 2022 Privacy Policy was found compliant, limiting the transparency infringement period to 29 July 2020 – 1 December 2022). The DPC found TikTok failed to verify, guarantee and demonstrate that the supplementary measures and SCCs were effective to ensure EEA user data remotely accessed by staff in China was afforded a level of protection essentially equivalent to EU standards, given that Chinese laws (Anti-Terrorism Law, Counter-Espionage Law, Cybersecurity Law, and National Intelligence Law) do not offer the same level of protection. TikTok relied on SCCs plus supplementary measures and had prepared Transfer Risk Assessments (TRAs) with a leading Chinese law firm, arguing the territoriality principle in Chinese law meant Chinese authorities could not lawfully compel access to data only accessed remotely and not stored domestically; the DPC rejected this argument. Supplementary measures (including encryption and "Project Clover," TikTok's €12 billion data security initiative) were deemed general security measures that did not address the risk of Chinese authorities accessing data under problematic laws. TikTok could not rely on Article 49 derogations (contractual necessity, compelling legitimate interests) since those apply only to occasional/non-repetitive transfers, whereas TikTok's transfers were systematic, repetitive, and continuous. TikTok also initially told the DPC it did not store EEA user data on servers in China, but in April 2025 informed the DPC it had discovered in February 2025 that limited EEA user data had in fact been stored on servers in China, contrary to its earlier evidence — the DPC stated it received inaccurate information and is considering further action. Fine factors weighed under Article 83(2): systematic transfers over years affecting a very large number of EEA users (including sensitive data), highly negligent character despite TRAs being carried out, high degree of responsibility given the scale of processing, and categories of data involved (daily life, location, private communications, financial data, user-generated content potentially revealing special category data); adverse financial consequences were treated as a moderate mitigating factor. Corrective measures required TikTok to bring processing into compliance within six months, with further transfers to China suspended if not achieved. The decision is under appeal; implementation was stayed by an Irish High Court order of 14 November 2025. [11][12][13][14][15][16]

**Case 2: Uber — €290 million (Dutch DPA / Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, decision 22 July 2024, announced 26 August 2024).** The largest fine ever imposed by the Dutch DPA, against Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI, San Francisco) and Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) as joint controllers, for violating Article 44 GDPR. For a 27-month period (6 August 2021 to 27 November 2023), Uber transferred EEA-based drivers' personal data to the US without appropriate safeguards, after removing SCCs from its joint controllership agreement effective 6 August 2021 (arguing SCCs could not be used when processing falls directly under GDPR scope). Data transferred included account details, taxi licences, location data, photos, payment details, identity documents, and in some cases criminal and medical data, retained on US servers in Uber's centralized IT infrastructure. The Dutch DPA rejected Uber's arguments that Article 3 and Chapter V were mutually exclusive, that drivers themselves were the exporters, and that Article 49 derogations applied (transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing, not incidental; transfer was not "necessary" for contract performance per C-252/21 (Meta Platforms), as there were practicable, less intrusive alternatives such as processing on EU servers). The DPA found a "transfer" occurred both when EU drivers' data was sent directly via the Uber app to UTI for US storage and when data related to GDPR rights requests was shared between UBV and UTI, and held that Chapter V applies to transfers between joint controllers subject to GDPR in different countries. The investigation began after more than 170 French drivers complained to the Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH), which submitted a complaint to the French CNIL on 12 June 2020; the case was transferred to the Dutch AP under the one-stop-shop mechanism. The fine represented up to 4% of worldwide annual turnover (Uber reported approximately €34.5 billion in worldwide turnover in 2023). This was the third fine against Uber by the Dutch DPA (after €600,000 in 2018 for a data breach and €10 million in 2023 for a nontransparent privacy policy). Uber has indicated it intends to object/appeal, calling the decision "unjustified" and "completely unjustified"; the company now uses the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. Also of note: in late 2024, the Dutch DPA fined Uber €10,000,000 for incomplete disclosure on data retention of EU driver data. [16][17][18][19][20][49]

**Case 3 (context/record): Meta Platforms Ireland — €1.2 billion (Irish DPC, May 2023).** The largest GDPR fine to date, for transferring EU user data to the US without adequate safeguards following the invalidation of the EU-US Privacy Shield, failing to protect European users' data from US intelligence agencies. [2][5][3][8]

**Recommended preventive controls for cross-border transfers:**
- Maintain a complete data-flow map identifying all third-country transfers, including remote access by personnel located outside the EU (which constitutes a "transfer" even if data is not stored in the third country).
- Ensure a valid transfer mechanism is in place and continuously maintained (adequacy decision, SCCs, BCRs); do not assume Article 3 extraterritoriality or Article 49 derogations eliminate Chapter V obligations — regulators have rejected these arguments.
- Conduct substantively robust Transfer Risk Assessments (TRAs) that include detailed analysis of destination-country law measured against the European Essential Guarantees; merely preparing a TRA is insufficient — they must form a defensible basis for conclusions about essentially equivalent protection.
- Design supplementary measures that meaningfully address specific government-access risks (e.g., strong encryption with key separation, pseudonymisation, data minimisation); general security measures alone are insufficient.
- Keep fair processing information/privacy policies up to date and transparently name all third-country destinations and describe processing activities (Article 13(1)(f)).
- Revisit TRAs for transfers to non-adequate countries on a scheduled basis and whenever local law changes; apply Article 83(2) factors as a self-risk-management framework (large-scale, long-term, core-service transfers involving sensitive data should receive enhanced scrutiny).
- Regularly review intra-group transfer contracts and avoid gaps when legal frameworks change (e.g., Privacy Shield invalidation in 2020; removal of SCCs without replacement).

[11][12][14][16][18][19][20]

### GAP 2: NO VALID LAWFUL BASIS FOR ADVERTISING / BEHAVIOURAL PROFILING / TARGETED ADVERTISING (INVALID CONSENT, UNLAWFUL LEGITIMATE INTERESTS, IMPROPER CONTRACTUAL NECESSITY)

Insufficient legal basis for data processing is the most common GDPR violation (669 fines, average €2.9 million, per CMS). The largest 2023–2026 cases in this category: LinkedIn (€310M) and Google (€325M, ePrivacy-adjacent), with the earlier Meta €390M (2023) and Meta €405M (2022) as context. [2][3]

**Case 1: LinkedIn — €310 million (Irish DPC, 24 October 2024).** LinkedIn Ireland Unlimited Company was fined €310 million (approx. $335 million) for breaches of transparency, fairness and lawfulness in processing members' personal data for behavioural analysis and targeted advertising. The DPC found LinkedIn failed to meet the thresholds for each of the three lawful bases it sought to rely on under Article 6(1): (a) Consent (used for third-party data) was not freely given, sufficiently informed, specific, and unambiguous; (b) Legitimate interests (used for first-party data for behavioural analysis/targeted advertising and third-party data for analytics) were overridden by data subjects' fundamental rights and freedoms — the DPC considered the rights and freedoms of members outweighed LinkedIn's commercial interests; (c) Contractual necessity (Article 6(1)(b)) was rejected since behavioural analysis and advertising were not essential to the service's core functionality. LinkedIn was also found to have breached transparency obligations under Articles 13(1)(c) and 14(1)(c) (failure to provide clear information about the lawful bases relied upon) and the principle of fairness under Article 5(1)(a). The inquiry originated from an August 2018 complaint by the French non-profit La Quadrature Du Net to the French DPA; the DPC launched the inquiry as lead supervisory authority on 20 August 2018 and launched a fresh inquiry in July 2024. Corrective powers: reprimand under Article 58(2)(b), three administrative fines totaling €310 million under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83, and an order to bring processing into compliance within three months. Draft decision was submitted to the cooperation mechanism in July 2024 under Article 60; no objections were raised. Microsoft had previously flagged an expected charge of about $425 million for a potential fine related to its LinkedIn unit. The decision may follow similar reasoning to the CJEU's ruling in Meta Platforms and Others v German Federal Cartel Office regarding lawful bases for personalized advertising on social networks. [59][60][61][62][63][5][4]

**Case 2: Google — €325 million (CNIL, 1 September 2025).** The CNIL imposed a record €325 million fine — €200 million against Google LLC and €125 million against Google Ireland Limited — for two breaches: (1) displaying advertisements in the form of emails within Gmail users' "Promotions" and "Social" tabs without consent, violating Article L.34-5 of the French Postal and Electronic Communications Code (CPCE) (direct electronic marketing — the CNIL relied on the CJEU's 25 November 2021 judgment in Case C-102/20, StWL v. eprimo, confirming ads mimicking private communications constitute "direct marketing" requiring prior consent; even after Google changed the visuals in April 2023, the ads still could not be clearly distinguished from real emails); and (2) obtaining invalid consent for advertising cookies during Google account creation, violating Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act. The CNIL found that, until October 2023, consent was not freely given — it was harder to refuse personalised advertising cookies than to accept them (dark patterns/asymmetric design), and users were not informed that cookie placement was a condition of accessing Google's services. The cookie breach affected more than 74 million accounts; 53 million individuals in France illegally saw the involved advertisements. Google's prior fines (€100 million in 2020 and €150 million in 2021 for cookie violations) were treated as aggravating factors confirming recidivism. The one-stop-shop mechanism does not apply because cookie/electronic prospecting operations fall under the ePrivacy Directive, not the GDPR; territorial jurisdiction was based on Google France as an "establishment." Google LLC and Google Ireland Limited were found jointly responsible as joint controllers. Google must cease displaying Gmail ads without prior consent and ensure valid cookie consent during account creation within six months, with €100,000 daily penalties for noncompliance. The proceeding was triggered by a noyb complaint in August 2022. This is the first major enforcement action explicitly targeting interface design choices that manipulate user consent decisions. [41][42][43]

**Case 3 (context): Meta — €390 million (Irish DPC, January 2023).** For changing the legal basis from consent to contract for Facebook/Instagram advertising, "forcing" users to accept terms that required them to accept personalized adverts to use the platforms — deemed a GDPR violation. [5][8][10]

**Case 4 (context): Meta — €405 million (Irish DPC, September 2022).** For mishandling children's (ages 13–17) data on Instagram, including public display of contact info and public-by-default teen accounts, and inadequate age verification/parental controls. (TikTok was also fined €345 million by the Irish DPC in September 2023 for violations regarding children's accounts, age verification, and transparency.) [5][8][10][25]

**Recommended preventive controls for lawful basis:**
- Maintain a documented legal-basis register for every processing purpose; validate that the basis is genuine before launch (consent must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and revocable; legitimate interests require a documented balancing test (LIA); contractual necessity must be truly necessary to deliver the core service, not used for advertising).
- Do not use "consent or pay"/binary models without careful assessment (the European Commission fined Meta €200 million under the DMA in 2025 for its "Consent or Pay" model, finding the binary choice did not allow genuine user consent).
- Ensure no processing of third-party data for advertising occurs without a valid independent basis.
- Provide clear, transparent information about lawful bases in privacy notices (Articles 13/14), and avoid unexpected or detrimental processing (fairness principle).
- For profiling, conduct DPIAs and document the necessity/proportionality analysis; align with CJEU/EDPB guidance on personalized advertising lawful bases.

[59][60][61][62][41][42][43][11]

### GAP 3: INADEQUATE TECHNICAL AND ORGANISATIONAL MEASURES (TOMs) / INFORMATION SECURITY FAILURES LEADING TO DATA BREACHES

Insufficient technical and organisational measures for information security is the third most common violation (418 fines, average €2.0 million per CMS). The largest 2023–2026 cases: Meta €251M (2018 breach), Meta €91M (plaintext passwords), Vodafone €45M (Germany), Intesa Sanpaolo €31.8M (insider access), Enel Energia €79.1M (inadequate systems security enabling agent abuse). [2][3]

**Case 1: Meta Platforms Ireland — €251 million (Irish DPC, 17 December 2024).** Following two inquiries into a personal data breach reported in September 2018 that affected approximately 29 million Facebook accounts globally (approximately 3 million in the EU/EEA). The breach originated from exploitation of user tokens: a vulnerability created when a video upload function was deployed in July 2017; Facebook's 'View As' feature combined with the 'Happy Birthday Composer' facility could be exploited to generate fully permissioned user tokens granting full access to other users' profiles. Between 14–28 September 2018, unauthorized persons used scripts to exploit this vulnerability, gaining the ability to log on as account holders for ~29 million accounts. Affected data categories included user full names, email addresses, phone numbers, locations, places of work, dates of birth, religion, gender, timeline posts, group memberships, and children's personal data. The DPC found infringements of: Article 33(3) GDPR (failure to include all required information in the breach notification to the supervisory authority — fined €8 million); Article 33(5) GDPR (failure to adequately document personal data breaches — fined €3 million); Article 25(1) GDPR (failure to ensure data protection by design — fined €130 million); and Article 25(2) GDPR (failure to ensure only necessary personal data was processed by default — fined €110 million). The DPC issued reprimands and fines totaling €251 million. DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle: "This enforcement action highlights how the failure to build in data protection requirements throughout the design and development cycle can expose individuals to very serious risks and harms, including a risk to the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals... By allowing unauthorised exposure of profile information, the vulnerabilities behind this breach caused a grave risk of misuse of these types of data." The draft decision was submitted to the cooperation mechanism in September 2024; no objections were raised. [21][22][24][5][4][8][10]

**Case 2: Meta Platforms Ireland — €91 million (Irish DPC, 27 September 2024).** Meta inadvertently stored certain social media user passwords in "plaintext" (without cryptographic protection or encryption) on its internal systems, first reported to the DPC in March 2019 (discovered in a routine security review in January 2019; Meta fixed the issue and proactively notified users; the passwords were not made available to external parties). The DPC found four infringements: Article 33(1) (failure to notify the DPC of the personal data breach); Article 33(5) (failure to document the breaches); Article 5(1)(f) (failure to use appropriate technical/organisational measures to ensure security of passwords against unauthorised processing); and Article 32(1) (failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including ensuring ongoing confidentiality). The inquiry was launched in April 2019; the draft decision was submitted to other CSAs in June 2024 under Article 60; no objections were raised. Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle: "It is widely accepted that user passwords should not be stored in plaintext, considering the risks of abuse that arise from persons accessing such data. It must be borne in mind, that the passwords the subject of consideration in this case, are particularly sensitive, as they would enable access to users' social media accounts." [64][65][66][67][68][5][4]

**Case 3: Vodafone GmbH — €45 million (German BfDI, decision 10 March 2025, announced 3 June 2025).** Germany's Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) imposed two fines totaling €45 million: (1) €15 million for failure to adequately review and monitor partner agencies (local shops operating under the Vodafone brand using Vodafone-provided hardware/software as processors) working on its behalf, violating Article 28(1) GDPR — malicious employees in partner agencies committed fraud through fictitious contracts or contract changes at customers' expense; and (2) €30 million for security deficiencies in the authentication process for the combined use of the "MeinVodafone" online portal with the Vodafone Hotline, violating Article 32(1) GDPR — these authentication vulnerabilities enabled unauthorized third parties to access eSIM profiles. Additionally, the BfDI issued a warning for violating Article 32(1) GDPR regarding vulnerabilities in certain distribution systems. The BfDI also criticized overly broad access granted to partners into customer systems. Vodafone cooperated continuously and without restriction, disclosed self-incriminating circumstances, accepted the fines, and paid them in full to the federal treasury; it improved and in some cases completely replaced its processes and systems, revised its selection and auditing of partner agencies, separated from partners identified as having committed fraud, and donated €7 million to organizations promoting data protection, media competence, digital literacy, and anti-cyberbullying. The BfDI will conduct a follow-up audit. BfDI President Prof. Dr. Louisa Specht-Riemenschneider: "Data protection is often mistakenly seen as an obstacle to IT investments. In fact, the opposite is true: Without IT investments, there is the threat of security incidents and sanctions from data protection regulators. Therefore, my appeal: Investing instead of incurring risks!" [26][27][28][29][30]

**Case 4: Intesa Sanpaolo — €31.8 million (Italian Garante, Decision No. 208, issued 26 March 2026, published 30 March 2026).** The Garante fined Intesa Sanpaolo S.p.A. following a data breach notification submitted in July 2024 under Article 33. An employee made over 6,600 unauthorized consultations of the banking information of 3,573 customers (including account details, transaction histories, credit card movements, and investment data) between 21 February 2022 and 24 April 2024, without any legitimate business reason. Affected clients included national politicians, public figures, Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), and ordinary customers. The bank initially notified only nine data subjects; the true scale emerged only after press reports in early October 2024 prompted the Garante to open its own investigation. The Garante found: the bank's access control model allowed operators to query the entire client base "in full circularity" (any employee could access any client's data across all branches) without proportionate counterbalancing controls — no prior authorization required for accessing out-of-portfolio data, alerts configured to allow repeated accesses to go undetected, no enhanced controls for high-risk clients (PEPs), and no automatic escalation mechanism to supervisors; the illicit accesses went undetected for over two years; the bank failed to notify the breach properly (initial notification understated scope, was incomplete as to breach perimeter, and Article 33 deadlines were not met — the bank downgraded the breach from high to medium risk, focusing on the internal actor rather than probability and severity of impact on data subjects, incompatible with EDPB Guidelines 9/2022); and the bank failed to notify data subjects under Article 34 (concluding no high risk; the Garante held that notification is a preventive protection measure and waiting for evidence of actual harm inverts that logic — the bank eventually notified clients only after a Garante order in November 2024). Violations cited: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) (integrity and confidentiality), the accountability principle, and inadequate technical and organizational security measures. Aggravating factors: ~3,500 individuals involved, financial nature of data, breach duration of over two years, incomplete and delayed notifications, exposure of high-risk individuals, and prior enforcement decisions against the bank. Mitigating factors: cooperation and corrective action (enhanced ex-ante and ex-post monitoring, new escalation procedures, dynamic data masking). [54][55][56][57][58]

**Case 5: Enel Energia SpA — €79.1 million (Italian Garante, Decision No. 81 of 8 February 2024, announced 29 February 2024).** The highest fine ever issued by the Garante at the time, for deficiencies in the processing of customers' personal data for telemarketing purposes. The case stemmed from a Guardia di Finanza investigation that fined four companies €1.8 million and seized their databases; Enel Energia acquired 978 contracts from these four companies even though they were not part of its sales network. Subsequent inspections revealed serious security shortcomings in the information systems used for customer management and service activation: Enel failed to implement necessary measures to prevent unlawful activities by unauthorized agents who exploited easy access points ("front doors") into the company's information systems, fueling an illicit business for years through nuisance calls, service promotions, and contract signings with no real economic benefit to customers. At least 9,300 contracts were activated as a result. Violations cited: Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 24(1), 25, 28, and 32 GDPR. The fine of €79,107,101 was upheld by the Court of Rome in judgment No. 12783/2025 (Case No. 14089/2025) published 18 September 2025, dismissing the company's objection; an appeal is pending. [21][31][32][33][34][22][23]

**Case 6 (context): Clearview AI — €30.5 million (Dutch DPA, 3 September 2024).** For scraping facial images from the internet without consent to create an illegal biometric database from 30B+ scraped images; the Dutch DPA is investigating whether it can hold Clearview AI directors personally liable. [1][3][5][8]

**Recommended preventive controls for TOMs/security:**
- Implement encryption at rest and in transit as a baseline; never store passwords in plaintext — use salted hashing per NIST/NCSC/OWASP guidance (salt and hash passwords as a minimum).
- Design access controls on a need-to-know/least-privilege basis with role-based access control (RBAC), prior authorization for out-of-portfolio access, enhanced controls for high-risk individuals (PEPs), automatic escalation to supervisors, and real-time anomaly detection/behavioral analytics for suspicious queries. A broad access model is not unlawful in itself but requires proportionate compensating controls.
- Conduct thorough due diligence of third parties/processors before engagement, implement continuous monitoring of vendor activities (not "set and forget"), establish clear contracts with binding data processing agreements (DPAs), enforce strong IAM controls (MFA, strict identity verification, least privilege), and incorporate third-party scenarios into incident response planning.
- Build data protection into the design and development cycle (Article 25) — test features for token/permission vulnerabilities before deployment, and apply data minimization by default.
- Maintain robust monitoring, logging, and alerting to detect unauthorized access; layer security controls (firewalls, least privilege, MFA, monitoring, logging, alerting, salted/hashed passwords).
- Document breaches thoroughly, including all information GDPR requires; implement a risk assessment policy and procedure.

[26][27][28][29][30][54][55][56][57][64][65][66][67][68]
