### GAP 11: UNLAWFUL PROCESSING WITHOUT LEGAL BASIS / FAILURE TO NOTIFY DATA SUBJECTS OF CHANGES IN PROCESSING (INCLUDING "CONSENT OR PAY" MODELS AND CONSUMER DATA TRANSFERS BETWEEN AFFILIATES)

**Case: Intesa Sanpaolo — €17.6 million (Italian Garante, Decision imposed 12 March 2026).** The Garante fined Intesa Sanpaolo for unlawfully processing the data of approximately 2.4 million customers without an appropriate legal basis when it unilaterally transferred their accounts to its wholly-owned digital bank subsidiary, Isybank SpA. The bank selected customers based on criteria including age (under 65), digital channel familiarity, absence of investment products, and low financial balances. Customers were not properly informed — the notice was placed in the app's archive section without push notifications or text messages; the transfer forced changes including new IBANs, lack of physical branches, and mandatory mobile app access. The Garante emphasized that the processing was unlawful because customers could not have reasonably anticipated this activity given the circumstances and the information they were given. Together with the €31.8M fine, Intesa Sanpaolo faced just under €50 million in fines within less than a month. [55][58]

**Context: Meta — €200 million (European Commission, 2025, under the Digital Markets Act).** The Commission fined Meta for its "Consent or Pay" model (introduced November 2023), requiring Facebook and Instagram users to either consent to data use for targeted ads or pay for an ad-free experience; the binary choice did not allow genuine user consent. [11]

**Recommended preventive controls:**
- Identify and document a valid legal basis before any new processing, including consumer data transfers between affiliates/subsidiaries; consent must be genuine and informed.
- Provide clear, action-oriented customer notices for material changes in processing (e.g., account transfers, controller changes, new data uses); do not bury notices in app archives without push notifications or other direct communication.
- Conduct DPIAs for large-scale profiling and high-risk processing, including segmentation/profiling of customers for migration to new services.
- Avoid "consent or pay" binary models without a carefully assessed valid alternative; monitor DMA/GDPR developments on this issue.

[55][58][11]

### GAP 12: AI TRAINING / GENERATIVE AI PROCESSING WITHOUT VALID LEGAL BASIS, AGE VERIFICATION FAILURES, AND INADEQUATE INFORMATION (EMERGING ENFORCEMENT AREA)

**Case: OpenAI — €15 million (Italian Garante, December 2024; annulled March 2026).** The Garante's investigation (initiated March 2023 after a temporary ban of ChatGPT in Italy) found: (1) OpenAI processed personal data to train ChatGPT without an adequate legal basis (training on users' personal data without first identifying a proper legal basis prior to the service's public launch on 30 November 2022; DPIA and LIA produced in May and November 2023 were not decisive in establishing a prior legal basis); (2) failure to meet transparency/information obligations toward users; (3) inaccurate processing of personal information of data subjects; (4) absence of age verification mechanisms (risk of exposing children under 13 to inappropriate responses); and (5) failure to notify the Garante of the March 2023 data breach affecting 440 Italian users. The fine was €15 million (approx. 1.58% of OpenAI's 2023 worldwide turnover): €9M for unlawful data processing, €320K for failing to report the data breach, €5.68M for failing to comply with corrective measures imposed in 2023. OpenAI was ordered to run a six-month public education campaign. The Court of Rome annulled the decision on 18 March 2026; the Garante may appeal. Context: The EDPB established a dedicated ChatGPT Taskforce in April 2023; in February 2024 OpenAI established OpenAI Ireland Limited, triggering the one-stop-shop mechanism and freezing several national investigations. The EDPB issued Opinion 28/2024 (December 2024) after the Irish DPC secured Meta's agreement to pause LLM training (June 2024; resumed May 2025 under revised conditions) and took legal action against X to halt Grok training (permanent suspension September 2024). [74][75][76][77][78]

**Recommended preventive controls:**
- Establish and document a lawful basis for AI training before processing personal data (legal basis cannot be applied retrospectively); conduct DPIAs and LIAs before deployment, not after.
- Implement effective age verification mechanisms where services may be accessed by minors (especially under-13 users).
- Provide clear, accessible information to users about how their data (and non-user data) is used for AI training, including rights to object, rectify, and delete.
- Apply privacy-by-design principles to AI systems; monitor EDPB guidance and national DPA enforcement; prepare for EU AI Act high-risk requirements before August 2026 (penalties up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover).
- Notify data breaches promptly, including AI-related incidents.

[74][75][76][77][78][10]

### GAP 13: EXCESSIVE / INTRUSIVE EMPLOYEE MONITORING (WORKPLACE PRIVACY)

**Cases (context, mostly just outside the August 2023 cutoff but directly relevant to the period's enforcement patterns):**
- **Amazon France Logistique — €32 million (CNIL, 27 December 2023).** Intrusive employee monitoring system using scanners to track activity; the CNIL found the monitoring excessively intrusive and retained data beyond necessary periods. [5][8][10]
- **H&M — €35.25 million (Hamburg BfDI, October 2020).** Collected sensitive employee data (medical records, diagnoses) via surveillance; recorded return-to-work meetings accessible to 50+ managers, exposing private details like health and religious beliefs; a network drive was briefly accessible to all employees. [5][8][10][53]
- **Spain (2024):** AEPD enforcement targeted employment sectors for disproportionate surveillance; enforcement priorities include workplace technologies and school surveillance systems. [47][48]

**Recommended preventive controls:**
- Conduct a necessity and proportionality assessment before deploying any employee monitoring (including scanners, keystroke logging, video surveillance, and activity tracking); prefer less intrusive alternatives.
- Limit monitoring data collection to what is strictly necessary, implement access restrictions on sensitive employee data, and set clear retention limits.
- Consult works councils/employee representatives where required; provide transparency to employees about monitoring practices.
- Conduct DPIAs for high-risk workplace monitoring programs.

[5][8][10][47][48]

### GAP 14: EXCESSIVE DATA RETENTION / FAILURE TO DELETE DATA WHEN PURPOSE IS FULFILLED

**Cases:** Aena €10.04M (biometric data stored for up to two years, exceeding data minimization limits — violation of Article 5(1)(c)); Doctissimo €380,000 (France, 2023, retained health data too long); Verkkokauppa €856,000 (Finland, 2023, failed to limit data retention periods); Yoti Ltd €950,000 (Spain AEPD, 2026, including €250,000 for data retention beyond stated period); Uber €10M (Netherlands AP, 2024, incomplete disclosure on data retention of EU driver data). [70][49][46]

**Recommended preventive controls:**
- Implement and enforce data retention schedules for all data categories; automate deletion where possible; regularly purge data that has exceeded its retention period.
- Document retention periods in privacy notices and internal policies; ensure deletion extends to backups and third-party processors.
- Apply data minimization by default — collect only what is necessary for each purpose.

[70][49][46]

### GAP 15: PROCESSING WITHOUT CONSENT / TELEMARKETING AND DIRECT MARKETING ABUSES (ARTICLE 6, 7 + NATIONAL LAWS)

**Cases:**
- **Enel Energia €79.1M (Garante, February 2024):** Telemarketing data misuse, unauthorized CRM access sharing, unlawful acquisition of contracts from illicit sources, nuisance calls, and contracts with no real economic benefit to customers (at least 9,300 contracts activated). (See Gap 3, Case 5.) [21][31][32][33][34]
- **Enel Energia €563,050 (Garante, Decision No. 170, published 26 March 2026):** Following complaints/reports from 2024–2025 about repeated unsolicited promotional calls despite registration with the Public Register of Objections and denial of consent; the Garante found breaches of GDPR Articles 5, 6, 7, 24, and 28, inadequate opt-out mechanisms, and failure to demonstrate effective control over telemarketing partners. [35]
- **Context:** TIM €27.8M (2020, aggressive marketing with millions of unsolicited promotional calls); Intesa Sanpaolo €31.8M decision references prior enforcement decisions against the bank; Sky Italia €842,062 (2024, telemarketing violations). [8][10][57][53]

**Recommended preventive controls:**
- Implement and enforce consent management for all marketing channels; honor opt-out registers (e.g., Public Register of Objections) and withdrawal of consent.
- Vet and continuously monitor telemarketing partners/agents; validate the provenance of purchased contract lists (verify sellers are part of the legitimate sales network).
- Maintain audit trails of consent and marketing communications; implement robust opt-out mechanisms that are actually effective.
- Conduct regular compliance audits of telemarketing operations, including call monitoring and contract validation.

[21][31][32][33][35][34]

### GAP 16: PERSONAL LIABILITY AND EMERGING ENFORCEMENT TRENDS (AI, DMA, INDIVIDUAL ACCOUNTABILITY)

- **Clearview AI personal liability:** The Dutch DPA is investigating whether it can hold Clearview AI directors personally liable following the €30.5 million fine, signaling regulators' recognition of personal accountability as a compliance driver. [1]
- **EU AI Act:** Full enforcement for high-risk systems begins August 2, 2026, with penalties up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover (higher than GDPR's €20 million or 4%). [10]
- **DSA first fine:** €120 million against X (December 2025). [6]
- **GDPR Omnibus proposals (November 2025)** mark the end of technology-neutral data protection law. [10]
- **Compliance gaps statistics (2026 Kiteworks):** only 33% of organizations have complete knowledge of where their data is stored (2026 Thales Data Threat Report); human error remains the leading breach cause at 28%; 87% of organizations lack joint incident response playbooks with partners; 89% have never practiced incident response with third-party vendors; 84% have no automated kill switch for partner access; median third-party disclosure lag is 73 days (vs. GDPR's 72-hour requirement); Black Kite found 53.77% of ~200,000 monitored organizations had at least one critical vulnerability despite an average cyber grade of A (90.27). I am a data privacy analyst conducting privacy risk assessments. I need to identify and analyze GDPR enforcement cases with fines exceeding €10 million across a broad range of EU member states from the past 3 years (roughly August 2023 to August 2026, given today's date is August 23, 2026). Specifically, I need the following deliverables:

1. The top 10 most frequent GDPR violation types found in these high-value enforcement cases, with brief descriptions of each violation type (e.g., Articles 5, 6, 9, 32, 25, 83, etc., as applicable).

2. The standard penalty range typically imposed for each of these violation types, based on the enforcement actions observed in these cases.

3. Specific compliance gaps that enterprises should avoid, as revealed by these enforcement actions — i.e., the concrete failings or weaknesses that led to the fines, so organizations can proactively address them.

Key parameters for the research:
- Fine threshold: strictly cases with fines over €10 million.
- Geographic scope: broad range of EU member states (not limited to a single country; aim to capture enforcement across multiple DPAs, e.g., Ireland, Luxembourg, Italy, Spain, France, Germany, Netherlands, etc.).
- Timeframe: past 3 years from the current date (August 2026), so roughly mid-2023 through August 2026.
- Preferred sources: official GDPR enforcement case databases (e.g., GDPR Enforcement Tracker, European Data Protection Board, national DPA websites and press releases, and official regulatory decision documents), rather than secondary news aggregators or SEO-heavy blogs. If the query is in English, prioritize English-language sources, but include official DPA sources in their original language where necessary with translation notes.
- The output should be structured to support a privacy risk assessment, meaning practical, actionable insights on what enterprises should avoid.

args.research_topic: Compile a comprehensive factual database of all GDPR enforcement cases with fines exceeding 10 million euros (€10,000,000) issued by data protection authorities across multiple EU member states during the period from roughly August 2023 through August 2026 (past 3 years from August 2026). Geographic scope: a broad range of EU member states across multiple DPAs (national data protection authorities) — include at minimum Ireland (DPC), Luxembourg (CNPD), Italy (Garante), Spain (AEPD), France (CNIL), Germany (multiple Land DPAs and BfDI), Netherlands (AP), Belgium (GBA/APD), Portugal (CNPD), Austria (DSB), and any others with qualifying fines. For each qualifying case, report: (1) the company/entity fined, (2) the country and DPA issuing the fine, (3) the date of the decision, (4) the exact fine amount in euros, (5) the specific GDPR articles violated (e.g., Articles 5, 6, 9, 25, 32, 83, etc.), and (6) a one-to-two-sentence summary of the underlying facts. Priority sources: official GDPR enforcement case databases such as the GDPR Enforcement Tracker (enforcementtracker.com), the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) register of enforcement decisions, official national DPA websites and press releases, and official regulatory decision documents. Use English-language official sources where available; where the official DPA source is only available in its original language (e.g., Italian, French, Spanish, German, Dutch, Portuguese), include a translation note. Avoid secondary news aggregators and SEO-heavy blogs. This list is the factual backbone for a privacy risk assessment, so accuracy of fine amounts, dates, and article citations is critical. Include a brief note on any major cases near the €10 million threshold that did NOT qualify, to confirm the threshold is being applied strictly.

Identify and analyze the top 10 most frequently occurring GDPR violation types found in high-value GDPR enforcement cases with fines exceeding 10 million euros issued between roughly August 2023 and August 2026 across multiple EU member state data protection authorities (including but not limited to Ireland DPC, Luxembourg CNPD, Italy Garante, Spain AEPD, France CNIL, German DPAs, Netherlands AP, Belgium GBA). For each of the top 10 violation types, provide: (1) the relevant GDPR article(s) and a brief plain-language description of what the violation type covers (e.g., Article 5 principles relating to processing, Article 6 lawfulness of processing, Article 9 special categories of personal data, Article 25 data protection by design and by default, Article 32 security of processing, Article 44+ international data transfers, Article 83 conditions for imposing fines, etc.), and (2) the typical penalty range in euros observed for that violation type based on the actual high-value enforcement actions, noting how many of the qualifying cases involved that violation type. Base this analysis on official sources: the GDPR Enforcement Tracker database, the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) decisions and enforcement register, and official national DPA press releases and decision documents. Note where multiple articles were cited together in the same enforcement action (violations are frequently bundled), and indicate which violation type tended to drive the highest penalties. Structure the output as a ranked list from most frequent to least frequent violation type, each with description and observed penalty range, suitable for use in a privacy risk assessment.

Analyze the concrete compliance gaps and underlying organizational failings that led to GDPR enforcement fines exceeding 10 million euros issued by EU data protection authorities between roughly August 2023 and August 2026 (across Ireland DPC, Luxembourg CNPD, Italy Garante, Spain AEPD, France CNIL, German DPAs, Netherlands AP, Belgium GBA, and other EU DPAs). The goal is to produce actionable, practical insights for enterprise privacy risk assessments — specifically, what concrete weaknesses, behaviors, and missing controls did regulators cite as the reasons for the fines, and what should enterprises proactively avoid. For each compliance gap identified, report: (1) the gap or failing in concrete terms (e.g., failure to maintain a lawful basis for advertising/targeting, insufficient technical and organizational measures leading to data breaches, illegal transfer of personal data to third countries like the United States without appropriate safeguards, excessive data retention, failure to honor data subject rights like erasure requests, profiling without proper notice, dark patterns, inadequate privacy impact assessments, lack of data protection by design and by default, governance and accountability failures including ineffective data protection officer roles, failure to cooperate with the supervisory authority, etc.), (2) the specific enforcement case or cases that illustrate the gap (company name, DPA, fine amount, year), and (3) a recommended preventive control or practice enterprises should implement to avoid the same failure. Base the analysis on official sources: GDPR Enforcement Tracker, European Data Protection Board (EDPB) decisions and guidance, and official national DPA press releases and decision documents. Prioritize the gaps that are most frequently cited or that produced the largest fines, and organize the output as a prioritized list of compliance gaps with concrete enterprise recommendations, suitable for direct use in a privacy risk assessment report.

# GDPR Enforcement Cases with Fines Exceeding €10 Million (August 2023 – August 2026)

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

The researcher performed five batches of web searches using the Tavily search tool:

**Batch 1 (Overview/ranking queries):**
- "GDPR Enforcement Tracker top 10 highest fines 2024 2025 list"
- "GDPR fines over 10 million euros 2024 2025 data protection authority list"
- "EDPB GDPR enforcement decisions fines over 10 million 2023 2024 2025"

**Batch 2 (Case verification queries):**
- "GDPR Enforcement Tracker cases 2024 2025 fines over 10 million euros Italy Spain Germany Luxembourg list"
- "Vodafone Germany 45 million euro GDPR fine 2025 articles Hamburg DPA"
- "Shein CNIL 150 million euro fine GDPR 2025 cookie consent"
- "TikTok 530 million euro GDPR fine Ireland DPC May 2025 articles 5 6 44 violation"

**Batch 3 (DPA-by-DPA queries):**
- "Luxembourg CNPD GDPR fine 2024 2025 over 10 million euros"
- "Italy Garante GDPR fine 2024 2025 over 10 million euros telemarketing Enel"
- "Spain AEPD GDPR fine over 10 million euros 2024 2025"
- "Netherlands Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens Uber 290 million Clearview 30.5 million GDPR fine"
- "Germany Hamburg Berlin Bavaria GDPR fine over 10 million euros 2024 2025"

**Batch 4 (Additional DPA queries):**
- "Luxembourg CNPD fine 2024 2025 Microsoft OR fines enforcement"
- "Italy Garante fine 2024 2025 over 10 million euro decision"
- "Belgium GBA APD fine 2024 2025 GDPR large fine"
- "Austria DSB Portugal CNPD fine over 10 million 2024 2025"
- "Germany data protection authority Berlin Hamburg fine 2024 2025 large 10 million"
- "LinkedIn 310 million GDPR fine DPC articles 5 6 13 Ireland 2024"

**Batch 5 (Borderline/borderline case queries):**
- "Intesa Sanpaolo 31.8 million euro GDPR fine 2025 Italy Garante articles breach"
- "Isybank 17.6 million GDPR fine Italy Garante profiling 2025"
- "Google 325 million euro CNIL fine 2025 Gmail cookies articles 82 French law"
- "TikTok 345 million GDPR fine Ireland September 2023 articles 5 6 children data"
- "Meta 91 million password GDPR fine Ireland 2024 articles 32 5"
- "GDPR fine 10 million threshold borderline 2024 2025 cases near threshold Ireland Luxembourg Spain France"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### A. Macro-Level GDPR Enforcement Statistics (Context for the Period)

**Cumulative statistics (CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2026, 7th edition, cut-off date 1 March 2026):** A total of 2,685 fines have been recorded in the CMS Enforcement Tracker database (3,062 if fines with limited information on amount or date are counted), an increase of +440 compared to the GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2025. The total sum of fines amounts to approximately EUR 6.11 billion, an increase of +487.6 million compared to the previous report. The average fine across all countries for the 2018–2026 reporting period was EUR 2,277,122. [1]

**DLA Piper GDPR Fines and Data Breach Survey (January 2026, 8th edition):** European supervisory authorities issued approximately EUR 1.2 billion (USD 1.42 billion/GBP 1.06 billion) in GDPR fines during 2025, closely matching the 2024 total and reversing the previous year's downward trend. The aggregate total of fines since the GDPR took effect on 25 May 2018 through 10 January 2026 now stands at EUR 7.1 billion (USD 8.4 billion/GBP 6.2 billion). There was a 22% annual increase in notified personal data breaches, averaging 443 notifications per day (up from 363) — the first time the daily average breach notification count has exceeded 400 since 2018. Ireland continues to lead enforcement, with the Irish DPC having issued EUR 4.04 billion (USD 4.77 billion/GBP 3.56 billion) in aggregate fines since May 2018. The largest fine ever imposed under the GDPR remains the EUR 1.2 billion penalty against Meta Platforms Ireland Limited in 2023. [97]

**DLA Piper GDPR Fines and Data Breach Survey (January 2025, 7th edition):** Data protection authorities in Europe imposed fines amounting to EUR 1.2 billion (USD 1.26 billion/GBP 996 million) in 2024, a 33% decrease from the previous year due to the absence of a record-breaking fine (the EUR 1.2 billion Meta penalty in 2023 skewed the prior year's figures). This was the first year-on-year decline in fines. Total fines since GDPR application in 2018 stood at EUR 5.88 billion. Ireland's DPC remained the dominant enforcer with EUR 3.5 billion in fines since May 2018 — more than four times the second-placed Luxembourg DPA (EUR 746.38 million). Big tech and social media companies continued to be primary targets: the Irish DPC fined LinkedIn EUR 310 million and Meta EUR 251 million in 2024, while the Dutch DPA fined a ride-hailing app EUR 290 million for third-country data transfers. Enforcement expanded into other sectors, including financial services (Spanish DPA fined a large bank EUR 6.2 million for inadequate security) and energy (Italian DPA fined a utility provider EUR 5 million for outdated customer data). Data breach notifications averaged 363 per day (up from 335), with the Netherlands (33,471), Germany (27,829), and Poland (14,286) remaining the top three countries for total breaches notified since May 2018. [6]

**CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2025 (6th edition, cut-off 1 March 2025):** Total of 2,245 fines with complete information (+159 vs. 2024 report), with 2,560 cases recorded overall when including limited-information cases. Total fines exceeded EUR 5 billion for the first time, reaching approximately EUR 5.65 billion (+EUR 1.17 billion vs. 2024 report). The average fine across all countries for 2018–2024 was approximately EUR 2.36 million. The highest GDPR fine to date was EUR 1.2 billion imposed by the Irish DPA in May 2023 (ETid-1844) — the first fine in the billions. Most common violations: (1) insufficient legal basis for data processing (669 fines, average EUR 2.9 million); (2) non-compliance with general data processing principles (644 fines, average EUR 3.8 million); (3) insufficient technical and organisational measures for information security (418 fines, average EUR 2.0 million); (4) insufficient fulfilment of data subjects' rights. Spain led in number of fines for the sixth consecutive year, followed by Italy and Romania; Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands led in average fine amounts. Clearview AI received fines from DPAs in France, Germany, Greece, Italy and the UK accumulating to more than EUR 100 million. [8]

**Additional statistics:** From May 2018 to August 2025, regulators issued over 2,800 GDPR fines totaling over €6.2 billion, with more than 60% (over €3.8 billion) imposed since January 2023. Top enforcement countries by number of fines: Spain (107), Romania (61), Italy (41). Top by fine amounts: Ireland (€1.18 billion), Germany (€45.9 million), Italy (€32.4 million). Eight of the 10 highest GDPR fines were imposed on US-based companies (Meta, Amazon, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Uber), totaling €3.9 billion (nearly 63% of all fines). [2] As of October 2025, total GDPR fines reached €6.7 billion; Spain issued the most fines in the EU (1,021 fines totaling ~€120,750,450 as of September 2025), while Ireland issued the largest fines (~€3.5 billion since May 2018). [9]

**GDPR fine tiers (Article 83):** Tier 1 (Article 83(4)): fines up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (whichever greater) for procedural violations. Tier 2 (Article 83(5)): fines up to €20 million or 4% of total global turnover of the preceding fiscal year (whichever higher) for serious violations including unlawful processing, invalid consent, processing special category data, violating data subject rights, and unlawful cross-border transfers. The term "undertaking" is equivalent to its meaning under Articles 101 and 102 TFEU — a whole corporate group can be treated as one undertaking, allowing total worldwide annual turnover to be used for calculating fines. [31][33][34][5]

---

### B. QUALIFYING CASES — Fines Exceeding €10 Million Issued August 2023 – August 2026

The following 15 cases exceed the €10 million threshold and were issued within the August 2023 – August 2026 window. Cases are organized by DPA.

---

#### IRELAND — DATA PROTECTION COMMISSION (DPC)

**Case 1: TikTok Technology Limited — €530 million (2 May 2025)**

- **Company/Entity:** TikTok Technology Limited
- **Country/DPA:** Ireland / Data Protection Commission (DPC) — as Lead Supervisory Authority for TikTok under the one-stop-shop mechanism
- **Date:** 2 May 2025 (final decision announced; decision made by Commissioners for Data Protection Dr Des Hogan and Mr Dale Sunderland)
- **Fine amount:** €530 million total — €485 million for the Article 46(1) GDPR infringement and €45 million for the Article 13(1)(f) GDPR transparency infringement
- **GDPR articles violated:** Article 46(1) GDPR (international transfers — failure to verify, guarantee and demonstrate that supplementary measures and Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) were effective to ensure essentially equivalent protection for EEA user data transferred via remote access to China) and Article 13(1)(f) GDPR (transparency — failure to inform data subjects of third-country transfers)
- **Facts:** The DPC's inquiry (launched September 2021) examined TikTok's transfers of EEA user personal data to China. TikTok allowed remote access to EEA user data for approximately 1.5 years, resulting in data being processed on devices in China. The DPC found that TikTok's own assessment of Chinese law (including the Anti-Terrorism Law, Counter-Espionage Law, Cybersecurity Law, and National Intelligence Law) identified aspects that preclude a finding of essential equivalence to EU law; the Transfer Risk Assessment (TRA) was high-level only and failed to consider specific circumstances of remote access. The transparency infringement related to TikTok's October 2021 EEA Privacy Policy, which failed to name third countries (including China) to which data was transferred and failed to explain that processing included remote access to data stored in Singapore and the U.S. by personnel based in China; the infringement period ran from 29 July 2020 to 1 December 2022, and TikTok's December 2022 Privacy Policy was deemed compliant. Notably, throughout the inquiry TikTok claimed it did not store EEA user data on servers in China, but in April 2025 it disclosed that limited EEA user data had in fact been stored on servers in China (discovered in February 2025) — the DPC stated it is considering further regulatory action on this issue. [29][30][28][27]
- **Orders:** TikTok was ordered to bring its processing into compliance within 6 months; if not compliant, transfers of EEA data to China would be suspended. The DPC submitted its draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism on 21 February 2025 under Article 60; no objections were raised. TikTok disagrees with the decision and plans to appeal in full, citing "Project Clover," a €12 billion data security initiative involving independent monitoring by NCC Group, European data enclaves, additional security barriers, and privacy-enhancing technologies. [29][28]
- **Significance:** This is the first international transfer enforcement relating to China and the first concerning remote access rather than data storage. [28]

**Case 2: LinkedIn Ireland Unlimited Company — €310 million (24 October 2024)**

- **Company/Entity:** LinkedIn Ireland Unlimited Company
- **Country/DPA:** Ireland / Data Protection Commission (DPC)
- **Date:** 24 October 2024 (final decision announced; notified to LinkedIn on 22 October 2024; decision made by Commissioners Dr Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland)
- **Fine amount:** €310 million (approximately $335 million) — three administrative fines totalling €310 million
- **GDPR articles violated:** Article 6(1)(a) GDPR (invalid consent — not freely given, sufficiently informed, specific, or unambiguous, used for third-party data for behavioral analysis and targeted advertising); Article 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interests — the rights and freedoms of members outweighed LinkedIn's commercial interests); Article 6(1)(b) GDPR (contractual necessity not valid for behavioural analysis); Articles 13(1)(c) and 14(1)(c) GDPR (inadequate information provided about legal bases); Article 5(1)(a) GDPR (violation of the fairness principle)
- **Facts:** The inquiry examined LinkedIn's processing of personal data of its members for the purposes of behavioural analysis and targeted advertising. The DPC found LinkedIn relied on invalid consent for third-party data, unlawfully relied on legitimate interests and contractual necessity for first-party data, failed to provide clear/transparent information about these legal bases, and breached the fairness principle. The inquiry began on 20 August 2018, originating from a complaint made by the French non-profit organisation La Quadrature Du Net to the French Data Protection Authority, which was transferred to the DPC as lead supervisory authority for LinkedIn. [72][69][71][70]
- **Orders:** A reprimand (Article 58(2)(b)), an order for LinkedIn to bring its processing into compliance (within three months), and administrative fines totalling €310 million (Articles 58(2)(i) and 83). The DPC submitted a draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism in July 2024 under Article 60; no objections were raised by peer EU/EEA supervisory authorities. [72]
- **Quote (DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle):** "The lawfulness of processing is a fundamental aspect of data protection law and the processing of personal data without an appropriate legal basis is a clear and serious violation of a data subject's fundamental right to data protection." [72][70]

**Case 3: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited — €251 million (17 December 2024)**

- **Company/Entity:** Meta Platforms Ireland Limited
- **Country/DPA:** Ireland / Data Protection Commission (DPC)
- **Date:** 17 December 2024
- **Fine amount:** EUR 251 million — €11 million for Article 33 GDPR violations and €240 million for Article 25 GDPR violations. (One breakdown reported: Art. 25(1) €130M, Art. 25(2) €110M, Art. 33(3) €8M, Art. 33(5) €3M.) [54]
- **GDPR articles violated:** Article 33 GDPR (incomplete data breach notifications) and Article 25 GDPR (failure to ensure data protection principles were built into the design of processing systems and failure to ensure that only necessary personal data is processed by default)
- **Facts:** The fine relates to a 2018 data breach affecting 29 million Facebook accounts worldwide, including 3 million in the EU/EEA, resulting from exploitation of user tokens ("View As" feature) by unauthorized third parties. The breach compromised names, email addresses, phone numbers, and children's data. The DPC found two categories of violations: Art. 33 GDPR for incomplete data breach notifications, and Art. 25 GDPR for failure to ensure data protection by design and by default. [13]
- **Case rank:** ETid-2484; ranks #8 of 369 in the Media, Telecoms and Broadcasting sector, #8 of 37 fines in Ireland, and #9 of 3,063 total fines tracked. [13]

**Case 4: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited — €91 million (27 September 2024)**

- **Company/Entity:** Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL)
- **Country/DPA:** Ireland / Data Protection Commission (DPC)
- **Date:** 27 September 2024 (final decision announced; notified to MPIL on 26 September 2024; decision made by Commissioners Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland)
- **Fine amount:** €91 million
- **GDPR articles violated:** Article 33(1) GDPR (failure to notify the DPC of the personal data breach); Article 33(5) GDPR (failure to document the breaches); Article 5(1)(f) GDPR (failure to use appropriate technical/organisational measures to ensure security of passwords against unauthorised processing); Article 32(1) GDPR (failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk)
- **Facts:** The inquiry was launched in April 2019 after MPIL notified the DPC in March 2019 that it had inadvertently stored certain social media user passwords in 'plaintext' (without cryptographic protection or encryption) on its internal systems. The passwords were not made available to external parties, and no signs of internal abuse were found. The DPC submitted a draft decision to other Concerned Supervisory Authorities across the EU/EEA in June 2024 under Article 60; no objections were raised. The decision included a reprimand (Article 58(2)(b)) and the €91 million fine (Articles 58(2)(i) and 83). [95][96][92]
- **Quote (DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle):** "It is widely accepted that user passwords should not be stored in plaintext, considering the risks of abuse that arise from persons accessing such data. It must be borne in mind, that the passwords the subject of consideration in this case, are particularly sensitive, as they would enable access to users' social media accounts." [95][96]

**Case 5: TikTok Technology Limited — €345 million (1 September 2023)**

- **Company/Entity:** TikTok Technology Limited
- **Country/DPA:** Ireland / Data Protection Commission (DPC)
- **Date:** 1 September 2023 (decision; announced 15 September 2023) [5][87]
- **Fine amount:** €345 million
- **GDPR articles violated:** Article 5(1)(a) GDPR (fairness — dark patterns nudging child users into more privacy-intrusive settings; added after EDPB binding decision following Berlin DPA objection); Articles 5(1)(c) and 5(1)(f) GDPR (data minimization; security/integrity); Articles 12(1) and 13(1)(e) GDPR (notice requirements must be concise and easily accessible); Articles 24(1), 25(1), and 25(2) GDPR (data protection by design and by default, including data minimization)
- **Facts:** The DPC's investigation covered TikTok's processing of children's data between 31 July 2020 and 31 December 2020. Findings: (1) child user profiles (ages 13–16) were set to public-by-default, violating data minimization, data protection by design and by default, and data controller obligations without adequately considering privacy risks to children; (2) the "Family Pairing" feature allowed non-child users who could not be verified as parents or guardians to pair with child accounts and send direct messages, posing "severe possible risks to child users" and violating the security principle; (3) TikTok failed to provide adequate, clear information to child users (ambiguous wording like "public," "anyone," "everyone"), infringing transparency rules in Articles 12 and 13; (4) TikTok used "dark patterns" to nudge child users into selecting more privacy-intrusive settings, infringing the fairness principle (Article 5(1)(a)) — this last finding followed an objection raised by the Berlin DPA and upheld by the EDPB, and was not included in the DPC's original findings. The decision reflected a binding decision of the EDPB pursuant to Article 65 GDPR. [87][89][90][91]
- **Orders:** Reprimand and an order to bring processing into compliance within three months. TikTok said it "respectfully disagrees" with the decision, particularly the level of the fine, noting the criticized features dated back three years and had been addressed before the investigation began (e.g., setting all under-16 accounts to private by default in January 2021). [90][91]
- **Quote (Data Protection Commissioner Helen Dixon):** The public-by-default setting was "precisely at the hands of TikTok because of the way they designed the platform, and we say that infringed the data protection by design and by the default requirements of the GDPR." [91]

#### NETHERLANDS — AUTORITEIT PERSOONSGEGEVENS (AP)

**Case 6: Uber Technologies Inc. and Uber B.V. — €290 million (22 July 2024 / published 26 August 2024)**

- **Company/Entity:** Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI, U.S.-based parent, San Francisco) and Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands-based EEA entity) — found to be joint controllers for the personal data of EEA drivers
- **Country/DPA:** Netherlands / Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP, Dutch DPA) — lead authority under one-stop-shop rules since Uber's European entity is in Amsterdam
- **Date:** Decision issued 22 July 2024; published 25/26 August 2024
- **Fine amount:** €290,000,000 (the largest single AP sanction; up to 4% of worldwide annual turnover — Uber reported approximately €34.5 billion in worldwide turnover in 2023)
- **GDPR articles violated:** Article 44 GDPR (and Chapter V GDPR) — transfers of personal data to the United States without appropriate safeguards
- **Facts:** Between 6 August 2021 and 27 November 2023, Uber unlawfully transferred the personal data of European Union drivers to the United States without valid Article 46 transfer mechanisms. Uber collected and retained sensitive information of European drivers on US servers — account details, taxi licences, location data, photos, payment details, identity documents, and in some cases criminal and medical (health) data. Uber previously used Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) but removed them from its joint controllership agreement effective 6 August 2021, arguing SCCs could not be used when processing falls directly under GDPR scope. The AP rejected all of Uber's defenses: (1) Chapter V is complementary to Article 3 GDPR (not mutually exclusive); (2) UBV was the "exporter" as it established contractual relationships with EEA drivers and defined data collection terms; (3) the transfers were systematic, repetitive, and continuous (not "incidental" under Article 49), and not objectively "necessary" since less intrusive alternatives (such as EU-based servers) were available (per C-252/21, Meta Platforms). Specific examples: driver app data from EEA drivers (including identity documents, health data, criminal records) stored directly on US servers; and structural data exchange between UBV and UTI when EEA drivers exercised GDPR rights requests. The infringement's severity was classified as "high" based on: systematic nature and over two-year duration; large scale (many EU drivers affected); and sensitivity of data transferred (special category data such as health and criminal records). The fine was imposed jointly on both entities. [47][48][49][46]
- **Origin:** The complaint originated from the French human rights group Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH) on behalf of 172 (more than 170) French Uber drivers, filed with the French DPA (CNIL) on 12 June 2020, and forwarded to the Dutch AP. [47][48][49]
- **Appeal:** Uber has indicated its intent to object to the fine. Uber has since ended the violation and now uses the successor to the Privacy Shield (EU-US Data Privacy Framework). [48]
- **Prior Uber fines by AP:** €600,000 in 2018 for a data breach notification violation, and €10 million in 2023 for a nontransparent privacy policy (which Uber has appealed). [47][48]

**Case 7: Clearview AI — €30.5 million (3 September 2024)**

- **Company/Entity:** Clearview AI (U.S. facial recognition company)
- **Country/DPA:** Netherlands / Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP)
- **Date:** 3 September 2024
- **Fine amount:** €30.5 million (largest European Clearview penalty), including penalty payments up to €5.1 million for non-compliance
- **GDPR articles violated:** Processing of biometric (facial) data without consent — scraping facial images from the internet to create a biometric database (implicitly violating Articles 5, 6, 9 GDPR); the Dutch DPA is also investigating whether it can hold Clearview AI directors personally liable
- **Facts:** Clearview AI scraped facial images from the internet without consent to create a biometric database from 30B+ scraped images. Clearview received fines from DPAs in France, Germany, Greece, Italy and the UK accumulating to more than EUR 100 million total across seven fines since 2020. [3][4][6][54]

#### FRANCE — CNIL

**Note on French cases:** Fines under the cookie/ePrivacy rules are issued under Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (transposing the ePrivacy Directive) and/or Article L. 34-5 of the French Postal and Electronic Communications Code (CPCE), NOT under the GDPR itself. The CNIL has asserted that the GDPR "one-stop shop" cooperation mechanism does not apply to these cookie operations since they fall under the ePrivacy Directive. They are included here because of their size and relevance to privacy risk assessment, but flagged as non-GDPR legal bases. [12][22]

**Case 8: GOOGLE (GOOGLE LLC and GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED) — €325 million (1 September 2025)**

- **Company/Entity:** GOOGLE LLC and GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED (jointly responsible — both determine the purposes and means related to the use of cookies and commercial prospecting)
- **Country/DPA:** France / CNIL
- **Date:** 1 September 2025 (Deliberation No. SAN-2025-004)
- **Fine amount:** €325 million total — €200 million against GOOGLE LLC and €125 million against GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED
- **Legal basis:** Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (cookies — ePrivacy, not GDPR) and Article L. 34-5 of the French Postal and Electronic Communications Code (CPCE) (direct electronic prospecting)
- **Facts:** Two breaches: (1) Google displayed advertisements in the form of emails inserted between private emails in the "Promotions" and "Social" tabs of Gmail without user consent — 53 million French users illegally saw these advertisements; the CNIL, citing a CJEU ruling of 25 November 2021, determined these advertisements constituted direct electronic prospecting requiring consent, and although Google made visual changes to ads in April 2023, the CNIL found they still could not be clearly distinguished from real emails; (2) until October 2023, consent for trackers during Google account creation was not free (it was harder to refuse personalised advertising cookies than to accept them) and not informed (users were not told that cookie placement was a condition of accessing Google's services) — the cookie breach affected more than 74 million accounts. The CNIL considered the Google group holds a central position in the online advertising market, Gmail is the second most widely used email service globally, and Google had already been sanctioned by the CNIL twice (in 2020 and 2021) for tracer-related breaches. [12][84][86][83]
- **Orders:** Injunction requiring Google to stop displaying ads between emails without prior consent and to obtain valid consent for advertising trackers within six months; penalty of €100,000 per day of delay if not complied with. [84][83]
- **Origin:** Complaint filed by NOYB on 24 August 2022; CNIL inspections conducted 2022–2023. [84][86]
- **Jurisdiction:** CNIL asserted material jurisdiction (ePrivacy) and territorial jurisdiction because GOOGLE France constitutes an "establishment" on French territory under Article 3 of the French Data Protection Act. [84]

**Case 9: SHEIN (INFINITE STYLES SERVICES CO. LIMITED) — €150 million (1 September 2025)**

- **Company/Entity:** INFINITE STYLES SERVICES CO. LIMITED, the Irish subsidiary of the SHEIN group
- **Country/DPA:** France / CNIL
- **Date:** 1 September 2025 (Deliberation SAN-2025-005)
- **Fine amount:** €150 million
- **Legal basis:** Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (cookies/ePrivacy — not GDPR)
- **Facts:** Following an August 2023 inspection of "shein.com," the CNIL's restricted committee found SHEIN violated Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act by placing advertising cookies on users' devices without obtaining consent — including before any banner interaction and even after users opted out or withdrew consent (85 cookies remained active after users refused; new third-party cookies were placed even after withdrawal requests). Consent banners lacked essential information and clarity, failed to identify third-party processors in second-level information, and used confusing dual consent mechanisms (banner + pop-up). The fine amount considered that the CNIL has repeatedly sanctioned similar breaches since 2020 and the massive scale of processing — an average of 12 million people residing in France visit the site monthly (20 million visits from French users between January–July 2023); the fine represented roughly 2% of SHEIN's European revenue in 2023, calculated based on the parent company's turnover. SHEIN argued the GDPR one-stop-shop mechanism applied and that its French entity was not an establishment, but CNIL dismissed these claims citing CJEU reasoning from Google Spain and Weltimmo. The company made changes to its website during proceedings, so no compliance orders were issued. SHEIN plans to appeal, calling the decision "politically motivated" and "disproportionate." SHEIN also received a separate €40 million fine in July 2025 from DGCCRF (France's consumer protection authority) for misleading pricing practices. [12][22][23][21]

**Case 10: ORANGE — €50 million (14 November 2024)**

- **Company/Entity:** ORANGE (French telecommunications operator)
- **Country/DPA:** France / CNIL
- **Date:** 14 November 2024 (published 10 December 2024)
- **Fine amount:** €50 million
- **Legal basis:** ePrivacy/Article 82 French Data Protection Act — displaying advertisements between emails (breach of Article L. 34-5 CPCE)
- **Facts:** CNIL fined ORANGE for displaying advertisements between users' emails without consent. This is an ePrivacy fine (not GDPR), included for completeness as a major French fine over €10 million in the window. [25][24]

**Case 11: Free Mobile — €27 million (13 January 2026)**

- **Company/Entity:** Free Mobile (French telecom operator)
- **Country/DPA:** France / CNIL
- **Date:** 13 January 2026
- **Fine amount:** €27 million
- **GDPR articles violated:** Article 32 GDPR (inadequate security), Article 34 GDPR (failure to communicate breach to data subjects), and Article 5(1)(e) GDPR (storage limitation)
- **Facts:** Inadequate security measures following an October 2024 data breach affecting ~24 million contracts. [54]

#### ITALY — GARANTE (Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali)

**Case 12: Enel Energia S.p.A. — €79.1 million (8 February 2024)**

- **Company/Entity:** Enel Energia S.p.A. (Italian electricity and gas company)
- **Country/DPA:** Italy / Garante
- **Date:** 8 February 2024 (order issued; decision published 29 February 2024)
- **Fine amount:** €79.1 million (€79,100,000; approximately $86.9 million) — the highest fine ever issued by the Garante at the time
- **GDPR articles violated:** Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR (failure to adequately assess risks and implement measures to prevent employee credential sharing); Articles 5(2), 24(1), and 25 GDPR (violation of accountability and privacy by design principles for failing to rein in illegal activities of other entities procuring contracts); and Article 28 GDPR (executing contracts with other entities that did not reflect actual personal data processing or include data controller obligations)
- **Facts:** The fine stemmed from an earlier investigation conducted by the Italian Guardia di Finanza, which fined four companies €1.8 million and seized their databases, as they were associated with unlawful activities. Enel Energia was found to have acquired 978 contracts from these companies outside its sales network. Subsequent inspections revealed serious security shortcomings in Enel's customer management and service activation systems, which allowed unauthorised agents to conduct various illicit activities, including making nuisance calls and signing contracts that provided no tangible benefit to customers. These violations resulted in the activation of at least 9,300 contracts over time. Mitigating factors included the company's introduction of an authentication system preventing credential sharing. [36][37]
- **Remedial orders:** Communicating the proceedings' outcome to interested parties; providing documentation certifying security measures against credential sharing; implementing system monitoring measures and restricting access from non-attributed IP addresses; ensuring sub-agent contracts comply with Enel Energia's contracts; and communicating with the Garante within 30 days regarding implementation. [37]

**Case 13: Intesa Sanpaolo S.p.A. — €31.8 million (26 March 2026)**

- **Company/Entity:** Intesa Sanpaolo S.p.A. (one of Italy's largest banks)
- **Country/DPA:** Italy / Garante
- **Date:** Decision No. 208, adopted 26 March 2026; published 30 March 2026
- **Fine amount:** €31.8 million (€31,800,000) — one of the largest fines the Garante has ever imposed; the bank may settle for half the amount (€15.9 million) under Article 166(8) of Italy's data protection code
- **GDPR articles violated:** Articles 5(1)(f) (integrity and confidentiality), 5(2) (accountability), 24 (controller responsibility), 32 (security of processing), 33 (breach notification), and 34 (communication of breach to data subjects)
- **Facts:** A single employee at the Agribusiness branch in Barletta, Puglia, accessed the private financial records of 3,573 customers without justification over more than two years, carrying out 6,637 queries across 460 working days between 21 February 2022 and 24 April 2024. Affected individuals included 34 national politicians, 43 prominent figures from entertainment, sport and media, 73 Intesa Sanpaolo employees and senior managers, and approximately 2,450 people from Bari and surrounding areas linked to the employee's personal sphere. The employee was dismissed for cause on 7 August 2024. The Garante found the bank's alert systems failed to detect the activity for over 19 months (first detected 9 October 2023), relying on quantitative thresholds rather than contextual checks; the bank's circular-access model permitted any Agribusiness manager to query the entire customer base without pre-authorisation or role-based limitations. The initial breach notification of 17 July 2024 reported only 9 affected customers (marked "complete"), while the bank internally knew of 3,572 affected individuals from at least 21 May 2024; the bank also improperly downgraded the risk classification against ENISA methodology and initially declined to notify affected customers individually until ordered to do so by the Garante (Provvedimento n. 659, 2 November 2024). Aggravating factors: two-year duration, ~3,500 victims, presence of politically exposed persons, inadequate pre-breach controls, incomplete/delayed notification, and three prior enforcement actions against the bank (Provvedimenti n. 270 of 27 May 2021; n. 272 of 28 July 2022; n. 202 of 26 May 2022). The bank implemented remediation through its "Programma Nemo" (pop-up prompts, pre-authorisation workflow, sensitive clients list expanded from 18 to 623 individuals, data masking, alert-analysis task force). [74][75][88]
- **Quote (Garante):** "The operational model used, which allowed operators to query the entire customer base in full circularity, was not in fact adequately balanced by controls designed to prevent and identify unauthorized access." [75]

**Case 14: Intesa Sanpaolo S.p.A. (Isybank transfer) — €17.6 million (12 March 2026)**

- **Company/Entity:** Intesa Sanpaolo S.p.A. (ISP) — processing related to its wholly-owned digital bank subsidiary Isybank SpA
- **Country/DPA:** Italy / Garante
- **Date:** 12 March 2026
- **Fine amount:** €17.6 million (approximately $20.3 million)
- **GDPR articles violated:** Articles 5 (lawfulness, fairness, transparency — profiling deemed not lawful, fair, nor transparent), 6 (no appropriate legal basis), 12 (transparency/insufficient notifications), plus general unlawful processing of data during corporate reorganization
- **Facts:** Between 2023 and 2024, ISP carried out a corporate reorganization involving the transfer of approximately 2.4 million customer accounts to its fully-owned digital bank, Isybank SpA. ISP selected customers as "primarily digital" based on criteria including age (under 65), digital channel familiarity, absence of investment products, and low financial balances. Customers were not properly informed — the notice was placed in the app's archive section without push notifications or text messages. The transfer forced changes including new IBANs, lack of physical branches, and mandatory mobile app access. The Garante found the profiling was unlawful because customers could not have reasonably anticipated the activity given the circumstances and the information provided. [80][76][79][81]

**Case 15: OpenAI (ChatGPT) — €15 million (December 2024; ANNULLED 18 March 2026)**

- **Company/Entity:** OpenAI (developer of ChatGPT)
- **Country/DPA:** Italy / Garante
- **Date:** Decision adopted 20 December 2024 (announced December 2024/January 2025); **ANNULLED by the Court of Rome (Tribunale Ordinario di Roma, case R.G. 4785/2025) on 18 March 2026**
- **Fine amount:** €15 million (approximately 1.58% of OpenAI's 2023 annual worldwide turnover) — breakdown: €9 million for unlawful data processing, €320,000 for failing to report a data breach, and €5,680,000 for failing to comply with corrective measures imposed in 2023. A separate procedural sanction was included for failure to notify a March 2023 data breach.
- **GDPR articles violated:** Articles 5, 6 (no adequate lawful basis for training-data processing prior to public launch on 30 November 2022), 12–15 (transparency and data subject rights), 33 (failure to notify a data breach)
- **Facts:** The Garante's investigation (begun March 2023 when it temporarily banned ChatGPT in Italy) found that OpenAI trained ChatGPT without an adequate legal basis, failed to meet transparency obligations, lacked sufficient age verification mechanisms, and failed to notify the Garante of a 20 March 2023 data breach that exposed chat histories and payment information of ChatGPT Plus subscribers during a nine-hour window, affecting 440 Italian users. OpenAI was also ordered to conduct a six-month institutional communication campaign across Italian media. OpenAI expressed intent to appeal, calling the fine "disproportionate," noting it was nearly 20 times the revenue the company made in Italy during the relevant period. [56][62][55]
- **Annulment:** On 18 March 2026, the Court of Rome annulled the €15M fine on jurisdictional grounds — OpenAI's February 2024 establishment of OpenAI Ireland Limited made the Irish DPC the lead authority under the one-stop-shop mechanism. The court did not rule on the merits, and the Garante removed the decision from its website. [55][99]

#### GERMANY — BfDI (Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information)

**Case 16: Vodafone GmbH — €45 million (3 June 2025)**

- **Company/Entity:** Vodafone GmbH (Vodafone Germany)
- **Country/DPA:** Germany / Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) — the Federal Commissioner at the time was Prof. Dr. Louisa Specht-Riemenschneider
- **Date:** 3 June 2025
- **Fine amount:** €45 million total (approximately $51 million) — split into €15 million for the Article 28(1) violations and €30 million for the Article 32(1) security flaws. This is the largest GDPR fine issued in Germany to date.
- **GDPR articles violated:** Article 28(1) GDPR (failure to sufficiently review and monitor partner agencies working on Vodafone's behalf in terms of data protection law) — €15 million; Article 32(1) GDPR (security weaknesses in the distribution system, specifically the 'MeinVodafone' portal) — €30 million, with a separate warning issued for this violation
- **Facts:** The BfDI discovered security vulnerabilities in Vodafone's distribution systems and inadequate verification of partner agencies. The first violation stemmed from fraudulent conduct by employees of third-party sales agencies that tricked customers into signing fictitious contracts or unauthorized plan changes; Vodafone had failed to adequately vet and monitor these partner agencies. The second violation involved technical security flaws in Vodafone's "MeinVodafone" online portal and hotline authentication processes, which allowed unauthorized third parties to retrieve customers' eSIM (embedded subscriber identity module) profiles; the regulator also criticized overly broad access granted to partners into customer systems. Vodafone has since improved its systems, revised its partner agency processes, and separated from fraudulent partners. BfDI noted Vodafone cooperated with the agency during proceedings and paid the fines in full to the German treasury; a follow-up audit will be conducted to assess the effectiveness of the corrective measures. - **Quote (Federal Commissioner Prof. Dr. Louisa Specht-Riemenschneider):** "Data protection is often mistakenly seen as an obstacle to IT investments. In fact, the opposite is true... Without IT investments, there is the threat of security incidents and sanctions from data protection regulators. Therefore, my appeal: Investing instead of incurring risks." [20]

- **Country/DPA:** Spain / AEPD

### C. Notable Cases OUTSIDE the Window (August 2023 – August 2026) — Provided for Context

The following cases do NOT qualify for the August 2023–August 2026 window (fines issued before August 2023), but are central to understanding the enforcement landscape:

- **Meta Platforms Ireland Limited — €1.2 billion (12 May 2023, Ireland DPC)** — Insufficient legal basis for EU-US data transfers following the CJEU's invalidation of the Privacy Shield; the largest GDPR fine ever imposed; record has held for over three years; roughly 60% larger than the next-highest figure. Under appeal. [1][3][32]
- **Amazon Europe Core — €746 million (16 July 2021, Luxembourg CNPD)** — Advertising targeting without proper consent, after a complaint by 10,000 people via French group La Quadrature du Net. The Administrative Tribunal rejected Amazon's appeal on 18 March 2025 (upholding the CNPD decision), but the Luxembourg Administrative Court ANNULLED the fine on 12/16 March 2026 on procedural grounds (the CNPD did not properly assess intentionality/negligence or weigh a more lenient measure); the case was remanded to the CNPD for reassessment, and the underlying violation was not overturned. [3][32][52][58]
- **Meta Platforms (Instagram) — €405 million (5 September 2022, Ireland DPC)** — Mishandling children's (ages 13–17) data on Instagram, including public display of contact info. [3]
- **Meta Platforms Ireland — €390 million (4 January 2023, Ireland DPC)** — Changing legal basis from consent to contract for Facebook/Instagram advertising, "forcing" users to accept terms. [3]
- **Meta Platforms Ireland — €265 million (25 November 2022, Ireland DPC)** — 2018 data leak affecting up to 533 million users (Facebook Search, Messenger Contact Importer tools). [3]
- **WhatsApp Ireland — €225 million (2 September 2021, Ireland DPC)** — Transparency violations; fine reassessed after EDPB intervention. [3]
- **Google LLC — €90 million / Google Ireland — €60 million (31 December 2021/6 January 2022, CNIL)** — Cookie refusal issues on YouTube/google.fr; €100,000/day penalty for delay. [3]
- **H&M — €35.25 million (1 October 2020, Hamburg Commissioner)** — Collected sensitive employee data (medical records, diagnoses) via surveillance; network drive briefly accessible to all. [3]
- **TIM (Telecom Italia) — €27.8 million (15 January 2020, Italian Garante)** — Unwanted marketing calls and consent violations. [5]
- **Criteo — €40 million (15 June 2023, CNIL)** — Behavioral retargeting company; trackers without consent, lack of transparency (UPHELD March 2026 by the Conseil d'État). [3][99]
- **Amazon France Logistique — €32 million (27 December 2023, CNIL)** — Intrusive employee monitoring system using scanners to track activity. [3]
- **Austrian Post — €18 million (23 October 2019, Austrian DSB)** — Political affinity processing of 2.2 million data sets; overturned 2 December 2020 by the Federal Administrative Court. [63]

### D. Near-Threshold Cases — Confirming Strict Application of the €10 Million Threshold

To confirm the threshold is being applied strictly, the following notable cases fall at or below €10 million and therefore do NOT qualify:

- **Uber B.V. — €10 million (Netherlands AP, 2023)** — Fine for a nontransparent privacy policy. This is exactly at the €10 million threshold and does NOT exceed it; under appeal. Included as the clearest borderline case. [47][48]
- **Google LLC — €10 million (Spain AEPD, 18 May 2022)** — Fined for Articles 6 and 17 GDPR violations related to sharing data from erasure/withdrawal requests with the Lumen Project (Harvard Berkman Klein Center database). Issued before the window; exactly at threshold. [43][42]
- **TIM — €9.5 million (Italy Garante, 7 August 2026)** — Fined for unlawful telemarketing practices and failing to handle data subject rights. In window but below threshold. [58]
- **OpenAI — €15 million (Italy Garante)** — Above threshold but ANNULLED on 18 March 2026 by the Court of Rome (jurisdictional grounds); no longer a standing fine. [55][62][99]
- **Luka Inc. (Replika chatbot) — €5 million (Italy Garante)** — No legal basis for processing, inadequate privacy policy, insufficient age verification; under appeal. [59]
- **France Travail — €5 million (France CNIL)** — Inadequate security. [12]
- **IQVIA — €5 million (France CNIL, May 2026)** — Health data warehouse safeguard failures. [99]
- **REWE International AG — €8 million (Austria, 2022)** — Below threshold and outside window. [64]
- **Acea Energia — €2 million (Italy Garante)** — Serious violations in processing data of over 1,200 customers; agents activated contracts without consent, sometimes with forged signatures. [59]
- **Unverified figures reported in only single secondary sources (not confirmed by official sources in this research):** "Apple €98.6 million (Italy)" [75]; "Meta (Facebook) €479 million (2025)" and "Google LLC €200 million (2025)" [44]; "Meta €1.3 billion (2023)" [44] — the last appears to be an erroneous rendering of the €1.2 billion Meta fine.

### E. DPA-Specific Enforcement Notes for Member States Without Qualifying Fines

**Luxembourg (CNPD):** No new fines over €10 million were found in the window. The CNPD's only qualifying-scale fine remains the Amazon Europe Core €746 million fine (July 2021), which was upheld by the Administrative Tribunal on 18 March 2025 but annulled by the Administrative Court on 16 March 2026 on procedural grounds (CNPD did not properly assess intentionality/negligence or weigh a more lenient measure; case remanded to CNPD for reassessment; underlying violation not overturned). Other CNPD activity in the window was small-scale (e.g., €175,000 fine on a credit institution for data subject right violations, April 2025; €7,000 fine for incomplete records of processing activities, November 2025). [52][58]

**Austria (DSB):** No qualifying fines were found in the window. The DSB's largest fines predate the window: Austrian Post €18 million (2019, overturned 2020) and €13 million (2021) for unlawful processing of party affinities — the €13 million fine was confirmed by the Supreme Administrative Court in July 2026. The DSB issued only 55 fines out of 4,030 proceedings conducted in 2023 (just 1.36% of all proceedings resulted in a fine); the CJEU (Case C-416/23, judgment 9 January 2025) struck down the DSB's arbitrary policy limiting data subjects to a maximum of two GDPR complaints per month. [62][63][64][65]

**Portugal (CNPD):** No qualifying fines. The CNPD issued just 2 fines totaling €47,000 in all of 2025, despite opening 3,201 processes, conducting 244 inspections (double the 122 in 2024), opening 2,037 investigations, and instating 88 administrative offence proceedings. The CNPD attributed the low sanction count to insufficient human resources (36 workers at year-end 2025), a shortage of staff with specialised knowledge in administrative offence proceedings, procedural complexity, paper-based processes, and structural deficiencies in the legal framework. Data breach notifications climbed 42% to 472 in 2025. [61]

**Belgium (GBA/APD):** No qualifying fines were found. The Belgian DPA has ~90 staff; a reference was found to a €100,000 fine against a telecoms operator for a 14-month data access delay. [61]

**Germany (Land DPAs):** No fines over €10 million from the German Land (state) DPAs were found in the window; the only qualifying German fine is the federal BfDI's €45 million against Vodafone (June 2025). The HmbBfDI (Hamburg) imposed fines totaling €775,000 in October 2025, a €492,000 fine on a financial company (October 2025), and a €900,000 fine on a credit collection agency for GDPR deletion violations (November 2024). Germany's most significant pre-window fines include H&M €35.25 million (Hamburg, 2020) and 1&1 Ionos €9.55 million (2019). Germany has no central supervisory authority — each of the sixteen federal states (Länder) has its own authority, with the BfDI overseeing federal public bodies, social security institutions, and telecom/postal providers. [66][67][50]

**Netherlands (AP) — other activity:** The AP has pursued substantial public-sector enforcement including the Belastingdienst (€3.7M fine, December 2021, for unlawful nationality-data processing in the childcare-benefits scandal — Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(c), 6, and 9 GDPR), Booking.com (€475K, 2021, late breach notification), and OLVG hospital (€440K, 2021, inadequate access controls). 2024–2026 priorities include algorithmic decision-making in the public sector, platform-worker data, credit-scoring and AI-driven assessment in financial services, and connected vehicles. [45]

**France (CNIL) — other qualifying-adjacent activity:** The CNIL's cookie action plan (initiated 2019) has produced a stream of sanctions under Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act: Google €150M + Facebook Ireland €60M (2022, dark-pattern banners), Microsoft Ireland €60M (22 December 2022, advertising cookies on bing.com without consent), and the ORANGE €50M (2024) and Google €325M / SHEIN €150M (2025) fines detailed above. [54][25][12]

1. Meta Platforms Ireland — €1.2 billion (Ireland DPC, May 2023) — unlawful EU-US data transfers
2. Amazon Europe Core — €746 million (Luxembourg CNPD, July 2021) — ad targeting without valid consent (annulled on procedural grounds March 2026, remanded)
3. TikTok — €530 million (Ireland DPC, May 2025) — unlawful EU-China data transfers
4. Meta (Instagram) — €405 million (Ireland DPC, September 2022) — mishandling of children's data
5. Meta (Facebook + Instagram) — €390 million (Ireland DPC, January 2023) — invalid legal basis for behavioural ads
6. TikTok — €345 million (Ireland DPC, September 2023) — children's data processing failures
7. Google — €325 million (French CNIL, September 2025) — Gmail inbox ads + invalid signup consent (ePrivacy)
8. LinkedIn Ireland — €310 million (Ireland DPC, October 2024) — invalid legal basis for behavioural ads
9. Uber — €290 million (Dutch AP, August 2024) — unlawful EU-US data transfers

[14][32][1]

The top 10 fines total roughly EUR 4.79 billion, representing close to 80% of the CMS Enforcement Tracker Report's EUR 6.11 billion cumulative total. Ireland's DPC issued 7 of the top 10 fines (worth ~EUR 3.75 billion combined). Nine of the top 10 fines stand as issued; the exception is Amazon's €746 million fine, annulled March 2026 on procedural grounds. [32]

### G. Key Enforcement Trends Relevant to the Period (2023–2026)

- **Coordinated enforcement:** The EDPB has coordinated enforcement through its Coordinated Enforcement Framework (CEF) since 2023. In 2026, the CEF is focusing on transparency and information obligations per the EDPB Strategy 2024-2027. The EDPB's 2024-2027 Strategy (adopted April 2024) is structured around four pillars: (1) advancing harmonisation and promoting compliance, (2) reinforcing a common enforcement culture, (3) addressing technological challenges, and (4) enhancing the EDPB's global role. No Article 65 binding decisions were issued in 2024 (first year since 2020). [1][10]
- **Cross-border transfers remain the highest-risk category:** Three of the five largest fines in 2024–2025 (TikTok, LinkedIn, Uber) involved data transfers outside the EU; TikTok's €530M decision shows transfer enforcement is now a settled enforcement lane. [4][99]
- **Payment/collection statistics:** Of Ireland's €4.04 billion in fines, only ~€20 million (0.5%) has actually been collected, as most major fines are under appeal; however, companies almost always implement corrective orders despite appealing headline numbers (e.g., Meta localised EU data infrastructure, LinkedIn rewrote consent flows within three months). [14]
- **2026 priorities:** EDPB Transparency Action (CEF 2026, launched 19 March 2026, testing Articles 12–14 compliance); EU AI Act high-risk provisions go live 2 August 2026 (penalties up to €35M or 7% of turnover — higher than GDPR's €20M/4%); Digital Omnibus (largest GDPR reform since 2018, proposed 19 November 2025); cross-border transfer enforcement continues (Schrems II reasoning intact). [99]
- **Personal liability:** The Dutch DPA is investigating whether it can hold Clearview AI directors personally liable following the €30.5 million fine — signaling regulators' recognition of personal accountability as a compliance driver. [6]

### Translation Notes

Where official DPA sources are only available in their original language, the following notes apply: The Italian Garante's decisions (Enel Energia, Intesa Sanpaolo, Isybank, OpenAI) are published in Italian on the Garante website; the details in this report were sourced from English-language legal analyses (Orsingher, VitalLaw, ICLG, DataGuidance, PPC.land, DSN Group, Lewis Silkin).
